Brazil · Retail

Brazilians keep spending on their dogs and cats even when money is tight. The country’s newly merged pet-store champion is turning that loyalty into steady profit.

Here is the Petz Cobasi Q2 2026 profit you should know about: Brazil’s largest pet-care retailer, formed by merging the Petz and Cobasi chains, grew its adjusted profit to R$70.3 million (about US$13.6 million) from April to June — solid growth in a quarter when prices barely moved.

What the Petz Cobasi Q2 2026 profit shows

Two profit figures are worth separating. Adjusted profit — the cleaner measure of the day-to-day business — rose 8.4% to R$70.3 million (about US$13.6 million).

Reported profit looks flashier at R$100.4 million (about US$19.5 million), up 43.5%. But that number is flattered by R$52.9 million (about US$10.3 million) of one-time tax credits from past years, so the adjusted figure is the fairer read of how the stores are actually doing.

Sales backed up the profit. Net revenue climbed 7.9% to R$1.7 billion (about US$329 million), and adjusted operating earnings rose 11% to R$186.7 million (about US$36.2 million).

Why this counts as real growth

Here is the part management is proudest of. Sales at stores open at least a year — the retail industry’s honesty test — grew 7.1%.

That growth came with almost no help from higher price tags. Pet-product prices were roughly flat, so the company sold more stuff to more owners rather than simply charging more. In retail, that is the healthy kind of growth.

Online is doing the heavy lifting. Digital sales rose to R$855.6 million (about US$166 million), now 40.6% of the business — a share most brick-and-mortar chains would envy.

The merger is starting to pay

Petz and Cobasi were fierce rivals before they joined forces. Combining them created scale — more stores, more buying power, one bigger online operation.

The balance sheet shows the benefit. The company ended the quarter with a net cash position of R$286.1 million (about US$55 million), up more than 80% from the previous quarter, while trimming spending on new stores. In plain terms, it is generating cash rather than burning it.

Why this matters if you live or invest in Brazil

If you own a pet in Brazil, Petz and Cobasi are probably where you buy the kibble, book the grooming and see the in-store vet. A stronger, better-run chain tends to mean wider stock, steadier prices and more services near you.

If you invest, the pet aisle is a quiet read on the Brazilian consumer. When families keep spending on animals through a high-rate, tight-budget stretch, it signals a certain resilience in everyday demand — and shows how a well-handled merger can turn two rivals into one cash-generating leader.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Petz Cobasi earn in Q2 2026? Adjusted net profit was R$70.3 million (about US$13.6 million), up 8.4% from a year earlier. Reported profit was R$100.4 million (about US$19.5 million), boosted by one-time tax credits. Why are there two different profit numbers? The reported figure includes R$52.9 million (about US$10.3 million) of one-off tax credits from prior years. The adjusted figure strips those out to show the underlying performance of the stores. What is Petz Cobasi? It is Brazil’s largest pet-care retailer, created by merging the Petz and Cobasi chains. It trades on the B3 exchange under the ticker AUAU3. How fast is the business growing? Net revenue rose 7.9% to R$1.7 billion (about US$329 million), and same-store sales grew 7.1% — almost entirely on higher volumes rather than price increases.

Brazil’s biggest homebuilder keeps growing while high interest rates cool the housing market around it. The trick is who it builds for.

What the Cyrela Q2 2026 profit shows

The bottom line grew 16% over the year, to R$452 million (about US$88 million). Revenue climbed faster still, up 18% to R$2.48 billion (about US$481 million), as buildings launched in earlier quarters were handed over and booked as sales.

Just as telling, the company held its margins. Gross margin — what is left after building costs — rose to 34.4%. In a business where inflation eats into every slab of concrete, keeping that number up is the hard part.

Why Cyrela grows while others slow

Brazil’s benchmark interest rate sits high, and expensive mortgages usually chill home sales. Yet Cyrela leans on wealthier buyers who lean less on financing, which softens the blow.

It also runs its own mortgage arm, CashMe, which lends to buyers and earns fees along the way. That unit chipped in R$111 million (about US$21 million) this quarter, up 54% from a year earlier — a cushion most rivals simply do not have.

The balance sheet got healthier, too. Adjusted net debt fell 12.5% from March to R$1.9 billion (about US$370 million), and the company generated R$272 million (about US$53 million) in cash. Less debt means more room to launch when the cycle turns.

The one soft spot

Not everything pointed up. The potential value of new launches for the first half slipped 11% from a year earlier, to R$5.6 billion (about US$1.09 billion).

That is worth watching. Today’s launches become tomorrow’s revenue, so a lighter launch pipeline can mean slower growth a year or two out. For now, a large backlog and R$12.8 billion (about US$2.48 billion) of finished inventory to sell keep the machine fed.

Why this matters if you live or invest in Brazil

If you are shopping for an apartment in São Paulo or Rio, Cyrela is often the name on the hoarding — and a builder this steady is more likely to deliver on time and stay solvent through a downturn. That is real peace of mind when you are handing over a deposit years before the keys.

If you invest, Cyrela is the sector’s bellwether. When the biggest, best-run homebuilder still grows profit through a high-rate stretch, it tells you Brazilian real estate is bending, not breaking — a useful read for anyone weighing property or property stocks here.

How is Cyrela growing while interest rates are high? It focuses on higher-income buyers who rely less on mortgages, and it runs its own home-finance arm, CashMe, which added R$111 million (about US$21 million) to results, up 54% over the year. Is there any weak point in the results? Yes. The potential value of new launches in the first half fell 11% from a year earlier to R$5.6 billion (about US$1.09 billion), which could slow revenue growth later if it does not recover. What happened to Cyrela’s debt? Adjusted net debt fell 12.5% from March to R$1.9 billion (about US$370 million), and the company generated R$272 million (about US$53 million) of cash in the quarter.

The farm-loan problem, explained simply

Banco do Brasil is the country’s farm lender. When crop prices sag and interest rates bite, farmers fall behind, and the bank feels it first.

That is exactly what happened. Loans overdue by more than 90 days climbed to 5.61% of the book, up sharply from 3.96% a year ago. Credit costs — the money set aside for loans that may go bad — rose 16% over the year, to R$18.5 billion (about US$3.6 billion).

The CEO argued the bank is now steering toward a safer mix of borrowers. A new federal measure, known as MP 1.376, is meant to give struggling farmers more room to renegotiate, which should slow fresh defaults.

What you get as a shareholder

The board declared R$584.9 million (about US$113 million) in interest-on-equity, a tax-friendly cousin of dividends common in Brazil. That works out to about R$0.102 (roughly US$0.02) a share, payable in September.

It adds to R$340.7 million (about US$66 million) already advanced in June. For a stock long prized by income investors, keeping the payouts flowing is the point.

Why this matters if you live or invest in Brazil

Banco do Brasil is woven into daily life here — salaries, pensions, farm credit and small-business loans all run through it. When its farm book wobbles, the tremor reaches grain towns and the wider economy, not just the share price.

So watch the delinquency line more than the profit line. If overdue loans keep climbing, the recovery is a head-fake; if they level off as the bank claims, this quarter marks the turn. Either way, the health of Brazil’s biggest agricultural lender is a fair proxy for the health of its farm economy — the engine behind the exports that move the real.

The half-year picture

Add the two quarters together and the bank has earned R$7.3 billion (about US$1.4 billion) so far in 2026. That is a long way from its full-year target of R$18 billion to R$22 billion (about US$3.5 billion to US$4.3 billion).

To hit even the low end, the second half has to be much stronger than the first. This quarter was a step; it was not the finish line.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Banco do Brasil earn in Q2 2026? Adjusted net profit was R$3.9 billion (about US$760 million), up 3.3% from a year earlier and 13.9% from the previous quarter. It beat the roughly R$3.6 billion (about US$700 million) analysts expected. Why has the bank been struggling? Its large farm-loan book soured as crop prices and high interest rates squeezed producers. Overdue loans rose to 5.61% of the portfolio, and credit-loss provisions climbed 16% over the year to R$18.5 billion (about US$3.6 billion). What dividend or payout was announced? The bank declared R$584.9 million (about US$113 million) in interest-on-equity, about R$0.102 (roughly US$0.02) per share, to be paid in September. Is Banco do Brasil on track for its 2026 target? Not yet. First-half profit of R$7.3 billion (about US$1.4 billion) is well short of the pace needed to reach the R$18 billion to R$22 billion (about US$3.5 billion to US$4.3 billion) full-year goal.

Sources: Banco do Brasil second-quarter 2026 earnings release; InfoMoney; Money Times; Seu Dinheiro. Dollar values converted at about R$5.16 to US$1.

World.title: Petroperú Names Luis Suárez Carlo Its New General Manager
World.content:
Peru · Business

Key Facts — Who Petroperú’s board named engineer Luis Alberto Suárez Carlo as acting general manager

— When effective 15 August 2026, through Acuerdo de Directorio N.° 087-2026-PP

— Replaces Gustavo Adolfo Villa Mora, general manager since 21 February 2026

— Churn the third general manager in 2026, at a firm with 11 board presidents since July 2021

— Why it matters the company is deep in debt and was cut to Caa1 by Moody’s in January 2026

A third boss in eight months inherits the same broken balance sheet, and the churn tells its own story.

Petroperú has a new general manager, and the appointment says as much about the company’s turmoil as it does about leadership. On 15 August 2026, the board of Peru’s state oil company named engineer Luis Alberto Suárez Carlo acting general manager.

Who Is Petroperú’s New General Manager?

Suárez Carlo is an engineer with more than 40 years of experience across the energy sector. His background covers hydrocarbons, industrial maintenance, asset management, corporate planning, and project management.

The board fixed his start date at 15 August 2026, moving fast after a broad shake-up. It approved the decision through a formal resolution, Acuerdo de Directorio N.

° 087-2026-PP. Officially, he takes the job in an acting capacity rather than as a permanent appointment.

In Spanish, his title is gerente general encargado, meaning acting general manager.

How Suárez Carlo Reached the Top Job

He replaces Gustavo Adolfo Villa Mora, who had run the company as general manager since 21 February 2026. Because the board itself was overhauled, the leadership reshuffle followed almost at once.

Before Villa Mora, Rita Lorena López Saavedra briefly led the company. She had served as acting general manager from 8 January 2026.

So Suárez Carlo is already the third person to hold the role this year. Meanwhile, the deep crisis he inherits has shown no sign of easing.

Why Petroperú Keeps Changing Bosses

The company has churned through leaders for years, not just months. Since July 2021, Petroperú has cycled through 11 board presidents alone.

Because each new team meets the same mountain of debt, few of them stay long. As a result, strategy keeps resetting before any plan can take hold.

Political pressure and shifting government priorities add to the instability. Therefore constant turnover has become the company’s normal state, rather than the exception.

The Talara Refinery Debt Explained Simply

Much of the trouble traces back to a single, giant project on Peru’s northern coast. Petroperú rebuilt its Talara refinery to modernize how the country makes fuel.

The overhaul was meant to be a national showcase for cleaner production. However, it is widely reported to have cost around US$6 billion by the end.

That figure is several times the original budget of roughly US$1.3 billion. Because the firm borrowed heavily to finish it, the debt still crushes its balance sheet.

How Much Does Petroperú Owe?

The numbers are staggering for a single state company. Moody’s put Petroperú’s adjusted debt at around US$6.3 billion as of 30 September 2025.

Some later reports placed the total burden even higher than that. Still, every estimate points to a firm living far beyond its own means.

Roughly US$2 billion of the load sits in international bonds. As a result, looming repayment schedules hang over the company’s daily operations.

The Losses Behind the Crisis

Petroperú has been losing money heavily for several years running. It reported a net loss of about US$468 million in 2025.

That came after an even deeper loss of roughly US$774 million in 2024. Although the gap narrowed, the company remains firmly in the red.

Unpaid bills to suppliers have also stacked up over time. By late 2025, Petroperú owed its suppliers more than 2,569 million soles.

Ratings Downgrades Pile Up

Credit-rating agencies have steadily lost patience with the company. On 28 January 2026, Moody’s cut Petroperú to Caa1 from B3.

It also attached a negative outlook to that new rating. In practice, such a grade signals a very real risk of default.

Fitch went a step further and simply walked away. On 9 January 2026, it withdrew its ratings, citing insufficient information.

How the Government Keeps Petroperú Afloat

The Peruvian state has stepped in to rescue the company again and again. Because Petroperú is treated as strategic, the government keeps writing large checks.

In 2026, a decree cleared fresh support worth up to US$2 billion. It channels that aid through a special-purpose vehicle set up for the rescue.

Earlier bailouts had already added capital injections and state guarantees. Even so, the company keeps coming back to the treasury for still more help.

The Push to Bring in Private Money

Peru also wants outside cash, but without calling it privatization outright. In 2026, a decree let Petroperú transfer up to 144 million soles to ProInversión.

That agency arranges public-private deals on the state’s behalf. Because the word privatization is politically toxic, officials carefully avoid using it.

Still, the underlying goal is not hard to read. The state clearly wants private partners to help shoulder the enormous burden.

What the New General Manager Must Fix

Suárez Carlo inherits a daunting list of problems from day one. First, he must steady the shaky finances around the Talara refinery.

He also has to keep fuel flowing reliably to Peru’s domestic market. Meanwhile, he must reassure lenders who are already deeply nervous.

His acting title, though, gives him limited room to manoeuvre. Therefore quick and visible results are likely to matter most.

What It Means for Peru

Petroperú is far more than just another company to the country. It supplies fuel nationwide and carries a strong measure of national pride.

Because taxpayers keep funding the rescues, the stakes are very public. For example, every bailout ultimately competes with money for schools and roads.

The new general manager’s core test is simple to describe. In short, he must somehow make Petroperú stand on its own two feet.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Petroperú’s new general manager?

Engineer Luis Alberto Suárez Carlo. Petroperú’s board named him acting general manager effective 15 August 2026.

Who did Suárez Carlo replace?

He replaced Gustavo Adolfo Villa Mora, general manager since 21 February 2026. Rita López Saavedra held the role before Villa Mora.

Why is Petroperú in financial trouble?

The costly Talara refinery overhaul left it deeply indebted. Losses and repeated bailouts have followed for years.

Is Petroperú at risk of default?

Moody’s cut its rating to Caa1 in January 2026 with a negative outlook. That signals a real default risk.

Sources: Petroperú corporate communiqué (Acuerdo de Directorio N.° 087-2026-PP), Gestión, El Comercio, RPP, Moody’s, Fitch and Peru’s Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) decrees.

World.title: Peru Court Archives Criminal-Association Charge Against Nadine Heredia
World.content:
Peru · Politics

Key Facts — The ruling on 3 July 2026 a Peruvian court archived the criminal-association charge against Nadine Heredia, Ollanta Humala and four former ministers.

— The case the charge came from the Gasoducto Sur Peruano investigation, over a southern Peru gas pipeline concession awarded in 2014.

— Not closed the archiving covered only the criminal-association charge; an aggravated-collusion charge in the same case remains pending.

— Separate matter this is distinct from the Odebrecht money-laundering case, in which Heredia was convicted in April 2025 and sentenced to 15 years.

— Where she is Heredia was granted asylum in Brazil in April 2025 and remains there.

For Peru’s former first lady, this is one thread pulling loose from a knot of cases. The pipeline charge is not the money-laundering conviction that drove her to seek asylum in Brazil.

Peru Court Archives Criminal-Association Charge Against Nadine Heredia. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Nadine Heredia has had a criminal-association charge archived by a Peruvian court. The ruling in the Gasoducto Sur Peruano pipeline case also covered her husband, former president Ollanta Humala.

What the Court Decided

Peru’s judiciary has archived a criminal-association charge in a long-running corruption case, one of several tied to the Humala years. The decision was issued on 3 July 2026, according to Peruvian media reports.

It also covered her husband, former president Ollanta Humala, and four former government ministers named in the same file. The charge stemmed from the Gasoducto Sur Peruano case, over a planned gas pipeline in Peru’s south.

The court upheld a defense motion arguing the charge could not proceed. Prosecutors have signaled they will seek to overturn the ruling.

The Charge That Was Archived

The archived charge was criminal association, known in Peru as asociacion ilicita. It accused the group of forming an unlawful organization to commit crimes.

The court accepted a motion of inadmissibility of action from the defense. That motion argued the facts did not amount to the offense as charged.

Judge Leodan Cristobal Ayala ruled the motion founded, ending that charge. The ruling applies only to the criminal-association count, not the whole case.

One Charge Ends, Another Remains

The archiving did not close the entire Gasoducto Sur Peruano case. A separate charge of aggravated collusion remains pending against the defendants.

That count is due to be examined at a later stage of the proceedings. So the case file stays open, even as the association charge falls away.

Reports say prosecutors and other parties plan to appeal the archiving. A higher court could still revive the charge if the appeal succeeds.

The Gasoducto Sur Peruano Case

The Gasoducto Sur Peruano was a major plan to pipe natural gas across southern Peru to homes and factories. The concession was awarded in 2014 to a consortium of companies.

That consortium included Brazil’s Odebrecht and Spain’s Enagas, among other partners. Prosecutors alleged that officials improperly acted to favor the winning group during the process.

The project later collapsed after Odebrecht could not secure the financing it needed. The company lost the concession in 2017, amid the wider corruption scandal engulfing it across Latin America.

Why Nadine Heredia Was Investigated

Nadine Heredia served as Peru’s first lady during Humala’s 2011 to 2016 term in office. She was also a leading figure in his Partido Nacionalista, or Nationalist Party.

Investigators examined her role in decisions linked to the pipeline concession and its award. Prosecutors had sought lengthy prison terms for the couple in the case.

In 2025, they requested 35 years for Humala and Heredia. Heredia has denied wrongdoing throughout the various cases against her.

A Separate Case From the Odebrecht Conviction

The pipeline case is distinct from the case that made Heredia best known outside Peru. That other case concerned money laundering tied to payments from Odebrecht.

It centered on illicit contributions to Humala’s 2006 and 2011 presidential campaigns. In April 2025, a court convicted both Humala and Heredia in that case.

Each was sentenced to 15 years in prison. The pipeline archiving does not undo or affect that separate conviction.

Asylum in Brazil

After the April 2025 conviction, Heredia left Peru for Brazil. Brazil granted her asylum, and she travelled to its capital, Brasilia.

She has remained in Brazil since then. Her lawyers later asked Brazil’s Supreme Court to block any extradition.

Humala, by contrast, was jailed in Peru after the ruling. The couple’s legal paths then diverged sharply.

Humala’s Conviction Overturned

Peru’s Constitutional Court annulled Humala’s money-laundering conviction on 31 July 2026. It found the alleged conduct did not fit the offense at the time.

Humala was released from prison shortly after the decision. In August 2026, an appeals chamber extended that reasoning to Heredia.

It annulled her 15-year sentence and lifted the order for her arrest. That relief concerned the money-laundering case, not the pipeline matter.

What Archiving Means Here

In Peru, archiving a charge halts prosecution on that specific count. For Heredia, it means no trial proceeds on the criminal-association charge.

It is not a finding that she is innocent of all accusations. Nor does it settle the collusion charge still on file.

An appeal could reopen the archived count at a higher court. For now, that one charge is set aside.

A Project That Was Never Built

The pipeline was meant to carry natural gas to homes and industry across southern Peru. Backers presented it as a lasting boost for the region’s economy.

Instead, construction stalled and the concession was withdrawn. Years of legal disputes followed, both inside Peru and beyond its borders.

Spain’s Enagas pursued international arbitration against the Peruvian state over the failed deal. The affair left a costly, half-finished project behind in the desert.

Why It Matters

The rulings mark a notable shift in years of corruption cases against the couple. Both had faced some of Peru’s most prominent graft investigations.

Their cases grew out of the region-wide Odebrecht bribery scandal that toppled leaders across Latin America. The pipeline decision shows how those cases can narrow charge by charge.

For readers abroad, it signals continued turbulence in Peru’s justice system. Since further appeals loom, the story is unlikely to end here.

Frequently Asked Questions

What charge against Nadine Heredia was archived?

A Peruvian court archived the criminal-association charge against Nadine Heredia in the Gasoducto Sur Peruano case. The ruling was issued on 3 July 2026.

Is the whole case against her closed?

No. Only the criminal-association charge was archived, while a separate aggravated-collusion charge remains pending.

Is this the same as her Odebrecht money-laundering case?

No, it is a separate proceeding. Heredia was convicted in the Odebrecht money-laundering case in April 2025 and sentenced to 15 years.

Where is Nadine Heredia now?

She was granted asylum in Brazil in April 2025 and remains there. Her lawyers have asked Brazil’s Supreme Court to block extradition.

World.title: Egypt Opens Its Market to Peruvian Blueberries
World.content:
Peru · Business

Key Facts — What Egypt has opened its market to fresh Peruvian blueberries, reported on 13 August 2026

— Who Peru’s plant-health agency SENASA negotiated the phytosanitary access

— Reach fresh blueberry from Peru now enters 76 international markets

— Scale 2025 exports hit US$2.457 billion, up 8.2% on the year

— Why it matters the US still buys more than half the crop, so Peru is spreading its risk

The 76th market is less about Egyptian appetite than about Peru’s scramble to find buyers beyond a tariff-heavy United States.

Egypt Opens Its Market to Peruvian Blueberries. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Peruvian blueberries can now enter Egypt for the first time. Peru’s plant-health agency, SENASA, negotiated the new phytosanitary access.

As a result, fresh blueberry from Peru now reaches 76 international markets.

What Egypt Just Agreed

Egypt has agreed to let fresh Peruvian blueberries enter its market. The opening was reported on 13 August 2026 after more than a year of technical talks.

Because the deal clears the plant-health hurdles that block most fruit trade, shipments can now begin. As a result, Egypt becomes a fresh commercial outlet in North Africa.

For Peru, the move adds one more destination to an already long list. Meanwhile, it signals how hard the sector is working to spread its risk across many buyers.

Why Peruvian Blueberries Needed a New Door

Peruvian blueberries depend heavily on a handful of rich, high-paying markets. However, that concentration has quietly become a strategic weakness.

The United States still buys more than half of Peru’s crop each season. Because new tariffs have squeezed that trade, producers now want credible alternatives.

Therefore each new market matters far more than its size alone suggests. In short, Egypt is less about volume today and more about long-term balance.

How SENASA Opened the Market

SENASA is Peru’s National Agrarian Health Service, the body that guards crops and exports. It negotiates the plant-health rules that let fresh fruit cross borders safely.

For the Egypt deal, SENASA led the detailed phytosanitary talks with Cairo. As a result, Peru met the pest and inspection conditions Egyptian authorities set for entry.

The agency has been unusually busy opening doors on many fronts. Meanwhile, it keeps adding agricultural market accesses across several countries through 2026.

Peru, the World’s Top Blueberry Exporter

Peru is the world’s largest exporter of fresh blueberries by a comfortable margin. It has held that lead since around the 2019 and 2020 campaign.

Because the desert-coast climate suits near year-round growing, output has climbed remarkably fast. As a result, Peru now ships more fresh blueberries than any other country.

MIDAGRI, the agriculture ministry, calls this a consolidated global leadership in the fruit. Still, officials know the position must be actively defended each and every season.

The Numbers Behind the 2025 Record

In 2025, Peru’s blueberry exports reached a record US$2.457 billion, according to official figures. That total was up 8.2% from the year before.

Market trackers put the calendar-year season even higher, near US$2,563 million. They also counted about 412,239 tonnes of fresh fruit shipped abroad.

In 2024, exports had already comfortably passed US$2 billion for the sector. Therefore the trend line points firmly and consistently upward.

Where the Berries Come From

Most of the crop grows on Peru’s dry, sunny northern coast. The La Libertad region leads the way by a wide and stubborn margin.

In the last campaign, La Libertad alone accounted for 49% of total export volume. Because the land and weather suit the fruit so well, the region dominates.

Other coastal valleys such as Lambayeque and Ica are expanding too. Meanwhile, growers keep planting newer, sweeter and firmer varieties for pickier buyers abroad.

The United States Problem

The United States remains Peru’s single biggest customer by a wide distance. It takes more than half of every season’s blueberry exports.

However, US tariffs have recently made that heavy reliance look risky. In 2025, Peru began steering more of its fruit toward China instead.

Because one large market can turn hostile almost overnight, spreading sales is simply prudent. As a result, Egypt fits neatly into a clear defensive strategy.

Why Counter-Season Timing Helps

Peru harvests its blueberries precisely when the Northern Hemisphere cannot. That timing lets it fill supermarket shelves during a global supply gap.

Because few rivals ship fresh fruit in those key weeks, prices tend to hold up. Therefore new markets can absorb the extra fruit without crushing returns.

Egypt, like many other buyers, wants quality berries when its own season is over. In short, Peru’s growing calendar is one of its strongest commercial cards.

What Egypt Adds to the Map

Egypt is an emerging blueberry market straddling the Middle East and North Africa. It gives Peru a valuable foothold in a fast-growing consumer region.

With Egypt now included, Peru reaches 76 international markets in total. Because that map keeps widening, no single buyer holds all the pricing power.

The volumes shipped to Egypt will most likely start small at first. Even so, a new door often opens onto a wider neighborhood of nearby buyers.

What It Means for Growers

ProArandanos speaks for the country’s blueberry producers and exporters as a group. Its members together represent about 80% of national blueberry production.

For these growers, extra markets mean steadier and more balanced demand over time. As a result, they can plan new plantings with a little more confidence.

Still, shipping logistics and market promotion remain very real challenges. Therefore the industry treats each opening as a starting point, not a finish line.

What Happens Next

The first commercial shipments to Egypt should follow in the coming harvest season. Because the paperwork is now cleared, exporters can start planning routes and volumes.

Peru is also actively chasing several other new markets during 2026. Meanwhile, it keeps defending its established lead in the United States, Europe and China.

For now, Egypt is a modest but genuinely telling win for the sector. In short, it shows a world-leading exporter refusing to stand still.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which country just opened its market to Peruvian blueberries?

Egypt opened its market to fresh Peruvian blueberries, with the access reported on 13 August 2026. Peru’s plant-health agency, SENASA, negotiated the phytosanitary terms.

How many markets can Peru’s blueberries now reach?

With Egypt added, fresh blueberry from Peru now reaches 76 international markets. The sector keeps opening new destinations to spread its risk.

Is Peru really the world’s top blueberry exporter?

Yes. Peru is the world’s largest exporter of fresh blueberries and has led since around 2019, with 2025 exports of US$2.457 billion.

Why does Peru want markets beyond the United States?

The United States still buys more than half of Peru’s crop, but tariffs have made that reliance risky. New markets like Egypt help diversify demand.

Sources: Exitos Noticias, Gestion, Peru’s MIDAGRI and SENASA, Andina, Reuters, IFPRI, ProArandanos, Fresh Fruit Portal and Freshplaza.

World.title: Peru Names César Luna-Victoria as SUNAT’s New Chief
World.content:
Peru · Business

Key Facts — Who César Luna-Victoria León, named national superintendent of SUNAT

— When start date of 6 August 2026, via Supreme Resolution 027-2026-EF

— Replaces Javier Franco Castillo, SUNAT chief since October 2025

— Background PUCP tax lawyer and former Fishing minister under Alberto Fujimori

— Context appointed days into President Keiko Fujimori’s new government

A veteran tax lawyer who once served in Alberto Fujimori’s cabinet returns to government under his daughter. Taking over an agency that keeps changing hands.

Peru Names César Luna-Victoria as SUNAT’s New Chief. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

SUNAT, Peru’s national tax and customs authority, has a new chief. César Luna-Victoria León became its national superintendent on 6 August 2026, days into President Keiko Fujimori’s government.

What Peru’s Government Decided at SUNAT

Peru’s executive named César Luna-Victoria León to lead SUNAT. The appointment was made through Supreme Resolution 027-2026-EF.

That decree was published in the official gazette on 5 August 2026. Meanwhile, SUNAT’s own staff records list his start date as 6 August 2026.

The same package sent Clara Urteaga to the Tribunal Fiscal, the tax court. So the government refreshed two key posts in Peru’s tax system at once.

Who Is César Luna-Victoria

Luna-Victoria is a lawyer trained at the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú. Moreover, he holds a master’s in law from the same university and teaches there.

Because his field is tax and corporate law, he is a familiar face in Peru’s tax circles. He has chaired the Peruvian branch of the International Fiscal Association.

Most recently, he worked as a partner at the law firm Rebaza Alcázar. Therefore he arrives at SUNAT with decades in private tax practice.

He is also linked to the Instituto Peruano de Derecho Tributario, a respected professional body. In short, his standing in Peru’s tax community is well established.

The Chief He Replaces at SUNAT

Luna-Victoria takes over from Javier Franco Castillo. Franco had run SUNAT since October 2025, when he was named by an earlier decree.

His resignation was accepted in the same resolution that installed the new chief. As a result, the handover was formalized in a single act.

The government thanked Franco for his services in the notice. Still, his exit adds to a long list of recent departures at the agency.

What SUNAT Actually Does

SUNAT is Peru’s national tax and customs authority. In short, it collects the central government’s taxes and controls the country’s borders and trade.

It also promotes compliance and pushes businesses toward formal registration. Because it funds most public spending, its performance shapes the national budget.

For that reason, the person who runs SUNAT holds real economic weight. So each change at the top draws close attention from business and investors.

The agency operates as a specialized arm of the Ministry of Economy and Finance. Meanwhile, it manages one of the largest data operations across the Peruvian state.

Why the Timing Around SUNAT Matters

The appointment landed just days after Keiko Fujimori was sworn in on 28 July 2026. Therefore it counts among the first moves of her new government.

Fujimori won the 2026 election after a turbulent stretch of Peruvian politics. As a result, her team has moved quickly to place its own people in key offices.

Naming a tax chief early signals where revenue policy sits on the agenda. In fact, few state jobs matter more to a government’s spending plans.

A Familiar Name From the Fujimori Years

Luna-Victoria is not new to government. He served as Minister of Fishing under President Alberto Fujimori between 1999 and 2000.

That history gives the appointment a notable symmetry. After all, he now returns to public office under Alberto Fujimori’s daughter, Keiko.

Supporters point to his long experience in tax and public management. Critics, by contrast, may read the choice through a political lens.

A Revolving Door at Peru’s Tax Agency

SUNAT has changed leaders at a striking pace. During Dina Boluarte’s presidency, the agency saw four chiefs named in roughly 18 months.

Franco’s own arrival in October 2025 was described as the sixth designation in under three years. So Luna-Victoria inherits a post marked by instability.

Frequent turnover makes long-term reform harder to sustain. However, a well-known technician could bring some stability if he stays in place.

The Numbers SUNAT Must Hit in 2026

SUNAT has projected collecting more than S/ 182 billion in tax revenue in 2026. That figure anchors the government’s spending plans for the year.

Collection has been rising into the handover. For example, Peru’s July tax take jumped 20.4% to about US$4.77 billion, giving the new chief a favorable backdrop.

Meeting the annual target now falls to Luna-Victoria’s team. Because targets are public, any shortfall would quickly become political.

A rising tax take gives the incoming chief early room to maneuver. However, sustaining that pace through the full year is the harder task.

Informality, the Structural Tax Problem

Peru’s biggest tax challenge is informality. Because a large share of the economy operates off the books, the tax base stays narrow.

SUNAT’s stated plan leans on technology and simpler processes to widen that base. Its motto has been to educate before it punishes.

Formalizing small firms and traders is slow, grinding work. Even so, it remains the surest path to lifting collection over time.

Informal activity spans street vendors, small workshops and unregistered firms. Because each formalized taxpayer adds durably to the base, the effort compounds slowly.

What to Watch Next at SUNAT

The first test is whether Luna-Victoria stays long enough to act. After years of churn, continuity itself would be a change at SUNAT.

Watch, too, for his stance on audits, digital platforms and cross-border income. These have been growing fronts for the agency.

Above all, watch the collection figures against the 2026 target. In short, the numbers will judge this appointment more than any speech.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the new head of SUNAT?

César Luna-Victoria León is the new national superintendent of SUNAT. He took office on 6 August 2026 under Supreme Resolution 027-2026-EF.

What is SUNAT?

SUNAT is Peru’s national tax and customs authority. It collects central-government taxes, controls customs and promotes formal business registration.

Who did Luna-Victoria replace?

He replaced Javier Franco Castillo, who had led SUNAT since October 2025. Franco’s resignation was accepted in the same decree that named the new chief.

Why does this appointment matter?

SUNAT funds most public spending, so its leadership shapes Peru’s budget. The move is also an early signal from President Keiko Fujimori’s new government.

Sources: El Peruano (Supreme Resolution 027-2026-EF), Peru’s Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF), the Andina state news agency, Infobae, SUNAT’s official records, El Comercio, La República, Reuters and Associated Press.

World.title: Panama Canal Traffic Rises as Cargo Tonnage Climbs 7%
World.content:
Panama · Business

Key Facts — What rose cargo volumes climbed faster than the number of ships, so bigger, fuller vessels are driving the recovery.

— Transits 10,726 ships crossed in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, up about 5.2% on a year earlier.

— Cargo the canal moved 389.96 million tons in that period, up about 7.2%, roughly 390 million tons.

— Draft depth was restored toward the normal 50 feet after the drought, then trimmed to about 48 feet for the dry season.

— Money the canal earned about US$5.7 billion in fiscal 2025 and sent roughly US$2.965 billion to Panama’s treasury.

The rebound is real, but it is uneven: more cargo is moving by weight than by ship count. And the water that makes it possible is never guaranteed.

A vessel makes its way through the Panama Canal. Cargo tonnage rose about 7.2% in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, as allowed draft was restored toward its normal 50-foot maximum after the 2023-2024 drought. Photo: Paul Harrison via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Panama Canal traffic is climbing back after two hard drought years, with cargo volumes rising faster than the number of ships. Official figures show tonnage up about 7% so far in fiscal 2026.

Even as the waterway juggles the water that keeps it open.

What Is Happening at the Panama Canal

The Panama Canal is busier again. After the 2023-2024 drought forced sharp cutbacks, ships are returning to the world’s most important shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific.

The recovery is measured in two ways, and they do not match. The number of ship crossings rose modestly, while the weight of cargo moving through rose faster.

That gap tells a clear story. Because bigger, fuller vessels are transiting, each crossing now carries more, so tonnage is outpacing the simple ship count.

What Actually Rose, in Plain Numbers

In the first nine months of fiscal 2026, running from October to June, 10,726 ships transited. That is up about 5.2% from the same stretch a year earlier.

Cargo told a stronger story. The canal moved 389.96 million tons, close to 390 million, an increase of about 7.2% over the prior period.

So both measures are up, but by different amounts. In short, the canal is not just handling more ships; it is handling heavier, more valuable loads.

How the Drought Hit the Panama Canal

The Panama Canal does not run on the sea. It works by lifting ships with fresh water from Gatun Lake, so rainfall directly sets how much it can do.

During the 2023-2024 drought, that lake dropped to worrying lows. As a result, the authority slashed both the number of daily slots and how deep ships could sit in the water.

At the worst point, allowed depth fell to around 44 feet. Because that forced ships to carry less, many operators paid more, waited longer or rerouted entirely.

How Deep Ships Can Now Sit

As the rains returned, the lake refilled and the squeeze eased. The authority steadily raised the maximum allowed draft back toward its normal ceiling of 50 feet.

Draft is simply how deep a loaded ship sits below the waterline. Therefore a deeper allowed draft lets a vessel carry more cargo through the locks safely.

Even so, water management never stops. For the 2026 dry season the canal has trimmed the limit again in small steps.

Toward about 48 feet, far gentler than the drought cuts.

Why Draft Depth Matters So Much

Draft may sound technical, yet it decides real money. The deeper a ship can safely sit, the more containers, grain or fuel it can load per trip.

When draft is cut, a vessel must carry less to float higher. As a result, its cost per ton rises, and some cargo shifts to other routes.

So the return of deeper draft is a quiet win for global trade. It means fuller ships, lower costs per ton, and fewer painful detours.

More Ships Crossing Each Day

Daily traffic has also recovered. By the end of June, the canal was averaging about 35 crossings a day, close to its normal working rhythm.

In full health, the waterway handles roughly 36 to 38 ships a day across its two sets of locks. The authority raised its daily slot count in steps as the lake refilled.

For shippers, more slots mean shorter waits and steadier schedules. That predictability matters as much as price when planning a long ocean voyage.

Why the Panama Canal Matters for Global Trade

About one in twenty tons of world seaborne trade passes through this narrow strip of Panama. It is a lifeline for goods moving between Asia and the US East Coast.

Container ships, grain carriers and gas tankers all rely on it. Because the alternative is a long haul around South America or Africa, delays here ripple worldwide.

When the canal falters, freight bills climb and store shelves feel it later. So its recovery is felt far beyond Panama, from Shanghai warehouses to Atlantic ports.

The Money Behind the Recovery

The rebound shows up on the balance sheet too. In fiscal 2025 the canal earned about US$5.7 billion, its highest annual revenue on record.

That money matters far beyond the locks. The canal handed roughly US$2.965 billion to Panama’s national treasury, helping fund the country’s public budget.

Higher tonnage and firmer tolls both feed that total. So a fuller canal is, quite literally, a richer Panama.

Why Water Is Still the Wild Card

For all the good news, the core risk has not gone away. The canal still depends on rainfall, and dry years can return without much warning.

That is why the authority keeps trimming draft during the 2026 dry season, even after a strong recovery. It would rather ease limits early than run the lake too low.

Longer term, Panama is investing in new water supply to shield the canal. Until that lands, every dry season remains a test the waterway must pass.

What to Watch Next

Watch the rains and the lake level first, since they set everything else. A wet season refills Gatun Lake and lets deeper drafts and more slots return.

Then watch tonnage rather than just ship counts. Because heavier loads drive revenue, that figure shows the real health of the trade route.

Finally, watch how far the dry-season trims go. If they stay mild, as in 2026, the recovery of the Panama Canal should hold through the year.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Panama Canal traffic rise?

In the first nine months of fiscal 2026. Ship transits rose about 5.2% and cargo tonnage rose about 7.2% versus a year earlier.

How deep can ships go through the canal now?

Depth was restored toward the normal maximum of 50 feet after the drought. For the 2026 dry season it has been trimmed in small steps toward about 48 feet.

Why does the Panama Canal depend on rain?

The locks lift ships using fresh water from Gatun Lake, which is filled by rainfall. When the lake drops, the canal must cut draft and daily crossings.

How much money does the canal make?

The canal earned about US$5.7 billion in fiscal 2025, a record, and sent roughly US$2.965 billion to Panama’s national treasury.

Sources: Autoridad del Canal de Panama (ACP) fiscal 2026 midyear traffic figures (10,726 transits, +5.2%; 389.96 million PC/UMS tons, +7.2%, October 2025-June 2026) and 2026 draft advisories; Reuters and ACP on fiscal 2025 revenue of about US$5.7 billion and the roughly US$2.965 billion transfer to Panama’s treasury. Verified by the Rio Times via two independent AI-assisted fact-check passes.

World.title: Burrell Boom man remanded on grievous harm charge after allegedly beating his common-law wife badly
World.content:
Burrell Boom man remanded on grievous harm charge after allegedly beating his common-law wife badly

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 30-year-old Burrell Boom man has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being charged with grievous harm following an alleged domestic assault on his common-law wife.

Howard Reyes, a labourer of Wesley Avenue, Black Berry Ridge, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, where he was charged in connection with an incident that allegedly occurred on August 10.

Police say Reyes’ common-law wife, a 28-year-old woman reported that she was inside a bedroom with her daughter at around 8:25 p.m. when Reyes entered in an aggressive manner and began questioning the child.

The woman alleged that as she and her daughter attempted to leave the room, Reyes blocked her exit before punching her in the jaw. She further alleged that he grabbed her by the throat and choked her, restricting her breathing, while threatening to kill her if she attempted to open the door.

The woman told police she eventually broke free and ran into the street, but Reyes allegedly followed her and punched her multiple times in the face and head. A passing motorcyclist reportedly intervened and restrained Reyes, allowing the woman to escape.

She later complained of pain to her jaw, head, neck and shoulder, as well as dizziness, and requested court action.

In court, prosecutor Cpl. Lumberton Ayala strongly objected to bail, citing the seriousness of the charge, concerns over domestic violence and the fact that a medical form detailing the extent of the woman’s injuries had not yet been received.

The Magistrate upheld the prosecution’s objection and denied Reyes bail. He was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until October 14, 2026.

World.title: 20-year-old Christian Ramos remanded over $700 armed robbery at Belama shop
World.content:
20-year-old Christian Ramos remanded over $700 armed robbery at Belama shop

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 20-year-old Belize City labourer has been remanded to prison after being charged in connection with an armed robbery at Guan Fa Shop in Belama Phase 2.

Christian Denver Ramos, of Wagner’s Lane, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with one count of robbery. He was denied bail due to the nature of the offence and remanded to the Belize Central Prison until October 19, 2026.

Police allege that at around 5:40 p.m. on Saturday, July 25, a 30-year-old shop owner was attending to a customer at the business on Albert Hoy Street when a man dressed entirely in black, wearing a black bucket hat and dark shades, entered and waited in line.

According to the police report, after the customer left, the man allegedly jumped over the counter, produced a black object resembling a firearm and demanded money.

Fearing for her life, Ma reportedly placed approximately $700 in cash from the day’s sales into a black backpack provided by the robber. The assailant then fled the shop in the direction of Chetumal Boulevard.

Northside Criminal Investigation Branch personnel later reviewed surveillance footage from inside the store. Police say the footage was displayed on a larger screen and an officer identified the alleged gunman as Ramos.

The matter remains before the court.

World.title: Cabinet pulls plug on BTL-SMART deal five days before Cabinet vote during planned protests
World.content:
Cabinet pulls plug on BTL-SMART deal five days before Cabinet vote during planned protests

By Breaking Belize News Staff: In a major and unexpectedly early turn in the weeks-long controversy over Belize Telemedia Limited’s proposed $80 million acquisition of SMART/Speednet, Cabinet announced Thursday that it does not support the transaction — five days before the date Government had previously set to deliberate and announce its position.

Cabinet said the acquisition had become a matter of “national concern” and noted that the Government of Belize, the Social Security Board and the Belizean people are the majority owners of BTL. After reviewing the available information and considering concerns raised by social partners, the media and the public, Cabinet said it had reached an informed position against the acquisition.

The timing of the announcement is particularly significant. As recently as Tuesday, August 11, Government officially stated that Cabinet would hear stakeholder presentations and then deliberate at its Tuesday, August 18 meeting before announcing its position. Instead, Cabinet moved on Thursday, August 13 — effectively pulling political support from the controversial deal almost a week ahead of schedule.

The decision also comes just ahead of escalating industrial and political action. The National Trade Union Congress of Belize had called on Belizeans to wear black on Friday, August 14, in protest against the acquisition, followed by a demonstration outside the Sir Edney Cain Building in Belmopan on August 18, timed to coincide with the Cabinet meeting. The Belize National Teachers’ Union had also confirmed that its members would participate in Tuesday’s rally, while the United Democratic Party had separately called supporters to protest the proposed deal that same day.

The four Social Partners — the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry, National Trade Union Congress of Belize, National Evangelical Association of Belize and Belize Network of NGOs — immediately welcomed Cabinet’s decision, saying it demonstrated the importance of “public scrutiny, collective action and meaningful engagement.”

However, they cautioned that Cabinet’s opposition does not by itself legally dispose of the proposed transaction. They said the Public Utilities Commission still has regulatory responsibilities under law and called for those processes to proceed independently and transparently, particularly regarding competition and compliance with Belize’s telecommunications framework.

The Social Partners are also demanding that BTL’s Board provide outstanding financial and valuation information and answer questions about how an $80 million transaction of such national significance was introduced, assessed and advanced in the first place.

BTL’s Board had voted on August 4 to move forward with the proposed acquisition, subject to continuing due diligence and other approvals. Since then, opposition had widened considerably, extending beyond the Social Partners to BTL’s own union, former employees, opposition parties and other sections of the public.

While further regulatory and corporate steps may technically remain, Cabinet’s declaration represents the most significant setback yet for the proposed BTL-SMART acquisition. What had been expected to culminate in a showdown at Tuesday’s Cabinet meeting — against the backdrop of planned protests in Belmopan — instead reached a dramatic political turning point five days early.

The Social Partners, while celebrating the development, say their work is not finished and that they will continue pressing for answers and accountability surrounding the transaction.

World.title: Cabinet rejects the Speednet acquisition
World.content:
Cabinet rejects the Speednet acquisition

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The deal that dominated national dialogue for weeks is dead. Cabinet announced on Thursday, August 13, 2026, that it does not support the proposed acquisition of SMART/Speednet by Belize Telemedia Limited, effectively ending the takeover, and the decision landed one day before the unions’ planned wear-black protest and five days ahead of the demonstration set for Cabinet’s own doorstep.

“After careful deliberation, it is Cabinet’s informed position that it does not support the proposed acquisition,” the official statement reads.

Cabinet framed the decision around ownership and obligation. The Government of Belize, the Belize Social Security Board, and the people of Belize are the majority owners of BTL, the statement notes, giving Cabinet “a duty and obligation to responsibly review all available data and relevant information” and to consider the views of its members, social partners including the media, and the public. The proposed acquisition, Cabinet acknowledged, “is a matter of national concern.”

The statement closed with thanks to “all those who engaged in good faith and constructive dialogue” and an assurance that Cabinet “remains determined to always listen respectfully to their voices and act in the national interest.”

The road to the rejection ran through weeks of mounting pressure. The National Trade Union Congress of Belize rejected the consolidation and announced two days of action, a national wear-black protest set for Friday, August 14, and a demonstration outside the Sir Edney Cain Building on Tuesday, August 18, deliberately timed to the Cabinet meeting where the final decision was expected. The teachers’ union council had agreed to join pending membership consultation. Public scrutiny had also been sharpened by the confirmed fact that the Briceño family retains its 22 percent stake in Speednet, though no wrongdoing was ever established in connection with the holding.

In the end, the decision arrived before a single placard was raised.

What becomes of Speednet now, and whether the unions stand down their planned actions, are the immediate questions. Breaking Belize News will follow the responses as they come.

World.title: CNN crowns Belize’s Great Blue Hole among Earth’s strangest wonders
World.content:
CNN crowns Belize’s Great Blue Hole among Earth’s strangest wonders

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): When CNN went hunting for the planet’s most unusual landscapes, its editors gathered 24 of them, ancient twisted forests, erupting volcanoes, a pink lake, rock towers carved by millennia of wind. And to represent the whole strange collection, the image they placed at the very top was Belize’s own Great Blue Hole.

The newly updated CNN Travel feature by journalist Joe Minihane spotlights the giant marine sinkhole off Belize’s coast as the lead entry among wonders spanning six continents, keeping company with Northern Ireland’s Giant’s Causeway, the Fairy Chimneys of Cappadocia in Turkey, Hawaii’s Kilauea volcano, the Chocolate Hills of the Philippines, and Australia’s bubblegum-pink Lake Hillier.

The numbers behind the fame remain staggering. At 300 meters wide, some 984 feet, and around 125 meters deep, about 410 feet, the Great Blue Hole is the biggest sinkhole in the world. Part of the Belize Barrier Reef System, it was formed as sea levels rose thousands of years ago, flooding its deep cave network and leaving the near-perfect navy circle that now stares up at every passing plane.

The feature nods to the man who introduced it to the world, renowned marine explorer Jacques Cousteau, whose expeditions made the Blue Hole a bucket-list pilgrimage for divers everywhere. And it notes the wonder is still giving up secrets: recent submarine trips have produced new 3D sonar maps revealing never-before-seen mineral formations near the hole’s bottom.

The CNN spotlight lands in a season when the world cannot seem to get enough of Belize. The country welcomed a record 1.4 million visitors, new nonstop routes from five more American cities begin this winter, and international media have spent the year discovering what Belizeans have always known, that this small country holds an outsized share of the planet’s magic.

Twenty-four wonders made CNN’s list. One of them is ours, and it made the cover.

World.title: International News: Trump says US controls Strait of Hormuz, but experts say reality is more complicated
World.content:
International News: Trump says US controls Strait of Hormuz, but experts say reality is more complicated

By Zoila Palma: Nearly six months into the US-Iran war, the strategic Strait of Hormuz remains at the center of a growing dispute over control of one of the world’s most important oil shipping routes.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that the United States has “total control” of the waterway, while Iran says it will not fully reopen the strait until Washington meets its conditions.

The ongoing disruption has sharply reduced maritime traffic and contributed to rapidly declining global oil stockpiles, CNN reports.

Despite Trump’s claims, experts say the strait is not fully controlled by either the United States or Iran. Only a fraction of the vessels that normally pass through the waterway are currently making the journey, with 14 ships crossing on Tuesday compared with roughly 120 per day before the war.

The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports, while merchant shipping companies remain concerned about attacks, mines and other threats that could endanger their vessels.

Experts say both countries retain significant leverage, but each faces limitations.

Iran has the advantage of geography because it borders the strait and can threaten shipping through mines, small boats and surveillance, while the United States has substantial military and economic power, including sanctions on Iranian oil and frozen Iranian assets.

However, US military forces in the region are stretched, and analysts say Washington’s ability to maintain pressure could become increasingly difficult if the conflict continues for an extended period.

Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo set for Saturday at National Agriculture Showgrounds
