World.title: CCJ image at stake
World.content:
DESCRIBING the current discord within the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) as deeply troubling, former Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding has recommended an urgent probe and speedy resolution, warning that delay could irreparably tarnish the institution’s reputation.

“Disagreements are normal and healthy in a panel of judges who may offer different interpretations of the facts and points of law. That is why a panel exists. One expects that such disagreements are expressed respectfully, unlike another jurisdiction where they are sometimes punctuated with personal abuse,” Golding said in a column sent to the Jamaica Observer on Thursday.

Golding weighed in on the turmoil which became public at the start of the week when the Sunday Express newspaper in Trinidad and Tobago published a series of e-mail involving CCJ President Justice Winston Anderson and colleague judges.

In the e-mail exchanges, a majority of the judges accused Justice Anderson of governing the regional court in an “authoritarian” and “dictatorial” manner.

The complaints, as reported by the Sunday Express, range from accusations of Justice Anderson unilaterally imposing a judicial dress code to allegations of “panel fixing” and attempts to influence the outcome of cases.

The newspaper reported that the internal correspondence showed that five of the CCJ’s six sitting judges challenged Justice Anderson’s leadership, with one warning of “creeping patterns of anti-democratic approaches” and another calling for an urgent meeting to address “a level of disenchantment that may well be approaching a crisis point if left unaddressed”.

In one of the e-mail correspondence, presiding CCJ judge Justice Chile Eboe-Osuji told his colleagues: “I have never seen before the level of dictatorship in the administration of a judiciary that I have witnessed at the CCJ in recent months. There is a serious concern, not that the new trend would include an attempt to use a body like the RJLSC (Regional Judicial and Legal Services Commission) as an unwitting instrument of dictatorship. The RJLSC performs important functions within the mandate properly conferred upon it in the CCJ agreement. It would be wrong of any CCJ president — who is also the chairperson of the RJLSC — to try and misuse that important body in that way.”

Explaining his use of the world “dictatorship”, Justice Eboe-Osuji said it was “because Winston himself told us early on in a judges’ meeting — soon after his assumption of office of president (July 2025) — that he did not see himself as ‘running a democracy’ and that he would run the court in any way that he deems fit”.

In his column on Thursday, Golding said, “What is alarming is that the disclosure involves accusations of autocratic behaviour by the president and his manipulation of panel selection aimed at influencing judicial outcomes.”

Added Golding: “More alarming is the fact that these accusations are made not by one or two judges, but all the other five. It is hard to believe that they could have all taken that position without due consideration.”

He said that without appropriate resolution, “this episode will tarnish the reputation of the court, perhaps irreparably. Even if it is resolved, it will have suffered a serious setback in its hopes of gaining acceptance as the final court for all Caricom member states”.

Golding said that responsibility for fixing this débâcle lies firstly with the RJLSC and called on the commission to “move swiftly to investigate the reports and assess the facts”.

Pointing out that removal of the president, if that is deemed necessary, can only be done on the recommendation of the RJLSC and with a 75 per cent majority vote of the Caricom heads of government, Golding said: “God forbid that that becomes another imbroglio similar to that regarding the reappointment of the Caricom secretary general.”

The former head of Government also said he was most surprised by the focus of some legal luminaries as well as The Gleaner newspaper editorial on the circumstances by which the information became public — through a leak of confidential e-mail.

“Without that leak we would most likely never have become aware of this dysfunction and the court could descend into unexplained chaos. The leak may have breached ethical rules for which remedies exist, but are we not entitled to know? Is that not what whistle-blowing is all about?”

Read the full text of Golding’s column on Page 12 of today’s Jamaica Observer.

World.title: Mystery development irks Kingston 8 residents
World.content:
A drone shot of the location where the proposed development is to be built on Broadway Close in Kingston 8. The grassy area to the left in the photo is where the multi-family development is expected to be erected.

RESIDENTS of sections of Manor Park in upper St Andrew are up in arms over what they regard as secrecy surrounding a planned development in the area.

The residents say they have tried, without success, to get information on the development slated for 2 Broadway Close, Kingston 8.

According to the residents, unofficial sources have indicated that a five-storey building is planned for the area but efforts to get the authorities to either conform or deny this have so far failed.

In a letter, which they shared with the Jamaica Observer, the residents claim that people who live on Broadway Close, Broadway Road, Harrow Drive, and Waterworks Road are worried about the proposed development.

“The developers posted a notice of intention to build at 2 Broadway Close on July 6, 2026. Within 48 hours, the Broadway Mews Association formally requested the plans. The developer responded that the plans were in progress and would be provided once completed. Since then, there has been no further correspondence,” the residents said in the letter.

“Despite multiple requests, the community has been left in the dark. The developers were aware of the community’s interest within 48 hours of the notice going up. Yet, they have chosen to ignore all subsequent requests for information,” the residents added.

They claimed that when the community submitted a formal request for plans under the Access to Information Act, they were told it could take up to 60 days to receive them.

“The Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) informed residents they had only 35 days to file an objection. This creates an impossible situation where residents are being asked to object to a developer whose plans they have not seen, may not receive before the deadline, and which the developer has refused to share,” the residents claimed in the letter.

Repeated attempts by the Observer sine last week to get a comment from the KSAMC have so far been unsuccessful.

The residents pointed to comments made recently by Dr Patricia Green, a registered architect and former head of the Caribbean School of Architecture at the University of Technology, Jamaica.

“Dr Green has highlighted this exact issue. When citizens contact the KSAMC, they are denied access to the development proposals. Without the drawings, how are we to object?” the residents charged in the letter.

They pointed out that under Section 18 of the Building Act 2018, once a notice of intention is posted people can object to the development even without seeing the plan.

“The law does not require you to have seen the plans. Under Section 7 of the Kingston and St Andrew Building (Notices and Objections) Regulations, the KSAMC must take into consideration all objections which may be made before making a decision.

“The Supreme Court has confirmed this right. In Wint v KSAMC [2022], the court held that residents have a legitimate expectation that their objections will be considered, and that failing to do so is a breach of natural justice. You can object based on what you already know — the restrictive covenants, the cul-de-sac, the gully course, the road problems, the inadequate notice. You do not need to wait for the plans. But the developer’s refusal to share them speaks volumes,” the residents said.

They told the Observer that they have also contacted the National Environment and Planning Agency for answers and the agency confirmed the area is zoned for residential purposes and that the half-acre lot is permitted for 25 habitable rooms.

But the greatest fear of the residents is that the developers could be allowed to go as high as five storeys. The tallest building in the area is currently two storeys.

“Legal experts have noted that developments on plots smaller than half an acre are a key warning sign of a bad development. Under the 2017 Provisional Development Order, multi-family developments are only permitted if the land exceeds 0.5 acres, unless compelling reasons are shown. The 2 Broadway Close site is exactly 0.5 acres, a fact that should have triggered additional scrutiny,” the residents claimed.

They further argued that with Broadway Close being a dead-end street, a five-storey, multi-family development will generate significant vehicular traffic that must enter and exit through a single point.

“The KSAMC is required to assess access and traffic flow as mandatory planning criteria. Emergency vehicles — fire trucks and ambulances — require adequate turning radius and access. The Jamaica Fire Brigade is a mandatory referral agency that must approve such developments. Residents are demanding that a traffic impact assessment be conducted and made public before any permit is granted,” argued the residents.

They added: “The certificate of title for 2 Broadway Close contains restrictive covenants that are binding on the land and its owners. No building other than that used for the purposes of a private dwelling house with appropriate outbuildings appurtenant thereto shall be erected on the said land or any part thereof. Restrictive covenants are contractual obligations imposed on purchasers by the original vendor, intended to limit the purchaser’s use of the land for the benefit of all land owners in the subdivision.

“They run with the land, meaning successive owners are bound by the same covenants. A covenant that precludes subdivision would limit the owner’s ability to legally construct an apartment complex.”

World.title: It’s an event scene!
World.content:
DJ Zacky (left) and his MC, Flex Supreme.

In recent years, a new generation of event promoters have emerged on the party scene, adding to night-time entertainment offerings.

But even though some of these promoters have been hosting successful events, there are some challenges that come with the territory.

Kyle Chin said securing dates and identifying an appropriate venue remain challenges.

“I got into event promotion as a youth, just by helping my older cousins promote their event in St Elizabeth about ten years ago. Officially, I have been doing my own events for the past three years,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

Known for Socaverse and B43, he added: “The cost of getting the permits to actually keep the event is also of concern as well as the high taxes that promoters face.”

Chin’s events target the 18 and older demographic. Socaverse is a soca/EDM music event and is held twice annually while B43 is held monthly.

“What sets us apart and what we are bringing to nightlife is the experience. We cater to individuals with the different genres that are played and the type of setup we use,” said Chin who works as a corporate broker.

Popular teenage disc jock DJ Zacky, who hosts the bi-weekly SATDEHZ, which is held at Oceano, says he would like to see more support from corporate Jamaica for promoters.

“…I’d like to see more support for young promoters through sponsorship opportunities, easier access to venues, and stronger partnerships… I believe that there can be more collaboration within the entertainment industry. Better regulation and security support would also help events operate more efficiently,” said DJ Zacky.

“[P]eople don’t always take you seriously until you’ve built a name for yourself. But as our events continue to prove themselves, and our attendance keeps growing, you can see people starting to view us differently and put more respect on our name. That journey has motivated us to keep raising the standard with every event,” DJ Zacky shared.

He revealed that his passion for entertainment and creating memorable experiences were what drew him to event promotion.

“I saw an opportunity to bring people together through well-organised events… Event promotion allows me to combine creativity, business, and networking into something I genuinely enjoy,” DJ Zacky, who has been involved in event promotion for over a year, said.

SATDEHZ, a drink-inclusive event that offers patrons a premium nightlife experience, targets the 18-35 age demographic.

“We cater to university students, young professionals, and anyone looking for a quality entertainment experience. We’re focused on creating a premium yet accessible experience. Through strong branding, creative marketing, quality DJs, and engaging social media campaigns, we want every event to feel unique and memorable,” the business Administration student at the University of Technology, Jamaica shared.

On his way to The University of the West Indies (UWI), Mona, where he will be pursuing a degree in management studies, DJ Kovert, a popular disc jock, is the co-promoter for FWD, a bi-weekly event held at Dulce Lounge in Barbican.

Dominic Bartley is his business partner in this series which wrapped up on July 29.

“I decided to get involved in event promotion because I’ve always had a passion for music and creating experiences where people can take a break from their everyday lives and truly enjoy themselves. As a DJ, I realised there was an opportunity to create events that reflected the energy and atmosphere that I wanted to experience in Kingston, especially for my generation,” says DJ Kovert.

“While I’ve been promoting public events for a little over a month, my experience actually started before that. During my time at Ardenne High School, I helped curate and organise several school socials and events, which gave me valuable hands-on experience in planning, marketing, and understanding what it takes to have a successful party. Those experiences built the foundation and confidence that encouraged me to step into the entertainment industry and begin promoting my own events.”

FWD primarily caters to the 18-30 demographic.

“Each FWD staging is designed to have its own identity, with different themes, concepts, and elements that keep the experience fresh for patrons… As a younger promoter, we also bring a fresh perspective on how events are marketed and how audiences connect with entertainment,” DJ Kovert shared.

He spoke with Splash on the improvements he would like to see in the sector.

“I would like to have more support and opportunities created for promoters, especially young promoters who are trying to build sustainable events. This includes stronger partnerships with sponsors, more collaboration between promoters, venues, artists, and other stakeholders, as well as more accessible resources to help events grow. The entertainment industry is a major part of Jamaica’s culture and economy, and creating a better support system for promoters would allow more creativity, innovation, and quality experiences to thrive.”

Lemar Smith, who is from Trelawny, is the new kid on the block as far as event promotion is concerned. His weekly Saturday night event is called Sapphire Saturdays and is held at Vuebar in Liguanea.

“I started promoting Sapphire Saturdays in May this year… Although I’m still relatively new to the industry, the experience has taught me a lot,” said The UWI student, adding, “Whether you’re a university student, young professional, entrepreneur, or simply someone looking for a great Saturday night out, Sapphire is designed to bring people together in a fun and vibrant environment… We also place a strong emphasis on high-quality photography, videography, and social media content so people don’t just attend the event they become part of the Sapphire experience. It’s about creating a lifestyle and a community, not just another party.”

Smith would like the entertainment sector to become more diverse.

“I’d like to see more promoters take chances on concepts that feature house music, Afro House, Amapiano, R&B, throwback nights, and other unique experiences. Giving people more variety not only benefits patrons but also creates opportunities for DJs, artistes, promoters, and creatives to showcase different styles. I believe diversity will help Jamaica continue growing as one of the Caribbean’s top entertainment destinations.”

World.title: Douglas hard on self despite three-medal haul
World.content:
Shanoya Douglas celebrates one of her two silver medals after winning the women’s 100m and 200m at the 21st World Athletics Under-20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, on Sunday. Douglas won three medals — gold in the women’s 4x100m and silver in the 100m and 200m — to take her total to five after winning gold and bronze two years ago in Lima, Peru. (Photo: Paul A Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Shanoya Douglas may have left the 21st staging of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships with three medals, but the highly rated sprinter believes she could have performed much better at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon, on Sunday.

Douglas, who entered the five-day championships as the World Under-20 leader in both the 100m in 10.98 seconds and 200m in 22.11, won gold as the anchor on Jamaica’s women’s 4x100m relay team and silver in both individual events.

The Jamaican women’s relay team won in a World Under-20 leading 42.89 seconds, the fourth-fastest time, ever, but Douglas said she was disappointed with her overall performance.

“I have mixed feelings in this championship. Normally, I always get gold individual medals but I got two silver this time,” she told the Jamaica Observer. “The gold in the relay means a lot for me because I wanted to continue our streak and it means a lot to be able to continue that streak, especially knowing that I’d broken it in the 100 metres.”

The result means Douglas has won five medals at the last two World Under-20 Championships, including another relay gold and a bronze in the 200m at the 2024 championships in Lima, Peru.

The haul puts her among Jamaica’s most successful performers at the championships, a distinction that appears to surprise her.

“You know I never realised that I had that many,” she said, while admitting that she expected more from herself in Eugene.

Douglas won the 100m and 200m doubles at both the Intersecondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA)GraceKennedy Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships and the Carifta Games this year. She is also tied for third all-time with American sprint legend Allyson Felix in the World U-20 200m rankings and is 10th all-time in the 100m, also at the World U-20 level.

Her two silver medals in Eugene, both behind American Mia Maxwell, have given her a different perspective.

“This championship has taught me a lot, knowing that it’s not always things gonna go your way, and I was saying that sometimes it’s good to control the controllable, but this time I was having difficulties controlling the controllables,” she said. “And I’ve been hard on myself this championship, and I was like, ‘Let’s come out here, put everything aside, and deliver for my country.’”

Jamaican women had won the previous four World Under-20 200m titles through Briana Williams in Tampere, Finland, in 2018; Tina Clayton in Nairobi, Kenya, in 2021; Alana Reid in Cali, Colombia, in 2022; and Reid again in Lima, Peru, in 2024.

Douglas was particularly hard on herself when asked to grade her performance on a scale of one to 10.

“A five,” was her instant response.

She said members of the Jamaican coaching staff told her she was being too hard on herself, but she explained that the standards she sets for herself are what drive her.

“When you have a standard for yourself and not been able to reach that standard that you set for yourself, it’s like a different mental struggle,” she said. “And it’s just I’ve not met my standard and the standard that I had for myself going to this championship.”

Despite her disappointment, Douglas believes the experience will benefit her as she begins her professional career. She will forgo another year in high school after signing a professional contract the week before travelling to Eugene.

“I’m still having hope. I have great faith in myself that in the future I will be able to perform way better going into the other championships, and this has taught me a lot,” she said.

Douglas also pointed to the championship format, which required the sprinters to run the first two rounds of their events on the opening day before returning for the final the following day.

“This has set me up for what is to come in the professional setting where facing difficulties will be a reality every day. So yes, it has taught me a lot,” she said.

She said she was able to rebound from what she considered below-par performances in Eugene and resisted the temptation to dwell too long on the moments when she performed well.

Douglas said the experience had reinforced an important lesson about the difference between expectations and performance on the day.

“This championship probably taught me that because you have the fastest time on paper, it’s who show up on the day. And it’s not that I didn’t show up on the day, it’s just that circumstances didn’t make me perform how I wanted to. And regardless of that or not, I’m trying to see the positive in it because I was able to leave the championship with a medal, three medals,” she said.

World.title: 2026 MG ZS: Luxury on a budget
World.content:
The 2026 MG ZS in luxury trim offers premium features at a very competitive price point. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Sports car brands that make SUVs have it tough with the car-buying public. The fact that MG, one of the most-storied British auto makers and a cornerstone of the quintessential English roadster, has given in to the SUV-pocalypse must have the faithful spitting their afternoon tea across their crumpet-laden tables. Still, history has proven them more wrong than right, as these companies with sporting intention are able to infuse the mundane family hauler with their original ethos. MG has done just that with the ZS.

EXTERIOR

SUVs tend to stay on the conservative side of things, whereas the ZS has adopted a previous trend held by the premium brands: Russian Dolling, the act of simply scaling corporate design up or down a specific model. Yes, there is the usual Grilleus Maximus styling across the MG family present on the ZS; however, it has only been possible with the updates made to its larger sibling, the HS, to tell them apart. Otherwise, the ZS is inoffensive, clean, and modern-looking with a bit of sporting purpose due to the standard 18-inch wheels on the luxury trim.

Adding to its visual appeal is its availability in a wider colour palette than many of the sub-compact SUV class rivals. Push past the black, white, silver, and grey to the Brighton Blue Metallic on Auto’s review unit, or the Emerald Green Metallic that instantly brings forth similar tones to the iconic British Racing Green.

INTERIOR

The ZS is feature-rich given its class and price point. Keyless entry gets one into a cabin similar to the exterior. It’s a clear, modern design, highlighted by soft-touch materials across the main contact surfaces. Drop into the 6-way powered driver’s seat for an ergonomic experience.

Button clutter is a thing of the past, as there are hard buttons for the most accessible functions, and the other controls are tucked away in the 12.1-inch infotainment touchscreen. Some functions can even be assigned to steering wheel-mounted buttons. These few physical controls available operate with assuredness.

Luxury trim buyers will enjoy a bit more digital instrumentation via their 7-inch gauge cluster. The system works smoothly, has a logical layout, and all the connectivity modern passengers want.

While the ZS is the smaller MG SUV, the cabin space is more than sufficient for all occupants, and the sense of space is enhanced by the glass-to-body ratio and the sunroof. Even with the large greenhouse, the cabin retains a low-noise quotient for further comfort. Storage, including trunk space, is more than sufficient for family treks.

Combine this with a number of automated or powered convenience features and the ZS is a very nice place to be.

ON THE ROAD

For many class rivals, it would just fall apart right here, falling into either the ‘too soft, I don’t want to drive it fast’ category, or the ‘too stiff, my passengers are going to throw up and complain’ side of the graph. Then there are those soft, yet unable to provide comfort; and hard, yet unable to provide any actual vehicular control. This is where the sports car legacy kicks in.

The real beauty of the ZS is its driving dynamics, clearly inherited from MG’s performance car know-how. The suspension is compliant, but firm enough to be sporty. At the first corner, at speed, there’s magically precious little body roll, instilling confidence to drive with some enthusiasm. Even better, the rest of the car can keep up, as the steering is direct in tracing the given driving line, and the brakes assure constant speed reduction. The 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder is more than willing to respond in unison with the transmission for rapid increases in velocity as demanded by the accelerator pedal. Even on the broken surfaces that make up the Jamaican internal road network, the ZS quickly makes one forget that it’s an SUV, taking on a car-like feel and making as much use of its front-wheels as possible.

For those that are more measured in their pace, the ZS can handle precious human cargo with the abundance of equipped safety systems, passive, and active for urban operations. Things are a breeze in stop-and-go traffic due to the auto hold function on the luxury trim.

Then there is the MG Pilot Driver Assistance suite. Put together, they keep the vehicle in check and the driver alert for potential accidents, while allowing the vehicle to be operated for short periods with minimal driver intervention.

VERDICT

With its size, price, comfort, and feature set, the 2026 ZS Luxury is already a top contender in the cut-throat sub-compact SUV segment. And while the brand faithful may scoff at it, or others mislabel it as another small SUV, MG did take time to work their magic. This is a brand known for driving excellence, and the ZS is a pleasure to be behind the wheel, packed to the gills with the family, or alone on a B-road. If that last part is important, then the 2026 ZS MG Luxury should be at the top of your list.

World.title: Help delivered, but…
World.content:
Tents, provided by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management, erected in the area of Coopers Pen, Trelawny, where 20 houses were demolished on Tuesday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Even as the Government mobilised multi-agency help for about 40 families whose houses were demolished a day earlier, a group of irate residents of Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny staged a peaceful protest Wednesday, demanding more. The residents said they want to be relocated, after their houses were demolished allegedly by the owner of land some of them have occupied for decades.

The protesters insisted that the Government, or the landowner, must provide them with alternative accommodation. They said the temporary tents provided by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), in which some of them spent Tuesday night, are not enough.

“We get tent last night, so we can lay a head for the night. What about today? What is going to happen? We want to know where we are going to relocate to. What is going to happen to the people them that their house push down?” asked demonstrator Jessica Haye.

In a Wednesday afternoon release, while emphasising that the demolition arose from a long-standing private matter, and that the Government of Jamaica was not a party to the underlying private dispute, the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) said a number of State agencies had been deployed “to address the immediate humanitarian and social welfare needs of affected families”. The Ministry of Labour and Social Security, ODPEM, Child Protection and Family Services Agency, Poor Relief Department within the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, and the Social Development Commission are among agencies involved. OPM said teams worked well past midnight, Tuesday, to help those who lost their homes.

“Assistance provided included food supplies, bottled water, toiletries, temporary shelter supplies, tents and lighting equipment. As part of the emergency response, ODPEM mobilised and transported relief supplies directly to affected families, including 40 family-size tents, cots, foam pads, solar lights, care packages, cases of bottled water and sanitary products. The Ministry of Labour will return on Friday, August 14, to provide additional support,” said OPM.

But while grateful for the help, residents said they expect more, and they laid out their demands during Wednesday’s protest.

“There is no way you can demolish a house like this, and no notification. No notification. We need justice,” said Haye, who stressed that many of them had not yet recovered from the devastation caused by last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

“We are not going to stop this [protest] until the prime minister [Dr Andrew Holness] hear. We naw stop. We go come out here day by day because we want justice. It must be a relocation!” she insisted.

Another demonstrator, Sylvia Fisher, said while they understood that the residents could not remain on privately owned property indefinitely, they should have been given notice and assistance to relocate.

“You can’t run in pon people so. And run pon people goods… and then now put you under tent! You have pickney to go back to school. It cannot work,” she said.

She said she has lived in the community for 32 years, while her father lived there for more than 50.

Fisher is adamant that the government has a responsibility to assist affected residents whom, she said, voted them into office.

“The government need to come see this cause a we the people make the government, and is we the people put politicians in power, and a we the people have power. So they must consider poor people. A no rich man, a poor people put them in a power,” she argued.

“We know we have to go, but please relocate we, relocate we. We live pon the land 20, 30, 40 years you just come pitch we off so. No! Find somewhere and put we. The private man who them say claims to own the land, him fi find somewhere and put we. A him come mash we up,” Fisher alleged.

Even as those who have lost their homes agitate, there are fears that the wrecking crew will return. Among the worried is 69-year-old Stanley Hill, who said he has lived on the property for 51 years.

He said a marker has been placed at the doorway of the small concrete house he has occupied for decades, indicating that it is earmarked for demolition.

“Now to the age a me now, me soon 70, me a 69-year-old. And me live there from me a little boy. Where me going go now as an old man? Me can’t make house again,” said Hill.

“I need somebody to talk to me so me know where me stand. Because me can’t come sleep under tree. And me don’t have no money. Me don’t have no bank account,” he added.

The OPM has given a commitment to keep an eye on what is happening in the community and “coordinate additional interventions”. It said it is aware that those affected include senior citizens such as Hill, children, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable individuals.

Said the media release issued Wednesday: “The Poor Relief Department of the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, along with the Social Development Commission, will undertake further assessments of affected residents and households. Assistance will be provided through the applicable government programmes and support frameworks. Furthermore, the Ministry of Local Government has indicated that drop-in shelters will be available to meet the needs of residents.

“The Government of Jamaica’s response is being coordinated across the relevant social protection, disaster management, child protection, local government and community development agencies, with the immediate priority being to ensure that vulnerable residents have access to essential assistance while individual and household circumstances are properly assessed.”

World.title: ‘My soul is hurting’
World.content:
A screen grab of Opposition spokesperson on Youth and Human Rights Isat Buchanan making a plea for children found with firearms to have greater access to diversion. He was speaking during a sitting of the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act on Wednesday at Gordon House.

APPEALING not just as a legislator, but also from his own experience with past convictions, Opposition Spokesperson on Youth and Human Rights Isat Buchanan has urged the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act to make simple possession of a firearm or ammunition an offence that can be referred to child diversion, rather than leaving it solely to a judge’s discretion under Section 37 of the Act.

He argued that children caught in possession should be given a chance to avoid a lifelong criminal record.

But the proposal drew resistance from committee chairman Delroy Chuck and other members, who warned that making simple firearm possession a scheduled diversion offence could remove judicial discretion and allow criminals to exploit children as gun carriers, knowing they could be sent to diversion if caught.

The emotional exchange unfolded on Wednesday as the committee continued reviewing the matrices and submissions on the Child Diversion Act, 2018.

During the sitting, Buchanan repeatedly pressed his colleagues to consider what may have happened before a firearm ended up in a child’s hands.

“We are well aware that there are adults who are using children, even children below the age of criminal responsibility, to lock firearms, let’s call it that, and to carry. So if we are going to be in the business of being able to pull these children and divert them from this deviant behaviour, possession simpliciter has to be a space that we can divert them and put them in programmes. If we leave it to the discretion under section 37 in that contemplation, I’m afraid that there will be children who won’t be able to benefit,” he said.

Possession simpliciter, in this debate, means the simple fact of being found in possession of a firearm or ammunition, without necessarily alleging that the child used the weapon in another offence.

Buchanan wants that form of possession added to the First Schedule of the Child Diversion Act, which sets out offences that qualify as diversion offences. His argument is not that children should automatically be diverted in every firearm case. Rather, he wants firearm or ammunition possession placed among the offences that can be dealt with through the diversion framework, instead of relying solely on the separate discretion currently available to judges.

That distinction became the heart of the disagreement.

Section 37(2)of the Act already gives a court a route to diversion even when an offence is not listed in the First Schedule, providing that a court may make a child diversion referral order for any other offence where it is in the interest of justice.

This formed the basis of Chuck’s opposition to Buchanan’s plea.

He argued that this existing discretion is important because it allows the court to examine why the child had the gun, how the child came into possession of it, and whether the child was being used by someone else before deciding whether diversion is appropriate.

“The child may well, deliberately want to control a gun. A 16-year-old may well, deliberately want to control a gun, and having been found with the gun, he says, ‘put me on child diversion’, or automatically it has to go to child diversion, and my answer is that may not be an appropriate case for child diversion,” he argued.

He also warned that criminals could exploit diversion by using children as gun carriers, knowing they might avoid conviction.

However, Buchanan maintained that the possibility of coercion is precisely why simple possession should be included. His argument became increasingly personal as the discussion continued.

“At 47, chairman, I am still dealing with the past of convictions that have nothing to do with firearms. If you want this version of a Jamaican child to be better than me, if at all, if there’s any good in me, and you see, chairman, I’ve interfaced with you many times…all I’m asking is to empower the Jamaica Constabulary Force to drape up a boy, take the gun from him and let the don realise that you can’t buy enough guns that we can’t confiscate,” he said.

Buchanan was himself convicted in Jamaica in 1997, when he was 17, of possession of cocaine, dealing in cocaine and taking steps to export cocaine. He served 21 days in prison and paid a fine. In 2000, he was convicted in the United States of conspiracy to import cocaine and was sentenced to 10 years in prison, serving about eight and a half years. The Jamaican conviction was later expunged from his police record in 2014. The General Legal Council subsequently approved his application to practise law after considering his convictions, rehabilitation and character references.

Using his circumstance as an example, Buchanan reiterated that the purpose of child diversion was to give children another chance, not simply to punish them for behaviour that may have been shaped by their environment.

He eventually yielded the floor, visibly frustrated by the resistance to his proposal.

“If the Parliament doesn’t want to, or this committee doesn’t want to agree with me and we don’t want to put it to a vote and we don’t want to be brave enough to protect our children.. I will yield, chairman, but I’m hurt by this. I must tell you my soul is hurting,” he said.

Buchanan’s proposal did not face opposition only from Government members.

Opposition Senator Donna Scott Mottley said she had long had concerns about aspects of the Firearms Act but was uncomfortable supporting the change without evidence showing how children charged with firearm possession are currently being treated in the courts.

“I do agree that there should be some guidance to the judiciary. Whether or not it should be a part of the schedule is what concerns me. Because our discussion does disclose that the judges have discretion. And I wonder if it is not more that the judges should be aware of the policy of the administration as it pertains to children rather than for us to have it in the schedule,” she said.

She also warned that the proposal required more analysis, particularly because of the possibility that it could be abused by people with influence.

State minister in the ministry of National Security and Peace Juliet Cuthbert Flynn was more firmly opposed to including firearm possession in the Child Diversion Act’s First Schedule.

“We do have a gun problem in Jamaica, and so with this proliferation of guns, and, you know, just our culture, I think a standard has to be set. And these children, they might be young, but I think they all know right from wrong,” she said.

By the end of the exchange, the committee had not reached a consensus on Buchanan’s proposal.

Chuck suggested that the committee could record itself as divided rather than take a formal vote, while maintaining that the existing Section 37 mechanism could still protect children in appropriate firearm cases.

World.title: Masicka declares career longevity with new album Forever Reign
World.content:
Masicka.

For Masicka, staying power has never been something to take for granted.

The dancehall star has spent years carving out his own space in a genre in which competition is fierce and staying relevant can be just as difficult as breaking through.

From the hunger of his early years to international stages, major collaborations, and a record deal with Def Jam Recordings, the journey has taken him further than he once could have imagined.

Now, as he prepares to release his third studio album, Forever Reign, on August 14, Masicka appears increasingly interested not just in how far he can go, but in how long he can stay.

The 17-track project finds the artiste reflecting on many of the experiences that have shaped him — faith, survival, ambition, loyalty, success, and the sacrifices that often remain hidden behind the glamour of an artiste’s rise.

Even the title is deliberate.

“Forever Reign means I’m here to stay. Yes, there’s room for everyone, but my lane is carved out, and we’re going to soak up the space,” Masicka said. “The most important thing is to stay humble and focused.”

That balance between ambition and humility runs throughout the album.

Masicka has never been shy about his desire to reach the highest levels of dancehall, but Forever Reign suggests that the journey has also given him a greater appreciation for the things that cannot be measured by streams, charts, or sold-out venues.

That is evident from the album’s opening track, 1 Psalm, featuring Damian “Jr Gong” Marley.

Rather than opening with a declaration of dominance, Masicka begins with prayer.

The collaboration sets a reflective tone as the two Jamaican voices come together on a record centred on faith, protection, forgiveness, and perseverance.

For Masicka, the message is simple.

“One prayer a day, if we can pray and ask God to forgive us for our sins and protect us, then we’re good,” he said.

From there, Forever Reign moves through the different sides of the artiste’s personality and experiences.

Tracks including Oak Tree, Pointless, Shakazulu, Spend, Good, Slip and Slide, Boasty, Cross the Waters, Wicked Spell, It’s Not Too Late, AK Fire, Time and Palace, Breaking Chains, and Parables exploring the album’s varying moods, with collaborations with Nigerian rapper Blaqbonez, KraffGad, and reggae singer Lila Iké.

One of the more personal collaborations comes on Honor Roll, where Masicka links with KraffGad. The younger artiste’s hunger reminds Masicka of an earlier version of himself — the young lyricist trying to establish his name.

“His style is different, and he reminds me of myself when I was coming up and hungry,” Masicka said. “All of the young youths are ‘bad’, and I respect anybody brave enough to embark on this journey. I never had any doubt he was going to shell down this record.”

It is perhaps one of the clearest signs of Masicka’s own evolution, helping to push his music to an even wider international audience.

Just one day after the album drops, Masicka will headline a major performance at Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York, on Saturday, August 15.

It is the kind of back-to-back moment that makes the title Forever Reign feel less like a boast and more like a statement of intent.

But if the journey so far has taught him anything, it is that longevity is built project after project.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
World.content:
Latvia's military warned that similar incidents may happen again in the future. "While the Russian aggression in Ukraine is ongoing, the recurrence of such cases when a foreign unmanned aircraft enters or approaches Latvian airspace is possible," it said.

An air raid alert was declared in four eastern Latvian municipalities at around 4 a.m. local time. The military urged people to stay indoors and away from exterior walls.

After the drone was downed, Sandra Kapteine, head of the Rugāji village administration, told the Latvian Information Agency that the incident “caused no casualties,” as the drone wreckage fell in a “wooded area.”

There has been an uptick in similar incidents over recent months in countries close to the war-zone. A week ago, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said a Ukrainian-made drone crossed Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded near the village of Kardam.

World.title: Spain and Morocco reinforce border amid fears of fresh Ceuta migrant surge
World.content:
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska traveled to Ceuta on Thursday to inspect border infrastructure and a new sea barrier designed to keep people from swimming into the city. The exclave’s security personnel has also been reinforced with an additional 300 police officers and 2,000 soldiers.

“We do this to dissuade anyone who aspires to enter Ceuta and Melilla irregularly,” said Grande-Marlaska. “None of them will remain in Ceuta, none of them will make it to the Iberian Peninsula, none of them will be given legal status.”

The rumored mass crossing has been cited by critics of Spain’s migration policies.

Austria’s conservative Europe, Integration and Family Minister Claudia Bauer, last week mentioned the rumored Aug. 15 surge in a written statement, demanding Madrid “immediately and significantly reinforce border protection in its African enclaves and ensure that this time it will hold.”

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government also cited the possibility of a mid-August mass arrival last week while justifying its decision to maintain border checks on travelers from Spain.

World.title: Farage’s victory over Binface won’t silence his critics
World.content:
But second-placed this time was Count Binface, a comedian with a trash can on his head who secured — by many thousands — his highest ever vote count in a palpable protest against Farage. None of Britain’s mainstream parties took part in the contest, branding it a circus.

The Reform UK leader’s refusal to turn up at the count to hear the result Friday — a move that would have seen him pictured alongside a cast of comedy characters — underlined the struggle for him to get back on the front foot he is used to contesting politics from.

More significantly, Farage’s triumph means that parliamentary investigations into his financial affairs will now resume. That could lead to another by-election — one in which serious rivals are far less likely to stand aside to allow Farage to face-off against a long list of no-hopers.

Count Binface waits with other candidates for the declaration of the winner of the Clacton by-election at Clacton Leisure Centre, eastern England, on Aug. 14, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

Labour MPs switched out their own leader in part because of Farage’s storming success at local elections in May, but the focus on this contest has also made it harder for Farage to land blows on Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

This week, Labour overtook Reform in POLITICO’s Poll of Polls after months on the back-foot for the governing party.

Snubbing the count

Clacton is Farage’s fiefdom. It was one of the most Brexit-voting constituencies in the country and was the place that first sent him to the Commons on his eighth time of trying.

World.title: Farage probe resumes after he wins Clacton by-election
World.content:
The by-election was called by Farage himself amid mounting scrutiny of his finances.

The right-wing populist has faced repeated questions over a £5 million donation from crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, received before he became Clacton’s member of parliament in 2024, as well as support from convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

Farage has given varying explanations for the support, and billed this election — called at a dramatic press conference railing against the mainstream parties — as a “people versus the establishment” chance for Clacton’s voters to be his judge.

On Friday, the website of Parliament’s standards commissioner was updated to make clear that a paused probe into the Harborne donation has now been resumed.

That tees up the prospect of a further electoral test for Farage in Clacton if he is found to have broken the rules. The Conservatives, likely to be the most competitive challengers, have made clear that they would stand in such a contest.

Farage on Friday broke with tradition by declining to attend the result declaration at Clacton Leisure Centre.

World.title: Machthaber: Wolodymyr Selenskyj
World.content:

World.title: Week Ender archives: Can Europe quit American Big Tech?
World.content:
This week and next, the Brussels Playbook Week Ender podcast is away for the summer holiday.

So, we thought we’d re-up this popular installment on Europe’s quest to become independent from U.S. tech.

In this episode first released in June, Sarah Wheaton is joined by “The Tech Coup” author and former Member of the European Parliament Marietje Schaake and POLITICO’s Laurens Cerulus, as they look at what happens when the systems running Europe’s schools, ministries, banks, businesses and security are controlled elsewhere. They also discuss whether Brussels can build real alternatives or simply learn to manage its dependence better.

The Brussels Playbook Podcast will be back to its regular schedule on Aug. 24.

World.title: The job Zelenskyy can’t fill: Ukraine’s envoy to Trump’s Washington
World.content:
Zelenskyy moved his reshuffle plans forward so he could offer the ambassadorship to Yulia Svyrydenko, the outgoing prime minister, according to a former senior Ukrainian official and a Republican foreign expert familiar with the background to the shake-up. But she declined, disrupting his plans.

“It is no secret that I counted on and offered Yulia Svyrydenko the post of ambassador to the United States,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference in late July. He added that he was looking for a candidate with the highest possible qualifications: “a person at the level of a deputy prime minister, minister, or prime minister.”

Since then, however, other prospective candidates have proved equally reluctant, spurning what would in any case be the difficult job of handling Donald Trump’s unpredictable White House.

Ukrainians with sufficient heft and skill for the ambassadorship are looking at it askance, “worrying that they would not enjoy the conditions they would need to do the job properly,” said Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, a prominent Ukrainian opposition lawmaker and former deputy prime minister who is a regular critic of Zelenskyy.

“Certainly that would be the case without having the ear of the president or his trust,” she added. That narrows Zelenskyy’s options sharply. The person would likely have to come from his tight inner circle of trusted aides, Klympush-Tsintsadze said, but there is no one there who seriously fits the bill.

“Framing it as if nobody wants the job would be a kind of oversimplification,” said a former Ukrainian diplomat who was granted anonymity in order to speak freely. “Of course, there are people who want the job, but there’s no one who really measures up to it. Zelenskyy is having a hard time filling the position.”

World.title: EU leaders are on holiday. The crises affecting the bloc aren’t.
World.content:
“Physical presence can signal much more effectively that these emotions are taken seriously and are heard,” she added.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez was just hours away from kicking off his weeks-long summer break when 72,000 migrants surged into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on July 30. The Socialist leader duly postponed his plans and traveled to the North African coastal city, where he delivered a televised address pushing back against criticism from other EU leaders.

But as soon as the emergency was deemed to be under control, Sánchez resumed his scheduled vacation at a state-owned villa on the island of Lanzarote.

His decision to take time off, even as the political aftershocks continued to roil the bloc, drew criticism from opposition politicians like Elías Bendodo, deputy secretary of the center-right People’s Party, who this week accused the prime minister of “unprecedented selfishness” for taking time off while the situation in Ceuta is “far from normal.”

“Sánchez insults the Spanish people by remaining on his beach vacation,” he added.

The Spanish government rejected the criticism, noting the prime minister is not only reachable but actively participating in remote meetings, and insisted the state remains fully operational even when its top leaders are away.

World.title: Can a massive Madonna help slow secularization in Poland?
World.content:
Europe's largest statue of the Virgin Mary will be inaugurated on Saturday in the Polish village of Konotopie. What will the huge monument mean for the village and for the Catholic faith in Poland in general?

With its grain fields, meadows and lake, the countryside around the tiny village of Konotopie in central Poland is idyllic. Towering above all this is a monumental statue of the Virgin Mary.

Home to just 120 residents and situated about 160 kilometers (99 miles) northwest of the capital, Warsaw, the previously little-known village of Konotopie has been in the headlines for weeks now as a result of the massive statue.

The snow-white structure, which is visible for miles around, is over 55 meters (180 feet) tall. The statue itself is 40.6 meters high and stands on a 15-meter-high pedestal shaped like a crown that is intended to serve as a viewing platform.

The figure dwarfs Rio de Janeiro's famous statue of Christ the Redeemer, which reaches a total height of 38 meters including its base.

A 'pile of concrete' or a 'fantastic achievement'?

The statue will be officially inaugurated on Saturday, August 15, the feast of the Assumption of Mary, a major holy day in the Catholic calendar.

Although final construction work is still underway and the site remains fenced off and guarded, thousands of people — both pilgrims and sightseers — have been flocking to see it for months.

Opinion about the project is divided.

"It's a nightmare," one critic of the statue told the weekly magazine Newsweek, "a complete waste. Instead of investing that money in useful projects, they financed a giant pile of concrete."

"This Mary is absolutely beautiful. My utmost respect. A fantastic achievement," said one devout lady visiting the site, according to the right-wing conservative weekly Sieci.

Wealthy, devout benefactor

The benefactor behind the statue, 75-year-old Roman Karkosik, hails from a nearby village and is one of Poland's wealthiest individuals.

Nearly 40 years ago, when the shortage economy of socialism gave way to free-market capitalism after the collapse of communism in eastern Europe, Karkosik was a young graduate from technical high school.

He started out as a bartender, but moved on to buying and selling scrap metal, producing soft drinks and later became the first entrepreneur in Poland to manufacture plastic bottles.

The inauguration ceremony for the Marian statue coincides with a major Catholic holy day, the Feast of the Assumption of Mary, on August 15 Image: Kuba Stezycki/REUTERS

Karkosik made a name for himself on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. Some journalists have compared his role in Poland to Warren Buffett's influence on Wall Street.

His fortune is estimated at roughly €442 million ($511 million), and he ranks 44th on Wprost magazine's list of Poland's richest people. He lives in an 18th-century manor in the town of Kikol, just two kilometers from Konotopie.

A 'gesture of gratitude'

Karkosik and his wife, Grazyna, avoid both public appearances and contact with the media.

The cost of the statue remains a closely guarded secret. Media reports speculate that the project may have cost as much as €23 million.

The Karkosiks have described the Marian statue as a "gesture of gratitude."

According to media reports, the devout businessman wanted to thank the Virgin Mary for his recovery from a serious illness. His two brothers, who were also successful businessmen, both died prematurely after illnesses.

This is not the first time Karkosik has provided money for a religious structure. Back in 2011, he funded the construction of a church at a nearby pilgrimage site.

Artist feared seeing the finished statue

"I was afraid to come to Konotopie to see what had become of my design in reality," sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski told Polish media. Worried that the hands and face of the Virgin Mary might appear distorted, Matejkowski only visited the site in July.

"I opened my eyes and was stunned. The Mother of God is opening her arms to embrace us," he said with satisfaction. "That was exactly my intention: for the figure to have a human character, to come toward us," he explained.

The statue of Jesus Christ the King of the Universe in Swiebodzin, one of the tallest Jesus statues in the world, is also in Poland Image: Monika Skolimowska/ZB/dpa/picture alliance

Matejkowski says the statue has the facial expression of his 11-year-old daughter and the delicate facial features of his wife.

Region hopes for economic boost

Konotopie is situated in one of Poland's economically weak regions. There are no major industrial employers here, and jobs are scarce.

Local leaders hope the Marian statue will stimulate economic growth.

"The monument is not only a spiritual landmark but also a strategic asset for the region. We expect it to attract more investors and tourists, which will benefit the local economy," Krzysztof Kowalewski of the authorities in the nearby town of Kikol told Polish media.

Mayor Renata Golebiewska has said that revenues at local restaurants and bars have already broken local records.

Not the first statue of its kind in Poland

Poland is well known for its monumental Christian structures.

Following Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, a massive basilica was built in the village of Lichen in central Poland, overshadowing even the cathedrals of Paris and Cologne in scale.

The basilica is 138 meters (453 feet) long, 77 meters wide, and features a dome with a diameter of 35 meters. It can accommodate 20,000 worshippers.

Since 2010, Poland has also been home to the world's tallest statue of Jesus. Located in Swiebodzin near the German border, the 36-meter-high statue stands on a 17-meter-high mound.

Rising secularization

Whether all these gigantic monuments can stop the ongoing secularization of Polish society, however, remains highly questionable.

Although Poland is still one of the most Catholic countries in Europe, public trust in the Church continues to decline.

For centuries, the Catholic faith was a key part of Polish identity.

A huge statue of Pope John Paul II, who was born in Poland and was head of the Catholic Church from 1978 to 2005, in Czestochowa Image: Waldemar Deska/dpa/picture alliance

In the 19th century, when the territory that now makes up Poland was not an independent state and was divided up among foreign powers, Catholicism played a major role in the resistance to Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia.

After World War II, despite ideological differences, the anti-communist opposition and the Catholic Church in Poland worked together against the communist dictatorship.

During this period, churches became refuges for persecuted dissidents, and several priests were murdered by the secret police.

Pope John Paul II, himself Polish, also played a significant role in the struggle against the regime.

Catholicism in modern-day Poland

Since Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, however, the Catholic Church has experienced a crisis similar to that seen across Europe.

According to a September 2025 survey conducted by the Polish polling institute IBRIS, only 35% of Poles still trust the Church, down from 58% in 2016. Distrust rose from 24% to 47% over the same period.

In 2026, the annual number of priests ordained in Poland fell below 200 for the first time since 2000. Church attendance has also been steadily declining, especially among young people.

Even a gigantic Madonna is unlikely to reverse that trend.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
World.content:
Jets have shot down a foreign drone over Latvia after it entered the Baltic state's airspace. Its origin remains unclear, but the incident adds to concern over repeated incursions along NATO's eastern flank.

NATO fighter jets have shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the alliance and Latvian authorities said Friday.

Two Italian Eurofighters were scrambled and one destroyed the unmanned aircraft, while two Turkish F-16s were also deployed under NATO command.

What happened over Latvia?

Latvia's military initially issued an air alert and urged people in affected areas to remain indoors and seek shelter.

Authorities said the foreign drone entered Latvian airspace over the Balvi region as a result of Russian electronic warfare activity.

It was not immediately clear where the drone originated, and NATO said an investigation was underway.

Latvian authorities did not identify the drone as Ukrainian.

However, the reference to Russian electronic warfare raised the possibility that a Ukrainian drone targeting Russia had been forced off course by interference.

How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukrainian forces had attacked targets in northwestern Russia overnight, according to Latvian media.

Has this happened before?

Latvia and other NATO countries along the alliance's eastern flank have faced repeated incursions by drones since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A stray drone was also shot down over Latvia in early June, while other Ukrainian drones heading toward northwestern Russia have previously entered Latvian airspace and crashed.

Romanian and Spanish fighter jets were also deployed on Thursday after drones entered Romanian airspace near Ukraine.

Why are Italian jets defending Latvian airspace?

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania do not operate their own fighter aircraft, so NATO allies rotate responsibility for policing their skies.

The Italian Eurofighters involved in Friday's interception are based at Siauliai air base in Lithuania.

World.title: Zambia suspends vote count after violence
World.content:
Zambia has halted the counting and publication of election results after violence targeting poll workers and reports of stolen ballots. The electoral commission says it will reassess the suspension within 24 hours.

Zambia's electoral commission has suspended the counting and announcement of election results nationwide with immediate effect, citing violence directed at election officials.

The commission said ballot papers had also been stolen in some cases and that it would review the suspension within 24 hours.

Why has Zambia suspended vote counting?

The Electoral Commission of Zambia said the decision followed incidents of violence targeting polling staff.

It added that ballot papers had been stolen in some locations, though it did not immediately give details on where the incidents occurred or how widespread they were.

The general election is a major test for President Hakainde Hichilema, whose economic reform program has been weighed against widespread frustration over the cost of living.

Around 8 million people were registered to vote in the southern African country of about 22 million people.

Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Voters were also choosing members of parliament and local councillors at more than 13,500 polling stations.

Were there problems during voting?

Long queues formed before dawn at polling stations in Lusaka, with some voters gathering around makeshift fires as they waited.

Local observers reported delays and frustration at some polling stations because of poor voter guidance, confusion over voter rolls and crowd-management problems.

European Union observers were monitoring the election.

Hichilema came to power in 2021 after defeating longtime rival Edgar Lungu, who served as president from 2015 to 2021 and died in 2025. Lungu's political legacy still looms over the election, with Hichilema's main challenger Brian Mundubile leading an opposition alliance backed by many of the former president's supporters.

World.title: Berlin's Russian House: A hub for propaganda and espionage?
World.content:
The Russian House stands in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it's being used to spread propaganda for Putin's Russia. Now, French authorities have said it is being used by the Kremlin for espionage.

The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it is the subject of fierce disagreements and has long been a bone of contention in Berlin.

The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore.

But now, more than 40 years later, French authorities have linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.

"In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin earlier this week.

In response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that there are two bilateral agreements between Germany and Russia regarding real estate matters that cannot be easily revoked.

"It is, so to speak, an agreement that governs both the Russian House here in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut that we operate in Moscow," Giese said. Any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other.

German tax money for Russian propaganda?

The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation.

Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany.

Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian."

Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website.

The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda.

Symbols of friendship remained on display in Berlin's Russian House in October 2023, more than year after the Russian invasion of Ukraine Image: Dmyrto Katkov/DW

Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, a Holocaust film was shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis.

In an interview in August 2025, Robin Wagener, a member of the Bundestag for the opposition Green Party, told DW: "It is time we recognized that this is not mutual cultural exchange, but Russian war propaganda in Germany."

Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow

The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes.

Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term.

Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine.

It is an open secret that the German government is shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow.

The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia.

A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts.

Berlin detains German-Ukrainian woman for Russian espionage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year.

Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible

According the cultural agreement, the contracting parties welcome "direct contacts between social groups and associations, including trade unions, churches, religious communities, artists' associations and political, cultural and other foundations."

However, in recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations."

This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties.

Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible.

This article was originally written in German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in August 2026 to reflect news developments.

World.title: Why women are breaking men's endurance records
World.content:
Sophie Woods has completed the 2,000-kilometer Via Alpina faster even than the fastest-ever man. DW explains why she is not the only woman breaking men's records in extreme sports.

New Zealand runner Sophie Wood, who competes under her maiden name, Sophie Grant, recently accomplished something truly remarkable.

Running for 29 days across the Alps, from Trieste to Monaco, Woods covered around 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) while climbing a total of more than 100,000 meters (328,083 feet) – on an average of three to four hours of sleep per night.

This made her the fastest person ever to complete the Via Alpina. The 42-year-old ultra-runner finished the route more than seven days faster than the fastest man ever to do so.

"It gives me goosebumps thinking about it, to take the overall record is amazing," Woods told DW.

"I was there for the adventure. I didn't really want to be running for longer than a month, that was enough."

The longer the distance, the smaller the gender gap

Woods is not the only woman to have broken a men's record in endurance sports in recent years.

In 2026, Rachel Entrekin won the Cocodona 250, a race covering roughly 400 kilometers in the United States, setting a new overall course record.

A year earlier, Tara Dower ran the Long Trail in Vermont. a distance of about 440 kilometers, in 3 days, 18 hours, and 29 minutes, beating the previous men's record by 2 hours and 40 minutes.

In 2019, Germany's Fiona Kolbinger became the first woman to win the Transcontinental Race. Cycling nearly 4,000 kilometers across Europe, she finished just under eight hours ahead of the second-placed male rider. That same year, Jasmin Paris became the first woman to win the 430-kilometer Spine Race in Great Britain, shattering the previous course record by more than 12 hours.

A comprehensive analysis by RunRepeat and the International Association of Ultrarunners examined over five million results from more than 15,000 ultramarathons. The findings showed that the longer the distance, the closer women came, on average, to matching men's times.

In 2019, Fiona Kolbinger became the first woman to win the Transcontinental Race Image: Mateusz Birecki/IMAGO

In the events analyzed, on average, the men were still 11.1% faster. At the 100-mile mark, the gap narrowed to just 0.25%. At distances exceeding 195 miles, the women were on average 0.6% faster.

'We're good at solving problems'

So why are women able to keep pace—or better—when the physical demands increase?

Certain physiological factors may play a role. On average, women possess a higher proportion of fatigue-resistant Type I muscle fibers and rely relatively more on fat as an energy source during endurance activities.

The advantages men typically enjoy—such as greater muscle mass and higher maximal oxygen uptake—may be less decisive in ultra-long events than in shorter races.

"Probably we are better at burning fat, and therefore it makes us able to go longer," Woods said – before pointing to other possible factors.

"I think we're good at putting our egos aside. And I think we're good at solving problems."

Competing in an ultramarathon is about much more than who can run the fastest. There are key decisions to be made about sleep, nutrition and physical pain. That's where her team comes in.

"I just put my life in their hands," she said.

"You kind of control everything you can and then you just throw it into chaos and see what comes out in the wash."

As little as 90 minutes of sleep, 7,000 calories a day

The extreme physical strain was evident in her sleeping patterns – towards the end, she was sleeping as little as 90 minutes a night. When she simply couldn't go any further, she would lie down right next to the trail.

"You just curl up on the side in a little mossy glen and hope that no one thinks you've died," she said.

"The sleep deprivation was one of the hardest parts of the whole thing."

Her alarm would often go off again as early as three in the morning.

Sophie Woods broke both the women's and men's records on the Via Alpina Image: Ulrich Wagner/IMAGO

At the same time, maintaining her physical energy was a huge problem, with her team estimating that she was consuming between 6,000 and 7,000 calories a day – through sports drinks, soft drinks, as burritos, falafel wraps, sandwiches, pasta, and McDonald's food. She ate much of this while on the move.

In the Dolomites, heat and pain added to the challenge.

"I bawled my eyes out in the Dolomites," she said.

"I was really hot. I was really sore. I was really swollen. I was shuffling along and I was just like: I don't know if I can do this."

Despite it all, she carried on.

Women long neglected in sports research

Despite setting the record, Woods wonders what she and other women could achieve if their bodies were studied as thoroughly as men's.

"As a woman, you need to be very careful when you read these studies to actually see who they are studying, because often it will be 10 male cyclists," Woods said.

"We have just been left behind in all of the research for decades," she said.

"As women, we are fighting for crumbs in the sporting world. We are fighting for more coverage, we are fighting for more research, we are fighting for more sponsorship."

The fact that several individual men's records have been broken by women doesn't mean that women are inherently better endurance athletes than men. Men still hold many records and are, on average, significantly faster over shorter distances.

However, in an interview with the BBC, sports physiologist Nicholas Tiller described very long endurance events as "the great equaliser."

Woods is simply not interested in who holds the advantage on paper.

"I think the bravest thing to do is to try," she said.

"Try the scary thing. It doesn't matter what happens in the end because at least you've tried."
