Prime Minister Donald Tusk has confirmed that he will seek to have Maciej Berek, a government minister who stepped down this week and who Tusk calls his “right-hand man”, appointed as a judge on Poland’s constitutional court. The move has generated considerable controversy given that Tusk’s ruling coalition has repeatedly pledged to “depoliticise” the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after the previous national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government appointed its former politicians to the court. At a press conference on Thursday, however, Tusk defended the idea, describing Berek as an “apolitical and nonpartisan” figure who would help “fix the Constitutional Tribunal” after it was rendered illegitimate by PiS. Premier @donaldtusk potwierdził, że @MaciejBerek – do tej pory minister ds. nadzoru nad wdrażaniem polityki rządu – będzie kandydatem na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. – To jeden z najwybitniejszych polskich prawników – uzasadnił szef rządu.https://t.co/RsKLhLjHhC — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) August 13, 2026 Berek is a longstanding associate of Tusk. During Tusk’s first period as prime minister, from 2007 to 2014, Berek was head of the Government Legislation Centre (RCL) while also serving as secretary of the cabinet. After Tusk returned to power in 2023, heading a coalition of parties ranging from left to centre right, Berek was appointed as a minister without portfolio and then, in 2025, was made minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of government policy. He has, however, been an extremely low-key figure, rarely speaking in public. Berek is also not a member of parliament, and indeed not even a member of any political party. On Tuesday this week, Tusk unexpectedly announced before a cabinet meeting that Berek, whom he called his “right-hand man”, was leaving the government in order to “move on to other tasks”. The prime minister did not say what those tasks would be, but multiple media outlets reported that Berek would be presented as a candidate to become a judge on the Constitutional Tribunal. Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though was never a member of the PiS party). When Tusk’s coalition came to power, it promised to restore the legitimacy of the TK, including by “depoliticising” it. In 2024, it approved legislation that would have banned anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. However, the measures were referred by the then-president, PiS ally Andrzej Duda, to the TK itself, which subsequently declared them unconstitutional, meaning they did not come into force. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 At a press conference on Thursday, Tusk confirmed the rumours that he would seek to make Berek a TK judge. He called Berek “one of the most distinguished Polish legal practitioners, who has made his apolitical and nonpartisan nature a hallmark”. Berek has a doctorate in law and, between his stints in government, worked as an assistant professor in the department of constitutional law at the University of Warsaw. “For him, compliance with the law and the constitution has always been paramount,” declared Tusk. “I don’t know anyone better equipped, better prepared, to help rectify the situation we face with the flawed Constitutional Tribunal.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: Nie mamy żadnych innych interesów w tej sprawie. Zależy nam na naprawieniu Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, żeby nie był na smyczy prezydenta i PiS-u, tylko wykonywał swoją robotę. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 The prime minister acknowledged that his government had tried to ban politicians from serving on the TK. But he said that Berek himself had recently told him that, “under the current political circumstances, we must do everything we can to remedy the situation” at the tribunal. “Since methods that are unconstitutional are being used from the other side, I must also demonstrate my determination and that we won’t give in to such methods,” added Tusk. Those remarks, in which Tusk also called Święczkowski’s leadership of the TK “embarrassing”, were a reference to the fact that the current PiS-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, and Święczkowski have refused to accept four new TK judges chosen by parliament earlier this year. “We have no interests in this matter other than to repair the Constitutional Tribunal so that it is not a tool and is not under the thumb of the president or PiS, but rather that it performs its work as objectively as possible,” said Tusk. A newly sworn-in @TK_GOV_PL judge says he will not take his seat until four colleagues appointed by parliament are allowed to take theirs. He said their appointments had been blocked "unlawfully", in the latest twist in a long-running disputehttps://t.co/X30rm1Gfzs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 However, there remain major potential stumbling blocks on Berek’s path to the TK, not least doubts over whether Tusk’s coalition partners will support his nomination in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, declared on Tuesday that, if rumours of Berek’s nomination were true, “he won’t get votes from The Left because we promised our voters that politicians wouldn’t end up on the TK”. Given that the government has only a majority of nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition to oppose Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. On Thursday, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. Jeżeli to się wydarzy (a raczej nie), to do niedawna czynny polityk nie dostanie głosów klubu @__Lewica, gdyż obiecaliśmy naszym wyborcom, że politycy nie trafią do TK. Ale IMHO to bardzo krzywdząca dla @MaciejBerek plotka, on by się jako państwowiec w życiu na coś takiego nie… https://t.co/QWFFmdy4V3 — Anna-Maria Żukowska 💁🏻‍♀️ (@AM_Zukowska) August 11, 2026 The next vacancy on the TK’s 15-judge bench is due to open on 18 September, when the nine-year term of Justyn Piskorski, one of the PiS-era judges regarded as illegitimate by the current government, ends. After that, a further vacancy will open in January. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Earlier this week, his chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Radio Zet that Nawrocki would “accept the oath if procedures are followed”. World.title: Poland reintroduces VAT cut and daily price caps to lower fuel costs for drivers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has announced that, from Monday, it will reintroduce some of the measures that were used earlier this year to lower prices for consumers at petrol stations amid the energy crisis triggered by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The package, known in Polish as CPN and which will be in place from 17 August until at least 31 August, includes reducing VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and introducing retail consumer price caps on fuels set daily by the energy minister. Announcing the measures on Thursday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said they should result in prices falling by around 1 zloty (€0.23) per litre. Currently, average retail prices are 7.29 zloty for 95-octane petrol and 8.09 zloty for diesel, according to Polish price monitoring service E-Petrol. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Polska będzie w absolutnej czołówce europejskiej, jeśli chodzi o najniższe ceny paliw. pic.twitter.com/ar3IZbzFHQ — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Tusk acknowledged that CPN will entail “serious costs” for the state budget. When similar measures (which also, unlike now, included cuts in excise duty on fuels) were in place between the end of March and end of June, they cost the state an estimated 4.7 billion zloty. On Thursday, the prime minister renewed his criticism of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for last month refusing to sign into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits this year. The government said that the tax, which would have raised an estimated 4 billion zloty, was intended to help cover the costs of fuel subsidies. The profits of many fuel companies have boomed during the crisis, with Polish state energy giant Orlen last week announcing record half-year results. Nawrocki’s chancellery, however, has argued that fuel companies would seek to pass the costs of tax increases onto consumers, thereby increasing prices. CPN was first introduced in March in response to soaring fuel prices in the wake of US and Israeli attacks on Iran and subsequent disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. CPN subsequently helped bring Polish fuel prices to among the lowest in the EU. Since the measures were withdrawn in June, prices at the pump in Poland have risen significantly, placing pressure on the government to again cushion the blow for consumers. E-Petrol reports that prices have recently started to fall, but remain well above the levels seen before the crisis. Economists at PKO, a major bank, wrote on Thursday that higher fuel prices in July, which stemmed from the expiry of CPN and an increase in global oil prices, were the main drivers of inflation accelerating from 2.5% in June to 3.0% last month. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector. It also saw its highest-ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets https://t.co/uhGWJVQvf3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 On Thursday, Tusk claimed that the re-introduced CPN would lead to Poland having among “the lowest prices in Europe”, helping “possibly millions of Polish drivers, on critical days, when they return from holidays”. But he also acknowledged that fuel would “still be expensive”. Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, however, criticised the government for what he claimed was a belated response to high prices. World.title: Polish household assets hit record 4 trillion zloty amid fastest growth in years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are building up wealth at the fastest pace in years, with the combined value of household financial assets surpassing 4 trillion zloty (€930 billion) for the first time, according to new data from the Polish Development Fund (PFR), a state entity. The figure reached 4.1 trillion zloty at the end of the first quarter of this year, up 4.3% from the previous quarter, said PFR. That was the largest quarterly increase in just over six years. On an annual basis, assets rose 15.3%, the fastest pace in five years. After deducting liabilities, household net financial assets stood at 3.2 trillion zloty, also a record. Net assets were up 18.4% from a year earlier and 4.9% from the previous quarter. Ponad 4,1 bln zł – tyle wynoszą już aktywa finansowe polskich gospodarstw domowych. To historyczny rekord. W najnowszej analizie PFR pokazujemy, że w ciągu roku wzrosły o 15,3% – to jedna z najwyższych dynamik w historii. Skala i tempo wzrostu aktywów pokazują też, jak duży jest… pic.twitter.com/fSx1yOZtkn — Mikołaj Raczyński (@MikRaczynski) August 7, 2026 The biggest contribution to the quarterly increase came from what PFR classifies as “other equity holdings”, which include shares in limited liability companies, partnerships, cooperatives and mutual insurance societies. They rose by 61.5 billion zloty. Bank deposits recorded the second-largest increase (44.4 billion zloty). Despite the strong rise in equity holdings, bank deposits and cash remained the largest components of household financial assets, accounting for 26.3% and 11.1% respectively. Pension and disability funds accounted for 10.5% of household financial assets. Meanwhile, shares listed on stock exchanges and regulated over-the-counter markets made up 2.9% of household financial assets. Their value is equivalent to 3% of GDP, one of the lowest shares in the European Union, where the average is 8.2%. Although shares make up only a small share of household assets, the Polish stock market has performed strongly in recent years, with its blue-chip index reaching a record high last week and breaking its previous high set 19 years ago. By contrast, Polish households have a relatively high level of cash holdings. Cash was equivalent to 11.5% of Poland’s GDP in the first quarter, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). PFR’s data also show that household liabilities in Poland increased by 5.2% year-on-year to more than 891 billion zloty in the first quarter, well below the rate of asset growth. Long-term loans accounted for 92.2% of liabilities, while short-term loans accounted for 5.1%. Rising household wealth reflects three decades of strong economic growth in Poland, accompanied by a rapid rise in wages and living standards. Earlier this year, state research agency CBOS found that a record 39% of Poles say they are financially comfortable, up from just 3% in the early 1990s. Separate data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that only 2% of the population live in severe deprivation, the lowest level on record. Poland last year rose to its highest-ever level in a measure of household prosperity in European Union member states, overtaking four other countries. That growth has also fuelled a rapid increase in the number of ultra-wealthy people in Poland, whose number has almost doubled since 2019. However, the PFR data show only total combined household assets and liabilities, not how they are distributed across society. The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. The personal data of almost 19 million people, including medical information, has been compromised in a major cyberattack on a company that provides services to thousands of medical facilities in Poland. “We are dealing with one of the largest incidents in Poland’s history,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on Wednesday. He urged people to use government services to check whether their data is affected and to “lock” their national identity number to prevent potential fraud. (￼🧵 1/2) 💬 Dziś doszło do poważnego wycieku danych w firmie MyDr, który może obejmować blisko 19 milionów osób korzystających z opieki medycznej. W związku z sytuacją krytyczną zostały natychmiast podjęte działania mające zabezpieczyć dane i wyjaśnić okoliczności incydentu –… pic.twitter.com/nIp6EvbKiu — Ministerstwo Cyfryzacji (@CYFRA_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The attack targeted MyDr, a company that provides services used by many medical facilities in Poland. Its data includes patients’ personal information, as well as medical details such as diagnoses and prescriptions. It was first reported on Monday by Zaufana Trzecia Strona, an IT security news service, which said that it had been contacted on Saturday by the alleged perpetrators, who claimed to have accessed the data of around 18.8 million people. The hackers, who have not been identified, had also sent a screenshot from the compromised database showing the personal data of “one of the most important politicians in Poland”, added Zaufana Trzecia Strona. Shortly afterwards, MyDr confirmed that it had “become the target of an external, deliberate criminal activity involving some of our data”. In an update on Wednesday, it said that, at the time of writing, there was no evidence that the data had been published anywhere. Największy wyciek danych osobowych w historii Polski i co możemy z nim zrobić – nasza analiza incydentu w MyDr i jego potencjalnych skutków.https://t.co/vXUmVfpPAP Opisujemy aktualny stan wiedzy i możliwe scenariusze rozwoju sytuacji. pic.twitter.com/uqhjz1CjZ1 — ZaufanaTrzeciaStrona @zaufanatrzeciastrona@infosec (@Zaufana3Strona) August 13, 2026 Gawkowski addressed the issue at a press briefing on Wednesday. He noted that “there is no indication we are dealing with an external attack…from Russia or any other country”. Poland has recently regularly been targetted by Russian state-linked hackers. It is “very likely” that cybercriminals are behind the attack on MyDr, said Gawkowski, who pledged that there would be an “uncompromising” response from the Polish security services. The minister advised Poles to check in a secure government database whether their data had been leaked. He also advised citizens to use the state web portal, known as mObywatel, to “lock” their identity number, known as a PESEL, which prevents fraudsters from using it. Around 12,000 medical facilities use MyDr’s services, the digital affairs ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The company claims that it processes three million medical consultations and 2.7 million prescriptions a month, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. A letter sent to a Polish court by Marcin Romanowski, who served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government and is now on the run from criminal charges, suggests that he is residing in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. The Polish authorities have been trying to locate and extradite Romanowski, whose whereabouts have been unknown since he fled Budapest earlier this year after Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who had granted him asylum, lost power. Były wiceminister sprawiedliwości ma przebywać w Tyraspolu, stolicy zbuntowanej mołdawskiej prowincji znajdującej się pod patronatem Rosji. Spod tego adresu w Naddniestrzu polityk PiS miał wystąpić o wydanie listu żelaznego.https://t.co/m05dtQv3KV — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) August 12, 2026 On Wednesday, following media reports that Romanowski had sent a letter to the Polish authorities from Transnistria, a spokeswoman for Warsaw’s district court, which is responsible for extradition matters, confirmed to news website Gazeta.pl that this was the case. “The letter and envelope indicate that the package was sent to the court from Tiraspol in Transnistria,” said judge Anna Ptaszek. “It bears his handwritten signature.” Przemysław Nowak, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, also confirmed to broadcaster RMF that Romanowski had sent the letter, in which he indicated that he was residing in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, and requested safe passage to Poland. The fugitive politician said that he would be willing to appear in court or before prosecutors, on the condition that he was not placed in detention, said Nowak, who added that prosecutors had not yet taken a position on Romanowski’s request. Transnistria is a region of eastern Moldova, bordering Ukraine, that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s, even fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. The territory’s flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Romanowski’s apparent presence in the Russian-linked territory was condemned by figures from Poland’s government. “I would say that Romanowski is now very likely under the influence of Russian intelligence,” said deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk, quoted by broadcaster TVN. Paweł Wojtunik, the former head of Poland’s Central Anticorruption Bureau (CBA), who previously worked in Moldova, wrote that “it is impossible to enter [Transnistria], let alone to live there, without the consent of the local KGB, which is directly managed by the Russian GRU and FSB [intelligence agences]”. – Dzisiaj powiedziałbym, że Romanowski z dużym prawdopodobieństwem jest pod wpływem rosyjskich służb – ocenił wiceszef MON Cezary Tomczyk. Sprawę skomentował też szef MSZ Radosław Sikorski.https://t.co/LuWw0bkh2j — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 12, 2026 Even a deputy leader of Romanowski’s own party, the national-conservative PiS, was unwilling to defend him. In an interview with Polsat News, Przemysław Czarnek noted that it is still not confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. But he agreed, when asked by the host, that it “would be crossing a line” for Romanowski to be in the territory. Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government between 2019 and 2023. He remains a member of parliament, despite having fled Poland in December 2024 after prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group. Those alleged offences relate to Romanowski’s time at the justice ministry, which was then led by Zbigniew Ziobro, who is also wanted on multiple charges. Both Romanowski and Ziobro obtained asylum in Hungary when the country was led by PiS-ally Orbán. The Polish government says that Hungary has revoked the refugee status and travel documents granted to fugitive ex-justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro by Viktor Orbán. Poland will now seek Ziobro's deportation from the US, where he fled after leaving Hungary https://t.co/TcVw0AiEMX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 However, after Orbán lost power earlier this year, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains. Last month, Poland requested his extradition, though that is a process that could take years. Romanowski, meanwhile, disappeared completely, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians have denied the allegations against them and have claimed to be victims of “political revenge” by the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk that took power in December 2023. They have argued that they would not be able to receive a fair trial in Poland while Tusk remains in power because of the government’s influence over the judicial system. On Wednesday, Romanowski’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, confirmed that his client had requested safe passage to Poland and that he was “outside the territory of the European Union”. However, he did not confirm that Romanowski is in Transnistria. Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges. The Polish government has appealed to Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, to reverse its decision to exclude Poland from its European roaming area. It says that Polish users, who will now face greater costs when travelling, should not be treated as “second-tier customers”. Starlink, which provides users with portable terminals that act as receivers for internet connections from its network of satellites, offers a “Roam” service that lets customers continue using their connection outside their home country without extra charges as long as they remain within their designated region. One region is Europe, in which Starlink has included 36 countries and territories. However, the firm makes clear that “Poland is not included in the Europe region”, meaning users registered in that country are not included in the Roam system. The company offered no explanation for Poland’s exclusion from the system. Some media reports have suggested that it is because terminals registered in Poland are used in Ukraine. However, Ukraine is itself not included in Starlink’s European “Roam” region. The company’s decision prompted an angry response from Polish government ministers. “I do not agree with a global technology company treating Poles worse than other Europeans,” wrote digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on X, the social media platform owned by Musk. “If Elon Musk’s SpaceX wants to operate in Poland, benefit from the Polish market, and earn from Polish customers, it must treat them fairly and on equal terms,” he added. “That is why I have appealed to SpaceX for the urgent restoration of equal terms for the company’s Polish customers.” Nie zgadzam się, żeby globalna firma technologiczna traktowała Polki i Polaków gorzej niż innych Europejczyków. World.title: Czech Villages Face Water Shortages as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Residents say they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pool.

Communities across the Czech Republic are struggling with worsening water shortages as wells dry up and small streams disappear after years of increasingly severe drought, according to local media on Thursday.



In the village of Krsy in the Plzen Region, tankers are delivering drinking water daily to a reservoir above the village. Some private wells have already run dry, while others are close to empty.

Residents said they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pools.

Authorities are urging households to connect to public water networks where available.

The shortages are also putting pressure on tourist destinations. In Horni Becva, in the Beskydy Mountains, the population doubles during the summer holidays.

The municipality’s two wells have been operating close to their limits, with firefighters called in to deliver water.

Hotels with wellness facilities are among the largest users, prompting local officials to ask businesses to reduce consumption.

Officials hope conditions will improve when the tourist season ends and autumn rains arrive.

World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: This Website Tracks How Many Trams Are Still Running Without Air Conditioning
World.content:
A new website is giving Prague residents a live picture of how many trams are operating without air conditioning, highlighting an issue that has become particularly noticeable during the city’s summer heat.

The service, Smrdime.cz, was created by developer Christoph Korb. Its name is a play on the Czech word smrdíme, meaning “we stink,” and refers to the uncomfortable conditions passengers can face inside overheated trams.

The website uses live data to calculate the share of Prague’s trams that are currently running without air conditioning. The figures change throughout the day as new vehicles enter and leave service.

When the service was checked on Thursday, August 13, Prague was experiencing temperatures of around 37 degrees Celsius. At that point, 188 of the 256 trams in operation did not have air conditioning, representing about 71 percent of the fleet being tracked.



Of the 147 air-conditioned trams available, 77 were operating at the same time.

The figures provide a snapshot rather than a fixed daily total. As trams are taken out of service and replaced, the balance between air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned vehicles changes continuously.

The project draws attention to a long-standing issue facing Prague’s public transport system: a substantial part of the city’s tram fleet still lacks air conditioning.

The website is based on data from two publicly available sources. Transport information comes from Golemio, Prague’s open-data platform, while weather information is provided by Open-Meteo. The two data sources are used to calculate the current situation displayed on the site.

Korb built the service with Anthropic’s Claude Code development tool. He has also published the project’s source code on GitHub, allowing other developers to inspect the project and contribute to its development.

World.title: From a Student’s Dream to a Japanese Bakery in Prague: The Story Behind Yaki-Pan
World.content:
For Hoan, opening a bakery in Prague was not a sudden business idea. It was a dream that had been taking shape for more than a decade.

After arriving in Prague as a student, Hoan watched members of the Vietnamese community build businesses across the city, most commonly in restaurants, grocery shops and nail salons.

She worked in grocery stores and restaurants herself, gradually gaining experience in the food industry while studying.

But after finishing school, she still was not sure what kind of business she wanted to open.



One thing was clear: she loved baking.

“Its my dream. It’s been my plan for a long time, more than 10 years,” she says.

Rather than opening another coffee shop, she decided to focus on what she knew best. She had visited bakeries around Prague and noticed what she saw as a gap in the city’s food scene: there were few places specialising in Japanese-style baking.

Around six years ago, she decided that she wanted to fill that gap herself.

The result was Yaki-Pan, a small bakery built around Japanese pastries and flavours. Before opening, Hoan spent roughly a year and a half — and much of that time at home — testing recipes and trying to recreate the textures and flavours she associated with Japanese baking.

Getting there was not straightforward.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Yaki-Pan (@yakipan_brunch)

Learning to work with Czech ingredients

For Hoan, authenticity was essential. She wanted the pastries at Yaki-Pan to resemble Japanese baked goods as closely as possible, but she quickly discovered that one of the most important ingredients presented a major challenge: flour.

Japanese flour differs significantly from the flour commonly available in the Czech Republic. The differences affect the texture, consistency and ultimately the finished pastry.

“The flour here is not the same as when I learnt,” she says.

Instead of simply following recipes she had learned elsewhere, Hoan had to adapt them to local ingredients. She experimented with different combinations of flour and spent months trying to achieve the texture she was looking for.

Three years ago, she travelled to China to study Japanese baking under professionals. There, she was able to work with Japanese ingredients and gain further experience. Returning to Europe meant starting another process of adjustment.

She considered importing Japanese flour to the Czech Republic, but eventually found it difficult to maintain as a long-term solution. Instead, she continued experimenting with locally available ingredients.

“I needed to test for about two years at my home,” she says.

The process has not necessarily ended with the bakery’s opening. Hoan continues to work on her recipes and ingredients, looking for ways to improve the pastries while staying as close as possible to the style she wants to create.

A warm welcome from Prague

If Hoan was worried that Japanese flavours might be unfamiliar to Prague customers, the first day quickly put those concerns to rest.

When Yaki-Pan opened, she had not prepared significantly more food than usual. Within 30 minutes, the bakery had sold out.

The first two months were particularly busy, especially at weekends. Today, the customer base includes tourists, Japanese residents and visitors who have become regulars.

Japanese customers have also played an important role in validating Hoan’s approach, frequently complimenting her on how closely the pastries resemble those they know from Japan.

Among the most popular items is shio-pan, a Japanese-style bread known for its soft texture and salty flavour. At Yaki-Pan, the vegan version has become one of the bakery’s bestsellers and regularly sells out.

Hoan’s own favourite pastry, meanwhile, changes from day to day.

The bakery’s success has also brought an unexpected question. Some customers have asked why a Vietnamese woman decided to open a Japanese bakery.

For Hoan, the answer is simple. “It’s my dream,” she says. “I put all my energy into my recipes.”

Her background, she suggests, is less important than the work she has put into learning the craft and developing the food.

Building Yaki-Pan’s future

For now, Hoan is focused on the bakery she has already built. Yaki-Pan is run by Hoan and her husband, and her previous experience working in restaurants has helped her manage the busy days herself.

The couple are already thinking about the next stage. They hope to add outdoor seating next year and, eventually, open another location.

But there is no immediate rush to expand.

“Now I want to put all my energy into this one,” Hoan says.

There are also plans to introduce another type of matcha, giving customers more choice alongside the bakery’s existing drinks.

For a business that began as an idea Hoan carried with her for more than 10 years, Yaki-Pan remains very much a work in progress. The recipes continue to evolve, customers continue to discover Japanese-style baking, and Hoan is still searching for the ingredients and techniques that bring her original vision closest to reality.

World.title: Prague Taxi Driver Arrested After Taking CZK 3.5 Million Left in His Car
World.content:
A 21-year-old taxi driver in Prague has been arrested after allegedly taking a suitcase containing CZK 3.5 million in cash that passengers accidentally left in his car.

The money was recovered by police after the driver eventually admitted what he had done and told investigators where he had hidden it. He now faces up to five years in prison.

The incident happened in late July, although police only released details of the case several days later.



The passengers were a married couple who had taken a taxi to Václav Havel Airport in the early morning. They were heading on vacation and only realized after reaching the airport that one of their suitcases was still in the vehicle.

The couple immediately contacted the driver and asked him to bring the suitcase back. According to police, he initially agreed, but the luggage never appeared despite further calls and reminders.

The couple eventually reported the matter to police. Given the amount of money involved, forensic specialists from the Prague 1 police precinct joined the investigation.

Investigators quickly located the taxi and detained the driver. A search of the vehicle, however, produced no suitcase.

The 21-year-old initially denied that the passengers had left anything behind, telling police that he had not found any luggage in the car.

His account later changed.

After being placed in a cell, the man confessed and revealed where he had hidden the cash. Police officers and forensic specialists then located the money in a forest near Kladno.

The investigation also uncovered an attempt to destroy evidence. Near the cash, investigators found the burned remains of the suitcase. Police say the driver had taken the items to the forest, piled them together and set them on fire.

The driver remains under investigation and could face a prison sentence of up to five years if convicted.

World.title: Six Prague Rooftops and Terraces to Visit Before Summer Ends
World.content:
Summer is already moving on, and Prague’s rooftop season won’t last much longer.

August is the time to make the most of the city’s terraces, sunset views and outdoor events before they disappear for another year.

Here are six rooftops and terraces worth visiting before autumn arrives.



1. REASON at Masaryčka

Eleven floors above Masaryk Station, REASON offers one of Prague’s newest rooftop dining spots, with views over the city and the Zaha Hadid-designed Masaryčka development.

This summer, its terrace is also home to the seasonal Frerejean Frères Champagne Bar, serving champagne by the glass, cocktails, oysters and light bites. The menu includes THE REASON KIR, made with herbs grown on the rooftop.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and cocktails above Masaryčka.

2. W Prague – ABOVE Rooftop

ABOVE Rooftop at W Prague brings a Mediterranean feel to the top of Wenceslas Square.

The daily Mediterranean Hour runs from 5 to 6 PM, with two spritzes and a Taste of the Mediterranean platter for CZK 990. Oysters are also served from Thursday to Saturday, alongside a programme of summer events and pop-ups.

This summer: Mediterranean Hour, sunset drinks and oysters in the centre.

3. MINUTY Rooftop Terrace

The rooftop at Fairmont Golden Prague offers views across Pařížská, Letná and the city centre from nine floors up.

MINUTY Rooftop Terrace by Golden Eye focuses on champagne, oysters, caviar and cocktails. The terrace is seasonal and is expected to remain open until September, weather permitting.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and caviar with a view.

4. Sky Lounge 360°

For the view alone, Sky Lounge 360° is hard to beat. The rooftop looks across Prague’s historic centre and becomes livelier during the summer months, with DJs, sunset events and Prague Rooftop Festival activities.

It is more about drinks and atmosphere than a long dinner — a good option for an evening that starts at sunset and continues after dark.

This summer: Sunset events, DJs and panoramic views.

5. Casablanca Sky Bar

On the sixth floor of The President Hotel, Casablanca Sky Bar looks out over the Vltava and Prague skyline.

With DJs, cocktails and regular sunset events, it has more of a party atmosphere than a traditional hotel rooftop. It is also one of the venues taking part in the Prague Rooftop Festival.

This summer: DJs, cocktails and sunset parties above the Vltava.

6. Monkey Bar

Monkey Bar at Falkensteiner Hotel Prague is a quieter alternative, with a green, jungle-style terrace close to the main railway station.

Every Thursday until the end of August, the terrace hosts BBQ & Beats, combining barbecue, live music and summer drinks. Frozen margaritas are also on the menu.

For daytime plans, there is Jungle Brunch, including a bottomless mimosa option.

This summer: BBQ & Beats every Thursday through August.

World.title: Brazilian Summer Vibes Coming to Střelecký ostrov This Weekend
World.content:
Prague’s Střelecký ostrov will turn into a Brazilian-inspired summer spot this Friday and Saturday, with live music, DJs, food, drinks and a riverside atmosphere.

The two-day event will take place from 12 p.m. to 10 p.m. on both days, bringing Brazilian music and summer energy to one of the city’s most picturesque islands.

Visitors can expect live Brazilian music and DJ sets, alongside a selection of food and drinks. The menu will include wine, cheese, Czech dishes, cocktails, frozen margaritas and frozen daiquiris.

The event offers a relaxed way to spend the weekend in central Prague, with music, drinks and food overlooking the Vltava.

World.title: Czech Rivers Reach Record Lows as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Rivers and streams across the Czech Republic are experiencing exceptionally low flows as a prolonged drought continues to worsen, with several waterways approaching or reaching their lowest levels since records began.

According to the latest data from the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute, the vast majority of monitored rivers and streams are flowing well below their long-term averages.

Some of the country’s smallest watercourses have dried up completely, while critical conditions are emerging on several major rivers.



The Elbe is among the most affected. Its flow has fallen to one of the lowest levels ever recorded and is approaching the historic minimum for the entire period of regular observations.

The Vltava is in a somewhat better position in some sections because the reservoir system is being regulated to help stabilize water levels. But even the Vltava has reached an unprecedented low in České Budějovice, where the river is recording its lowest measured flow.

The effects of the drought are particularly visible at the Orlík Reservoir. As water levels have fallen sharply, the remains of a former hydroelectric power plant at Dubrava have emerged from beneath the reservoir.

The plant was built in 1929 but was demolished and flooded in the 1960s when the Orlík Reservoir was created. Its remains have now resurfaced as the reservoir continues to shrink.

The worsening conditions are not limited to rivers and reservoirs. Groundwater levels are also declining, affecting wells and raising concerns about the availability of water supplies in some areas.

Hydrologists are not expecting a significant improvement in the coming days. According to the medium-range weather forecast, there are currently no clear conditions that would bring a substantial recovery in river flows or groundwater levels.

World.title: Orbán fails to block return of billions in state assets as Hungary’s top court rejects Fidesz
World.content:
Hungary’s Constitutional Court has rejected a petition submitted by Fidesz challenging the constitutional amendment concerning public interest asset management foundations, known as KEKVAs.

The court dismissed the petition without examining its substance, ruling that it did not have the jurisdiction to review the challenged constitutional provision. The decision concerns the 16th amendment to Hungary’s Fundamental Law, adopted under the new Tisza government,

which abolished the public interest asset management foundations into which the previous Orbán government had transferred thousands of billions of forints in state assets.

Constitutional Court says it lacks jurisdiction

According to the Constitutional Court’s decision, the full bench rejected the Fidesz petition because the court lacks the necessary jurisdiction to carry out a substantive review of constitutional amendments. The issue stems from the Fourth Amendment to Hungary’s Fundamental Law in 2013, when

the Fidesz-led parliamentary majority removed the Constitutional Court’s power to conduct substantive constitutional reviews of amendments to the Fundamental Law.

Since then, the court has generally been limited to examining whether constitutional amendments were adopted in accordance with the required procedural rules, rather than assessing their substantive constitutional content.

Fidesz had argued in its petition that the disputed provision did not establish a general constitutional institution for the future. Instead, the party claimed that it introduced transitional rules specifically concerning identifiable foundations that were already operating when the amendment entered into force.

The Constitutional Court nevertheless concluded that it could not examine the substance of the challenge.

Two constitutional judges dissent

The decision was not unanimous. Outgoing Constitutional Court President Péter Polt and Constitutional Court Judge Tünde Handó issued separate opinions, arguing that the petition should have been examined on its merits.

Their dissent sets them apart from the majority of the court, which considered itself unable to rule substantively on the constitutional amendment.

The decision is particularly significant given the political and financial importance of the KEKVAs. Under the previous government, substantial amounts of public assets were transferred to such foundations, including assets connected to Hungarian universities and other public interest institutions.

Separate decision on Sulyok still pending

The Constitutional Court has also been asked to consider another politically significant constitutional amendment. According to 24.hu, the court has not yet ruled on the challenge seeking to annul the constitutional amendment that ended President Tamás Sulyok’s mandate. A decision on that case has been postponed.

World.title: Croatia wildfire forces at least 58 Hungarians to evacuate, one is injured: foreign minister monitors the situation
World.content:
At least 58 Hungarian citizens have been evacuated from areas affected by the devastating wildfire on Croatia’s Dalmatian coast, Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said on Friday.

Around 45 of those evacuated were accommodated in a sports hall, while another 13 were taken to a separate location. Croatian authorities and the Red Cross are providing them with assistance. The wildfire broke out near Omiš on Thursday evening and spread rapidly through dry vegetation and pine forest before reaching residential areas.

One Hungarian tourist injured

According to the Foreign Ministry, one Hungarian citizen was taken to a hospital in Split with a minor limb injury. No other Hungarian injuries are currently known. The Hungarian consular service remains in contact with the hospital and is monitoring the situation in case additional Hungarian citizens require medical assistance.

Hungarian consular officials spent the entire night responding to calls from citizens in the affected area and contacting people registered for consular protection. The exact number of Hungarians seeking consular assistance is not yet known, as officials are still contacting affected citizens individually to establish what help they require.

The ministry’s 24-hour consular emergency number is +36 80 36 80 36.

Seven Hungarians escaped on foot

The requests for assistance have mainly concerned evacuation, accommodation, safe onward travel and personal belongings or vehicles left behind.

Two Hungarian families, consisting of seven people in total, reportedly had to escape the affected area on foot. Their vehicles may have been destroyed by the fire, according to the Foreign Ministry.

Two Hungarian police officers currently serving in Zadar are also assisting with the consular response. Following consultations with Hungary’s Interior Ministry, they have been asked to remain in the area and continue supporting the operation. Their accommodation is being provided by Hungary’s embassy in Zagreb.

More information on the wildfire: Hungarian tourists flee as huge wildfire engulfs Croatian coast near Omiš

Minibuses sent from Hungary

Two minibuses have been sent from Hungary to collect the 13 Hungarian citizens evacuated to the second location. The Hungarian embassy in Zagreb and the Consular Service are currently contacting all known Hungarian citizens affected by the fire, assessing their individual needs and coordinating with Croatian authorities.

Where necessary, Hungarian officials will also help organise onward travel, accommodation and other consular assistance.

Fire contained, but firefighting continues

According to Anita Orbán, Croatian authorities have managed to prevent the fire from spreading further, although firefighting operations are continuing with the assistance of specialised aircraft. No further evacuations are currently known to have taken place.

The wildfire near Omiš forced around 1,000 residents and tourists to flee the affected area. At least 36 people were injured, seven of them in life-threatening condition.

The fire spread to residential areas overnight amid strong winds, causing significant disruption along the popular Dalmatian coast. Hungarians still in the affected region are advised to follow instructions from Croatian authorities and contact the Hungarian Consular Service if they require assistance.

World.title: Hungary’s new president Baka already more popular than predecessor Sulyok ever was, poll finds
World.content:
Hungary’s newly elected President András Baka has already achieved a level of public support that his predecessor, Tamás Sulyok, never managed to reach, according to a new poll commissioned by Telex.

The survey, commissioned by Telex and conducted by the 21 Research Centre on 11 and 12 August – the day Baka was elected and the following day – examined how well Hungarians knew the new president and whether they considered him suitable for the position.

The findings suggest that although Baka was largely unknown to the public before his nomination, he quickly won substantial support, particularly among voters of the governing Tisza Party.

Most Hungarians have heard of Baka

Some 84% of respondents had heard about Baka’s nomination as president. However, only 57% felt sufficiently familiar with him to say whether they considered him suitable for the role. Among those who expressed an opinion, 72% said Baka was suitable for the presidency, while 28% disagreed.

Across the entire sample, 41% considered him suitable for the post, compared with 16% who said he was unsuitable. The remaining respondents either did not know enough about him or declined to answer.

Baka’s initial level of recognition is difficult to compare directly with previous presidents because of the unusual circumstances surrounding his nomination. His name only became widely known after Prime Minister Péter Magyar posted a photograph of himself with Baka and Tisza politician Ruff Bálint on 5 August.

Before that, relatively few voters were likely to have remembered Baka as the former head of Hungary’s Supreme Court, a position from which he was removed in 2011.

András Baka. Photo: MTI

Baka starts with stronger ratings than Sulyok

Despite his relatively low public profile, Baka appears to be starting his presidency from a considerably stronger position than Sulyok ever enjoyed.

The 21 Research Centre’s earlier research found that Sulyok’s popularity remained relatively low throughout his presidency. By contrast, Baka has already attracted a significantly higher level of support just days after becoming president.

That does not necessarily put him among Hungary’s most popular political figures, however. Former presidents János Áder and Katalin Novák both reached much higher levels of popularity at their peaks. Still, Baka has already surpassed Sulyok’s highest recorded level of popularity, according to the polling data.

Tisza voters overwhelmingly back the new president

Baka’s support is strongly connected to current party preferences. Among Tisza voters, 69% consider him suitable for the presidency, while just 1% believe he is unsuitable. By comparison, only 8% of Fidesz voters consider Baka suitable, while 47% consider him unsuitable.

Among voters of other parties and those without a party preference, 20% consider him suitable and 17% unsuitable. A much larger 63% in this group either do not know enough about him or did not express an opinion.

The figures suggest that Baka has managed to attract some sympathy outside the Tisza camp, despite being nominated by the party at a particularly politically polarised moment.

At the same time, the researchers caution that Tisza voters were much more likely to have heard about Baka’s nomination and therefore much more likely to form an opinion about him. A large proportion of those who remain uninformed are Fidesz, Mi Hazánk or unaffiliated voters, meaning winning over these groups could prove considerably more difficult.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Is Baka independent or close to Tisza?

The poll also asked respondents how they viewed Baka politically. Some 37% considered him independent, while 15% believed he was close to Tisza. Another 47% could not decide, while just 1% considered him a Fidesz politician.

There is a clear link between perceptions of Baka’s independence and his perceived suitability for the presidency. Among those who consider Baka suitable, 88% see him as independent, while only 7% regard him as a Tisza-aligned figure.

Among those who consider him unsuitable, the picture is almost reversed: 76% believe he is close to Tisza, while just 9% consider him independent.

Have you read this? New President Baka could stand up firmly to PM Magyar – so why is the opposition attacking him so viciously?

Baka also tops the list of preferred presidential candidates

Respondents were also asked to name, without being given a list, the person they considered most suitable for the presidency. The question produced highly fragmented results, with 62% unable to name anyone. Among those who did provide a name, however, Baka came out on top, with 14% mentioning him. Sulyok was named by just 5%.

Other names receiving one or two percent of mentions included chess grandmaster Judit Polgár, Péter Márki-Zay, Ákos Hadházy, Viktor Orbán, Mi Hazánk’s presidential nominee Máté Tóth, Katalin Novák, historian Ignác Romsics, former justice minister Péter Bárándy, Ágnes Forsthoffer and András Schiffer.

Fidesz voters were more likely to mention Sulyok, Orbán, Schiffer and former justice minister Judit Varga, although they were generally less likely to name anyone than Tisza voters.

The fact that Sulyok received just 5% of spontaneous mentions is also notable. According to the analysis, this suggests that even among Fidesz voters, relatively few appear to have a strong personal attachment to the outgoing president. Much of their opposition to his removal may therefore be connected to the procedure itself rather than support for Sulyok personally.

World.title: Hungarian tourists flee as huge wildfire engulfs Croatian coast near Omiš
World.content:
A major wildfire has swept through the Croatian Dalmatian coast near Omiš, forcing around 1,000 residents and tourists to evacuate overnight – including Hungarian holidaymakers.

The blaze broke out on Thursday evening near Lokva Rogoznica, south of Omiš, and rapidly spread through dry vegetation and pine forest amid strong and changing winds. The flames reached residential areas and parts of Omiš, destroying homes, cars and other property.

The situation was described by Croatia’s national fire chief as one of the most serious wildfires in the country’s history.

Dozens injured as flames approach Omiš

The fire started at around 8.20 PM on Thursday near the main coastal road. Strong winds quickly pushed the flames through the dry vegetation and forest, eventually bringing the fire into the Omiš area.

According to the latest information from Split hospital, 36 people required medical treatment, with 14 remaining in hospital. Seven of those injured were in life-threatening condition, while most of the casualties suffered burns or smoke inhalation.

The fire also caused significant damage to property as flames reached residential buildings and vehicles.

The rapidly changing wind has made the firefighters’ work particularly difficult, with the flames spreading in different directions. Some parts of Omiš were also left without electricity overnight.

Požar koji je počeo u Lokvi Rogoznici stigao je u noći do Omiša a u ranim jutarnjim satima očekuje se dolazak kanadera. pic.twitter.com/bWSy4Opzgb — HINA (@Agencija_HINA) August 14, 2026

Nearly 300 firefighters battle the blaze

By Friday morning, 286 firefighters and 93 vehicles were involved in the firefighting operation. Crews were sent from several Croatian counties and Zagreb to reinforce local teams.

Four Canadair CL-415 firefighting aircraft were also deployed in the early hours of Friday, while a Croatian Navy vessel was placed on standby in case a sea evacuation became necessary.

Emergency accommodation centres were opened in Omiš, Dugi Rat, Makarska and Split. Around 1,000 people spent the night at the sports hall in Omiš, while people from the most endangered areas were evacuated both by road and by boat.

The main coastal road, the Jadranska Magistrala, was closed on the affected section, as was part of the Omiš bypass towards Makarska. The evacuations and road closures caused major traffic congestion in the town.

Hungarian tourists among those forced to flee

The wildfire has also affected Hungarian holidaymakers staying in the area. Hungary’s Foreign Ministry said that Hungarian nationals known to the consular service and those who had contacted the service were currently safe. Hungarian officials reportedly liaised directly with Croatian authorities overnight to help Hungarian citizens leave the affected areas safely.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said the situation was being monitored continuously and that the Hungarian consular service remained in contact with affected Hungarian citizens and local authorities.

Hungarians currently in the area are being urged to follow instructions from Croatian authorities and contact the Hungarian Consular Service immediately if necessary.

The ministry’s 24-hour consular emergency number is +36 80 36 80 36.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Fire continues to threaten the area

The blaze has been particularly difficult to contain because of the strong, shifting winds and extremely dry conditions. Reuters also reported that the fire forced hundreds to evacuate and that emergency services provided shelter for around 1,000 people.

Authorities continue to work to prevent the flames from spreading further around Omiš and the surrounding settlements. For tourists still in the region, the authorities’ evacuation instructions should be followed without delay, particularly as the direction and intensity of the fire can change rapidly.

World.title: Warning at Lake Balaton: Experts urge swimmers to take precautions
World.content:
Algae levels in Lake Balaton have continued to rise, with the highest concentration recorded in the Keszthely Basin. Experts are now urging swimmers in the area to take extra precautions and shower after bathing due to the growing dominance of filamentous cyanobacteria.

According to the latest measurements by the HUN-REN Balaton Limnological Research Institute, the increase in algal biomass that began in the second half of July has continued in recent weeks. However, significant differences remain between the various parts of the lake.

Algae levels highest in the Keszthely Basin

Measurements taken on 10 August 2026 found the highest a-chlorophyll concentration in the Keszthely Basin, at 80 micrograms per litre (µg/l), according to the institute.

The Szigliget Basin followed with 54 µg/l, while 32 µg/l was measured in the Szemes Basin. The water was considerably clearer in the Siófok Basin, with concentrations of 19 µg/l recorded near Tihany and 21 µg/l near Balatonfűzfő.

This means a clear west-to-east gradient in algal biomass continues to be visible along the lake. The pattern was also confirmed by the latest Sentinel-2 satellite imagery taken on 9 August.

Filamentous cyanobacteria are taking over

Researchers have also observed a significant change in the composition of the lake’s algal community.

The algae previously found in large quantities have declined considerably, while filamentous cyanobacteria have become dominant across the entire length of Lake Balaton.

One species in particular, Raphidiopsis raciborskii, has become widespread. The species is characteristic of late-summer conditions and is capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen. Researchers have also noted the presence of Planktothrix, which cannot fix atmospheric nitrogen.

Despite the increased algal biomass, the situation may not look alarming to people on the beaches. Unlike earlier in the summer, the algae are not currently accumulating in large visible patches in sheltered areas. Instead, they are mostly distributed evenly throughout the water column.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Experts advise swimmers to shower after bathing

Although there is currently no visible mass accumulation of algae, researchers are urging people swimming in the Keszthely Basin to take precautions.

Experts recommend showering after every swim in the Keszthely Basin.

Researchers stress that monitoring will remain particularly important for the rest of the summer, as a considerable part of the bathing season is still ahead.

It’s important to note that the latest findings do not mean that Lake Balaton’s beaches are unsafe across the board. However, the rising algal biomass and growing dominance of filamentous cyanobacteria mean that swimmers in the most affected areas should pay particular attention to the latest guidance from researchers.

World.title: Türkiye-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan defense pact: what could it mean for Hungary?
World.content:
The Türkiye-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan defense pact signed in Mecca could reshape security cooperation in the Middle East, bringing together a NATO member, a nuclear-armed state and one of the Gulf’s most influential powers. Hungary is not a party to the agreement and faces no direct obligations under it, but Türkiye’s NATO membership and Budapest’s increasingly close defence ties with Ankara mean the pact could have indirect consequences for Hungary.

According to Anadolu Agency, Türkiye’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday that the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement was designed to strengthen joint military capabilities and was not directed against any particular country. The agreement was signed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on 7 August.

The three countries plan to establish high-level political and military coordination mechanisms involving defence and foreign ministers, chiefs of general staff and armed forces commanders. Cooperation is expected to expand gradually from command-post and field exercises to joint operations involving land, naval and air forces, air defence and unmanned systems.

Türkiye-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan defense pact creates no direct obligation for Hungary

For Hungary, the most important point is that the agreement does not extend any new defence commitment to Budapest.

Hungary is a NATO member, but it is not part of the Mecca agreement. If Saudi Arabia or Pakistan were attacked, Hungary would therefore have no obligation to assist either country under the new pact.

The situation could become more complicated if Türkiye itself became directly involved in a regional conflict.

NATO’s Article 5 states that an armed attack against one member within the treaty’s geographical scope is considered an attack against all. However, this does not mean that every conflict involving Turkish forces automatically becomes a NATO conflict. NATO’s founding treaty defines where Article 5 applies, while individual allies decide what form of assistance they consider necessary if collective defence is activated.

An attack on Turkish territory could therefore potentially become a NATO issue involving Hungary, while an attack on Turkish forces operating elsewhere in the Middle East would not automatically have the same effect.

This distinction is crucial when assessing the Hungarian implications of the new arrangement.

If you missed it – Deterrence needs a balance sheet: The rise of Europe’s defence finance ecosystem

Türkiye insists the agreement will complement NATO

Ankara has repeatedly stressed that the new mechanism is not intended to compete with NATO.

Turkish officials describe the agreement as a regional security structure that complements existing alliances. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has nevertheless compared its mutual-defence principle technically with NATO’s Article 5: an attack against one participant is to be regarded as an attack against all three.

That makes Türkiye’s role particularly significant. It is now connected simultaneously to NATO’s collective-defence system and to an emerging Middle Eastern mutual-defence framework.

For Budapest, this could matter in NATO consultations if Türkiye were required to commit substantial forces to a crisis in the Middle East. It could also influence Ankara’s military priorities and the capabilities it makes available for NATO missions.

Péter Magyar with Mark Rutte and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. Photo: Péter Magyar/Facebook

Hungary has unusually close defence ties with Türkiye

Hungary has developed increasingly close military and defence-industrial relations with Türkiye in recent years.

The Hungarian Defence Forces described Türkiye in 2025 as a recognised military partner and highlighted plans to expand cooperation in joint exercises, training and defence-industry capabilities. Senior Hungarian and Turkish military leaders have also repeatedly described their bilateral relationship as a strategic partnership.

The industrial relationship is becoming increasingly important as well.

Hungarian technology group 4iG signed agreements with Turkish defence companies Nurol Makina and Aselsan in December 2025. The cooperation covers the Hungarian Gidrán armoured vehicle programme and plans for a Hungarian-based partnership in areas including military communications, counter-drone technology and air-defence systems.

Those areas closely overlap with the priorities identified in the Türkiye-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan defense pact, which include unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence, air defence, joint production and technology cooperation.

This creates a potential economic angle for Hungary. If the three-country framework generates major new defence programmes or orders for Turkish manufacturers, companies operating within Turkish-Hungarian industrial partnerships could eventually benefit. There is, however, no announced Hungarian participation in the Mecca agreement or its defence projects at present.

As we wrote before: Here’s what Péter Magyar said about his first NATO summit

Hungary has also been seeking stronger defence relations with Saudi Arabia.

Defence Minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky met Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman in 2025 to discuss military and defence-industry cooperation. Talks with Saudi Arabian Military Industries also explored possible cooperation in defence technology, research and development.

This means Budapest already maintains defence-related relationships with two of the agreement’s three participants.

For Hungary, the Mecca pact is therefore less about acquiring new military commitments and more about watching how a close NATO ally and important defence-industrial partner develops a second security network outside Europe.

If the agreement remains primarily a framework for exercises, technology and deterrence, its effects on Hungary may be limited. If it evolves into a functioning military alliance capable of deploying forces during major Middle Eastern crises, however, its implications for NATO planning, Hungarian-Turkish defence cooperation and regional stability could become considerably more important.

If you missed it – PM Magyar at NATO summit: “Ukraine is the victim, Russia the brutal aggressor”, announces bilateral meeting

Why closer cooperation between major military powers matters for Hungary

For Hungary, the significance of the Türkiye-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan defense pact goes beyond the question of whether Budapest has any formal obligations under it. As a medium-sized European country whose security depends heavily on NATO’s collective defence system, Hungary has a clear interest in maintaining close relations with states that possess substantial military capabilities, advanced defence industries and the ability to contribute to regional stability.

Türkiye is particularly important in this respect. The Hungarian Defence Forces have described the country as one of NATO’s strongest military powers, highlighting its operational experience, modern military technology and large domestic defence industry. Budapest and Ankara have consequently placed increasing emphasis on joint exercises, training and defence-industrial cooperation. According to the Hungarian Defence Forces, strengthening military-to-military relations and expanding defence-industry capabilities have become important elements of the partnership.

From a Hungarian security perspective, cooperation among militarily capable states can be valuable in several ways. It can improve deterrence, accelerate the development and production of modern weapons systems, and create larger networks for military logistics, maintenance and technological development. NATO itself places considerable emphasis on multinational capability development and interoperability, arguing that modern armed forces must be able to communicate, deploy and operate effectively together before a crisis develops into an armed conflict.

This is especially relevant at a time when European countries are being asked to strengthen their own military capabilities and defence industries. NATO’s 2026 defence policy continues to emphasise higher investment, greater production capacity, innovation and stronger cooperation between governments and defence companies.

For Hungary, therefore, closer cooperation between Türkiye and other major regional military powers could potentially create opportunities beyond diplomacy. If it leads to new joint technologies, larger production programmes or greater Turkish defence-industrial capacity, some of those benefits could eventually reach Hungary through existing Hungarian-Turkish projects.

At the same time, closer military cooperation does not automatically translate into greater security. New regional blocs can also create competing strategic commitments or draw participating states more deeply into conflicts. For Budapest, the favourable scenario would therefore be one in which the new pact strengthens deterrence and defence capabilities without weakening Türkiye’s NATO commitments or increasing instability in the Middle East.

Seen from this perspective, the development of the pact matters to Hungary not because Budapest is expected to join it, but because Hungarian security increasingly depends not only on its own military modernisation, but also on the strength, technological sophistication and reliability of the countries with which it cooperates.
