World.title: Popular Lebanese restaurant Al Beiruti to open in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Al Beiruti, a popular Lebanese restaurant, is set to build its first Iraqi branch in Iraq Mall in Baghdad, adding another significant regional dining name to the capital’s growing restaurant scene.

The Baghdad inauguration will be the next chapter of Al Beiruti’s regional development, after previous launches in Jordan and Qatar, as well as its established presence in the UAE.

The restaurant announced that its Iraq Mall restaurant is about to open, with a local franchise arrangement handling the expansion.

Al Beiruti has become a renowned location for Lebanese food in the Middle East, providing both classic dishes and a more modern restaurant experience.

The menu includes Lebanese favorites, including manakish, fattoush, hummus, baba ghanouj, and grilled halloumi, as well as shawarma, wraps, and mixed grills. Larger meals include steak, chicken escalope, and grilled salmon.

Al Beiruti joins a growing number of international and regional food and beverage companies in Baghdad, as new malls and commercial expansions change the city’s retail and entertainment markets.

Iraq Mall has emerged as a focal point of that expansion, drawing new restaurants, boutiques, and entertainment ideas as consumer spending and private-sector investment continue to rise in the capital.

World.title: Baghdad and Erbil agree on unified digital customs system across Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Baghdad and Erbil have agreed to fully adopt the digital ASYCUDA customs system across border crossings, with non-oil border earnings shared equally by the federal and Kurdistan regional governments.

The deal is a significant step toward standardizing customs processes across Iraq and addressing long-standing disagreements over border revenues and claimed import quantities.

ASYCUDA, designed by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), digitizes customs declarations, payments, and clearing processes, allowing authorities to better monitor products entering the nation and the income they earn.

Linking customs operations to Iraq’s banking and electronic payment systems may help limit the potential for underreporting, revenue leakage, and corruption at border crossings.

The deal comes as Iraq’s Finance Ministry and Central Bank work to digitize customs, payments, and government financial data in collaboration with UNCTAD.

A combined computerized customs system for Baghdad and Erbil might give more accurate revenue data while resolving one of the two governments’ ongoing financial issues.

The change is also significant for Iraq’s overall economy.

More open and uniform customs processes might facilitate cross-border commerce, boost governmental revenues, and enhance the business climate as Iraq pursues more foreign investment and closer integration with international markets.

World.title: Iraq’s Chief Justice Faiq Zidan meets Syrian President Al-Sharaa in Damascus
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zidan met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus on Thursday, marking another high-level Iraqi outreach to a neighboring Arab state as Baghdad seeks to bolster regional relations under rising security problems.

Al-Sharaa welcomed Zidan and an Iraqi delegation to the People’s Palace, which also included Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais.

According to the Syrian president, the talks focused on extending judicial and legal cooperation between Iraq and Syria, as well as resolving mutual concerns.

The visit also resulted in more practical conversations among the two nations’ judicial officials. Iraqi and Syrian authorities agreed to set up joint judicial committees to continue working on cases involving Syrian prisoners and other cross-border legal issues.

Zidan’s visit is crucial as he is one of the most prominent persons in Iraq’s state institutions, and it coincides with Baghdad’s increased diplomatic, security, and judicial interaction with its neighbors.

The Damascus meetings come after a separate Iraqi security group visited Riyadh, where senior military official Abdul Amir al-Shammari met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman.

Zidan had also just visited Ankara as part of a larger Iraqi effort to build ties with Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Turkey.

That approach has become more urgent in light of the regional escalation involving Iran-backed Iraqi forces.

In late July, the United States and Saudi Arabia conducted synchronized attacks against locations used by Iran-aligned organizations in Iraq, after Riyadh accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones against Saudi energy infrastructure.

The incident put Baghdad under strong pressure to prevent armed organizations from exploiting Iraqi territory to launch assaults on neighboring nations and also highlighted the potential that militia activity may harm Iraq’s improved ties with Arab governments.

Against this setting, Zidan’s encounter with Al-Sharaa is significant beyond regular court cooperation.

Iraq and Syria share a long border and confront shared concerns such as terrorism, organized crime, prisoners, and cross-border security. Baghdad also has a strategic interest in preserving stable ties with Damascus, as Iraq strives to boost regional connections and prevent unrest from spilling over its borders.

Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s administration sees recent diplomatic efforts as part of a larger effort to strengthen Iraq’s ties with its neighbors while keeping the nation out of the developing conflict between Iran and its regional adversaries.

Baghdad has increasingly emphasized that choices on security, armament, and relations with neighboring governments must be made by Iraqi official authorities rather than armed groupings.

The travels to Damascus and Riyadh therefore convey an essential message: although Iran-aligned militias have exacerbated tensions between Iraq and certain of its neighbors, Iraqi official institutions are working directly with those nations to restore cooperation and avoid further escalation.

Strengthening judicial, diplomatic, and security ties with Syria, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey might serve as an essential regional buffer for Iraq as it seeks to safeguard its sovereignty, control armed groups, and avoid being drawn further into the region’s crises.

World.title: Iraq’s Al-Shammari visits Riyadh to meet Saudi Defense Minister
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A top Iraqi security team has traveled to Riyadh for meetings with Saudi Arabia’s leadership, as Baghdad and the Kingdom work to improve security and military cooperation after weeks of heightened tensions in Iraq involving Iran-backed militias.

First Lieutenant General Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman on Thursday to discuss military cooperation, regional developments, and increased coordination between the two nations.

According to reports from the visit, the conversations included cross-border drone concerns, air defense, and intelligence collaboration.

The conference is especially significant in light of the combined US-Saudi attacks on Iran-linked militia locations in Iraq on July 29.

Washington and Riyadh said the operation targeted Iran-backed terrorists’ weapons and logistical facilities in response to a series of drone assaults on Saudi oil installations that they said originated in Iraqi territory.

The strikes drastically escalated tensions between Baghdad and Riyadh, highlighting the Iraqi government’s problems in preventing armed groups from exploiting its territory to target neighboring nations.

Thursday’s visit indicates that both parties are now attempting to move beyond that conflict via direct military and intelligence collaboration.

Prince Khalid underlined Saudi Arabia’s commitment to Iraq’s security, stability, and economic growth, identifying it as an essential neighbor with whom the Kingdom has strong political and social relations.

The meetings in Riyadh follow Saudi intelligence head Khalid bin Ali al-Humaidan’s visit to Baghdad last week, during which he met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and reiterated an offer for the Iraqi leader to visit Saudi Arabia.

Baghdad’s security cooperation with Riyadh has grown more vital as the government seeks to prevent Iran-backed militias from drawing Iraq into a larger regional conflict.

Al-Zaidi has frequently said that Iraqi soil should not be used to attack other nations and has stepped up efforts for weaponry to be put solely under state control.

The most recent Iraqi trip to Riyadh symbolizes more than just normal defense diplomacy. It is part of a joint effort by Baghdad and Saudi Arabia to restore security trust after the July escalation and prevent militia activities from dragging the two neighboring nations into conflict.

World.title: Rare blind fish found in underground river in Iraq’s Anbar desert
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security and environmental teams have discovered a fascinating underground water system deep under the dry Anbar desert, where rare eyeless fish thrive in total darkness.

The location is in the Al-Khasfa region near Haditha, and crews traveled through a remote desert cave and sinkhole system to access running groundwater hundreds of meters under the surface.

The expedition’s footage shows little, pale fish moving in the subterranean water in the lack of sunshine.

The fish have evolved to live in darkness by losing their eyes and pigmentation, giving them a characteristic white-to-pink look.

The crew traveled more than 500 meters into the cave system despite challenging terrain and low oxygen levels.

The difference between above- and underground has piqued interest: underneath what seems to be an isolated and very arid stretch of western Iraqi desert, there is flowing freshwater and a specialized ecology.

Initial investigations have also suggested a link between the subterranean water system and the Euphrates basin, with the watercourse possibly running for a long distance under the desert.

However, environmental experts have highlighted that the blind fish themselves are not a novel finding.

Qais Najeh, the chairman of the Anbar Environment Directorate, stated that experts first confirmed the occurrence of eyeless fish in Al-Khasfa in 2010.

Similar fish have also been discovered in subterranean water near the Sheik Hadid mausoleum in Haditha district.

According to experts, the fish may grow to be roughly 49 millimeters long and survive in rather steady groundwater temperatures ranging from 20 to 22 degrees Celsius.

Their lack of vision and pigmentation are adaptations to generations of living in perpetually dark subterranean habitats.

The recent mission is nonetheless noteworthy because it has refocused attention on one of Iraq’s least-known natural ecosystems, perhaps allowing scientists to better research the subterranean water network, its geology, and the creatures that rely on it.

The fish’s severely limited environment renders it vulnerable.

Changes in groundwater levels, pollution, or human intervention might endanger a population that has acclimated to highly particular subsurface circumstances.

The Al-Khasfa location offers a unique dimension to Anbar, a region best known for its wide western desert and the Euphrates.

Hidden under that terrain lies an environment few Iraqis have ever seen: flowing subterranean water that feeds fish who have evolved to survive their entire lives without sunshine.

World.title: Israel reopens once-closed West Bank settlement
World.content:
GANIM – Israel officially reopened the West Bank settlement of Ganim on Thursday, more than 20 years after it withdrew from the community, in a move emblematic of the current government’s policy of rapid settlement expansion.

The smell of freshly-poured asphalt hung in the air above Ganim’s new and only street, where future residents and their families — who had come to help with the move — smiled at the sight of their pre-fabricated homes.

“A month ago there was nothing here. A rocky mountain, barely any trees, barely any shade. We’re arriving now,” new resident Reut Baran, 35, told AFP in front of her new home.

In a nearby truck, dozens of brand new air conditioning units still in their boxes were waiting to be installed.

Matan Berkovitch, a 25-year-old who moved into the new settlement with his wife and child, said he was satisfied with the government’s policy towards settlements as he looked around a brand new home just connected to the electric grid.

“I’m happy to be part of a time like this where there are ministers in the government who support and guide us in the right direction and know how to get things done properly,” he said.

Berkovitch’s mother Carmit, who came from Jerusalem to move him in, said another one of her sons would soon study at the religious school in the settlement, and expressed pride at their active part in the settler movement.

“Here, this is the Land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said at the ceremony, after arriving by helicopter.

Ganim is one of four Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank that Israel evacuated under former prime minister Ariel Sharon’s disengagement plan in 2005.

The move came partly because of their isolated location in the north of the territory among many Palestinian cities and villages.

Under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, settlement construction and expansion have soared, including with the official re-establishment of three of the four evacuated communities — Ganim, Sa-Nur and Homesh.

In Ganim, about two dozen pre-fabricated homes have already been installed, while steamrollers and other construction machinery busily created new space for future houses on the hillside on Thursday.

About a hundred people from Israel and other West Bank settlements attended the ceremony, including Katz and Yossi Dagan, head of the Israeli authority in charge of settlements in the northern West Bank.

“The era of evacuation is over — from here, we only build,” Dagan said.

In the valley below, Palestinians who spoke to AFP feared Ganim’s construction would make their lives harder, or even mean eventual displacement.

On both sides of the road leading to the settlement from Israel, the army has demolished stores in recent days and blocked several dirt roads to Palestinian communities with piles of rubble.

Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the territory, which are illegal under international law, among some three million Palestinians.

Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased dramatically since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip.

World.title: Carrick urges Man Utd to push for more signings to boost title bid
World.content:
London – Michael Carrick has urged Manchester United to splash the cash to keep pace with their Premier League title rivals.

United have spent around £85 million ($114 million) on Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Karl Darlow since the end of last season.

But that outlay pales in comparison to some of United’s fellow title contenders, with Manchester City, Arsenal and Chelsea all paying huge fees for high-profile signings.

Carrick knows United need more quality and depth if they are to challenge for a first English title since 2013, while also competing in the Champions League.

Remarkably, United have never spent more than £89.5 million on a single player — the fee paid for Paul Pogba in 2016.

And ahead of his first season as permanent United boss after a successful interim spell last term, Carrick called on the club’s hierarchy to push for more new recruits.

“I think we’ve done really good business and we’ve got really some top, top, top players,” Carrick told reporters on Thursday.

“We’re delighted with that. We always want to improve. We want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that. That never stops.”

Carrick led United to a third-place finish in the Premier League after he replaced the sacked Ruben Amorim.

But with United so far spending less than promoted sides Coventry and Ipswich, some fans are becoming restless as their Premier League opener at Hull on August 22 looms into view.

“Money’s money, I get that. It’s still about the football, and that’s where the competition lies,” Carrick said.

“Certainly the situation is what it is as well, whether that’s finances or whatever. For now, we’ve got to make the most of it, but we’ve got to keep pushing and push everything and every boundary that we can to be able to win again.”

Asked why United were not spending on the level of other clubs, Carrick added: “To be honest, I haven’t got the answers for that. We’re working with pushing everything that we can to make the best of it.”

Having spent last season on loan with Barcelona, Marcus Rashford is back at United this week after returning from the World Cup.

Barcelona declined their option to buy the 28-year-old England forward and questions remain over his United future.

“He’s our player, and he’s a good player and he gives us something a little bit different in the group,” he said.

“Marcus can offer us so much. He has done, and he can do again, so in that respect it’s quite exciting.”

Several United players have backed the team to dethrone Arsenal as champions and the understated Carrick wouldn’t rule out a title push.

“We’ve definitely got the potential to achieve something really special,” he said.

“I’m not hiding from the fact, and we should aim to do that, but I can’t give you a definite answer on that.

“It’s certainly what we’re pushing to do because we have to, because that’s the club we are.”

World.title: Leicester’s Thai owners put troubled club up for sale: reports
World.content:
London – Former Premier League champions Leicester have been put up for sale by the club’s Thai owners, according to reports on Thursday.

Just 10 years after their fairytale Premier League title triumph, Leicester will play in English football’s third tier for only the second time in their history this season.

The Foxes, who won their first FA Cup in 2021, have endured a dire period featuring successive relegations from the Premier League in 2025 and the Championship in 2026.

Last season, they were docked six points after breaching the Football League’s profit and sustainability rules, sparking their slump into League One.

A BBC report on Thursday said Leicester’s Thai owners King Power — run by the Srivaddhanaprabha family — have commissioned a leading US investment bank to help find a buyer, with the club’s assets said to be listed at more than £200 million ($269 million).

King Power bought Leicester in a £35 million deal in 2010.

Aiyawatt Srivaddhanaprabha took over as Leicester chairman following the death of his father Vichai in a helicopter crash outside the club’s King Power stadium in 2019.

Following last season’s relegation, Aiyawatt said he should shoulder the “blame” for the club’s predicament but also stressed the “structure will change”.

Russell Martin’s side kick off their promotion bid with a trip to Notts County on Saturday.

World.title: Gandhi's letter to India, as told through TOI
World.content:
A fast unto death announced by

in Puneâs Yerawada jail in 1932 was to change the course of Indiaâs political history. Imprisoned for the Civil Disobedience Movement, Gandhi announced the fast in a Sept 13 letter to British PM Ramsay MacDonald that was shared with the press.

His aim was to oppose a separate electorate for Dalits, proposed under the Communal Award of August 1932.

âI have to resist your decision with my life,â Gandhi wrote, saying his fast would begin on Sept 20. âAs a man of religion that I hold myself to be, I have no other course left open to me.â

The award classified Dalits as a minority whose representatives would be elected only by Dalit voters, just as Muslims, Christians and Sikhs would elect their own representatives. Gandhi believed this would divide Hindu society; BR Ambedkar supported it as a safeguard for Dalit political representation

Gandhi acknowledged that he might be wrong. If his judgement was âwarpedâ, he wrote, his death would be âa penance for my errorâ and would lift the burden from those who had âchild-like faithâ in his wisdom.

His week-long fast led to the Poona Pact, negotiated by Madan Mohan Malaviya and Ambedkar and accepted by Gandhi. It abandoned a separate electorate but reserved seats for Dalits within the general electorate, becoming a milestone in Dalit representation and a precursor to reservations for SCs and STs in independent India.

Suspending Satyagraha

Gandhi also used a letter to the press to announce the suspension of Satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act.





Writing on July 21, 1919, he asked satyagrahis to âswallow the bitter pillâ and halt their campaign after protests had turned violent.

The act allowed the colonial government to detain political prisoners for two years without trial. Gandhiâs campaign against it, launched in March 1919, was his first nationwide political mobilisation after returning from South Africa. Despite his appeals for peaceful hartals, fasts and prayers, violence erupted in several places.

Gandhi was prevented from entering Punjab and arrested; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on April 13 made the situation explosive.

Attacks on police stations and railway property, and deadly clashes between protesters and authorities, led him to pause civil disobedience.

For Gandhi, non-violence was not merely tactical. Amid divisions within Congress and Subhas Chandra Boseâs different course, he wrote from Sevagram on July 21, 1941

In the July letter, published under the headline âSATYAGRAHA. Civil Resistance Suspendedâ, Gandhi disclosed that the governor of Bombay had conveyed âa grave warningâ from the Government of India that renewed civil disobedience could threaten public security.

Writing from Mani Bhavan in Bombay, Gandhi conceded that the suspension was painful. Yet he remained unyielding on the law: âSatyagrahi will pay for its removal with their lives if it cannot be removed by lesser means.â He also warned the Raj: âIf my occasional Civil Resistance be a lighted match, Rowlatt legislationâ¦is a thousand matches scattered throughout India.â

For Gandhi, non-violence was not merely tactical. Amid divisions within Congress and Subhas Chandra Boseâs different course, he wrote from Sevagram on July 21, 1941: âWith me, no doubt non-violence is an end in itself, though it is also a means for the attainment of the freedom of the country.â

A year earlier, he had underlined its voluntary nature: âNon-violence cannot be imposed upon anyone. It has to come from within.

â

The South Africa Years

Gandhiâs letters to the editor predated his emergence as a leader of Indiaâs freedom struggle. During his 21 years in South Africa, where he first used Satyagraha as a method of resistance, he repeatedly drew attention to discriminatory laws against Indians

In a Dec 19, 1901 letter, he described the restrictions in the Transvaal, where Indians could not hold land, were required to live and trade only in designated areas, and were barred from footpaths.

In the Orange River Colony, he wrote, an Indian could not even enter without special permission, except as a domestic servant or labourer.

After returning to India, he continued to write about the poor conditions of Indians legally settled in South Africa. In an Aug 29, 1919 letter, he blamed the âgreedy Europeans of Natalâ for importing Indian indentured labour at miserably low wages while ignoring local Zulu workers, all in pursuit of âenormous profitsâ.

Cow Slaughter And Eid

Gandhiâs correspondence also addressed social fractures, particularly Hindu-Muslim relations. In a 1919 letter written around Bakrid, he recounted a conversation with Maulana Abdul Bari of Lucknowâs Firangi Mahal, a prominent supporter of the Khilafat Movement.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Gandhi quoted the Maulana as saying: âIslam will fall to pieces if it ever takes and never givesâ¦. If we take from you, we must give to you.â Abdul Bari had urged his followers to abstain from cow slaughter.

On Bakrid, he sent Gandhi a telegram: âIn celebration of Hindu-Muslim unity, no cow sacrifices in Firangi-Mahal this Bakri-Id.â

More than a century later, these letters are more than historical records. They reveal Gandhi not only as a politician confronting colonial power but as a public figure wrestling with representation, violence, communal division and moral responsibility. Through TOIâs pages, his words travelled beyond the immediate battles of the freedom struggle, leaving an intimate record of how he tried to shape public opinion â and India itself.

World.title: Karnataka BJP MLA's daughter booked for 'assaulting' woman cop over temple entry queue
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The daughter of Karnataka BJP MLA B Suresh Gowda was booked for allegedly abusing and assaulting a woman police sub-inspector following an argument at a temple in Mandya district in Karnataka, police said on Friday.

The incident took place on August 12 at the Maramma Temple in Ukkada village during Bhima Amavasya celebrations, news agency PTI reported.

According to the complaint filed by the woman police officer, she was deployed at the temple for security duty when

, the MLA's daughter, allegedly sought permission to enter the sanctum without waiting in the queue.

The police officer alleged that she asked Aishwarya to wait to avoid inconvenience to other devotees.

According to the complaint, Aishwarya then identified herself as the daughter of an MLA and questioned why she was being stopped.

The argument allegedly escalated, with Aishwarya abusing the officer and hitting her on the head. The complainant also alleged that she was threatened and prevented from performing her official duties.

Based on the complaint, the Kyathanahalli police registered an FIR under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including charges related to assaulting a public servant, causing simple hurt, intentional insult and criminal intimidation, a senior police officer said.





However, the case has taken another turn, with Aishwarya filing a counter-complaint against the police officer.

Police said an inquiry into her allegations has been initiated, but no FIR has been registered on the basis of her complaint so far. Further action will depend on the findings of the inquiry.

Speaking to reporters, Tumakuru Rural MLA B Suresh Gowda apologised for his daughter's conduct and said that anyone found guilty should face legal consequences.

"If she has committed a mistake, it is wrong. Whoever has done the mistake should face the consequences under the law," he said.

The

legislator said his daughter had visited the temple with her two young children and had requested permission to enter briefly because waiting in the queue could have caused inconvenience.

He also claimed that another person had been allowed to enter ahead of her, prompting his daughter to question the decision.

While acknowledging that the argument had escalated, Gowda said his daughter should have shown greater restraint, particularly because she comes from a political family.

"I apologise on behalf of my daughter if she has made a mistake," he said.

The MLA also called for a departmental inquiry into the incident and urged authorities to take action against anyone found responsible.

âLal Qila ta nishana hove gaâ: Delhi HC bomb threat ahead of Independence Day mentions khaki-clad attackers

The US military has reportedly lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones during its war with Iran, representing about 25 per cent of its fleet. The Reaper is used for surveillance and targeted strikes and can cost between $30 million and $50 million, depending on its sensors and weapons, according to the US Air Force.

The losses could therefore represent more than $1.3 billion in equipment costs, according to three US officials familiar with Pentagon data, quoted by the Washington Post.

The Supreme Court said students had a right to protest peacefully and stayed any coercive action against NALSAR students or faculty by the BCI or state Bar Council.

World.content:

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

For years, India has spoken about the enormous amount of energy locked inside its agricultural residue, cattle dung and organic waste. The challenge has been turning that potential into a commercially viable industry.Now, the government is making one of its most serious attempts yet.The Union Cabinet on August 6 approved GOBARdhan, the National Circular Bioenergy Scheme, with a total outlay of Rs 23,731 crore for FY 2026-27 to FY 2035-36. The scheme has set a target of ten-fold increase in domestic production of Compressed Biogas (CBG) and brings together everything from assured demand and pricing to capital assistance, pipelines and credit under a single framework.The idea sounds simple: take waste that would otherwise be burnt, dumped or left to decompose, and process it in a biogas plant and turn it into fuel that can be used much like natural gas.But the government's ambition goes much further.It wants villages to become centres of energy production, farmers to become suppliers to the energy industry and organic waste to become an economic resource rather than a disposal problem.The question is whether the new scheme can solve the problems that have held back India's CBG industry for years.GOBARdhan is not an entirely new idea.The initiative was originally launched in 2018 under the Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen as a waste-management programme. Its focus was on converting cattle dung, kitchen waste, crop residue and other organic material into biogas and bio-slurry, helping villages manage waste while generating useful products.The 2026 version is much broader.The government has now positioned GOBARdhan as a national framework for the Compressed Biogas industry, bringing several existing measures under one umbrella and placing the scheme under the ministry of petroleum and natural gas.These include the Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation (SATAT) initiative, the Market Development Assistance scheme for organic manure, the Biomass Aggregation Machinery scheme, pipeline infrastructure support and central financial assistance for CBG plants.In simple terms, the government is moving from âhow do we manage organic waste?â to âhow do we build an industry around it?âThe process begins with organic material such as cattle dung, agricultural residue, press mud from sugar mills and municipal organic waste.This material is fed into an anaerobic digester, where microorganisms break it down in the absence of oxygen and produce biogas. The raw biogas contains methane along with carbon dioxide and other impurities.The gas is then purified to remove these impurities and compressed.The resulting Compressed Biogas, or CBG, has properties comparable to natural gas and can be used within the existing gas ecosystem. This is one of its biggest advantages: India does not necessarily need to create an entirely separate fuel infrastructure for it.The process also produces organic material that can be processed into fertiliser.That means one plant can potentially create several economic outputs:Waste â CBG + organic manure + rural jobs + additional income opportunitiesThis is the circular economy the government is trying to build.The biggest reason is energy security.India currently imports nearly 50% of its natural gas requirement, according to the government's latest GOBARdhan backgrounder. That leaves the country exposed to international gas prices, shipping disruptions and geopolitical shocks.Domestic CBG offers a way to produce a portion of that gas from resources that India already has in abundance.The government estimates that lower dependence on imported fossil fuels under GOBARdhan could eventually save more than Rs 40,000 crore in foreign exchange. That is a government projection rather than a guaranteed saving, but it illustrates the scale of the ambition.There is also an environmental argument.Agricultural residue that is not economically used can become a waste-disposal problem, while organic waste dumped in landfills can generate methane and other emissions. Converting such material into fuel gives it an economic value while potentially reducing waste-related emissions.For farmers, the attraction is an additional market for residue and dung.For energy companies, it is another source of domestic gas.For the government, it is a way of connecting waste management, rural development and energy security.This is where the GOBARdhan story becomes more complicated.India's push for CBG production predates the new scheme by several years.The government launched SATAT in October 2018, with an ambitious target of establishing 5,000 CBG plants producing 15 million tonnes a year.But the industry struggled to scale at the pace initially envisaged.A 2022 review by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Petroleum and Natural Gas found that against the target of 5,000 plants by 2023-24, only 40 had been set up at that point. The committee also highlighted problems with financing, multiple approvals, pricing and feedstock availability.One of the biggest problems was that a CBG plant needs much more than a piece of land and a digester.It needs a reliable supply of biomass, equipment to collect and transport that biomass, storage facilities, technology, financing and, crucially, a buyer for the gas.One big complication with agricultural residue is that it is seasonal.Crop waste may be available in large quantities for only a few months of the year, forcing plants to invest in storage and logistics if they want to operate throughout the year. The parliamentary committee specifically flagged this issue.Bansal estimates that India generates around 230 million tonnes of surplus agricultural residue annually, suggesting that the problem is not a shortage of biomass but the difficulty of turning dispersed and seasonal supplies into a reliable, year-round feedstock chain.GOBARdhan's focus on biomass mapping, aggregation infrastructure and district-level planning is therefore critical to making plants operate at high utilisation.There was also a financing problem.Banks and investors were wary of projects whose revenues depended on uncertain feedstock supplies and evolving CBG prices. The committee noted concerns over the low internal rate of return of plants and called for more remunerative pricing.This is the gap GOBARdhan is now attempting to close.Kapil Bansal, partner, energy transition and decarbonization at EY-Parthenon India, told TOI that the biggest change is that GOBARdhan tackles the entire CBG value chain rather than individual bottlenecks.Earlier measures addressed issues such as biomass aggregation, organic manure, pipelines and financial assistance separately, but developers continued to face uncertainty around demand, pricing and financing.âThe sector is moving from a project-led approach to a market-led approach, where demand, pricing and financing visibility are available before developers invest,â Bansal said.The combination of assured offtake, a ten-year pricing framework, capital assistance, pipeline connectivity and credit guarantees, he said, should improve project bankability and give investors greater confidence.The government has structured GOBARdhan around six major components, each designed to address a different weakness in the existing CBG ecosystem.1. Assured demand for CBGPerhaps the biggest change is that producers will have greater certainty that someone will buy their gas.City Gas Distribution companies will procure CBG in line with a notified obligation that rises from 3% in FY 2026-27 to 4% in FY 2027-28 and 5% from FY 2028-29 onwards for the CNG transport and PNG domestic segments.This creates a predictable demand signal.For investors, that matters because a plant is much easier to finance when there is greater clarity about who will buy its output.GOBARdhan introduces a government-backed CBG price of Rs 2,110 per MMBTU, with a minimum ten-year framework.The objective is to give producers greater revenue visibility and make projects more attractive to investors and lenders.This directly addresses one of the problems identified in the earlier CBG ecosystem: uncertainty over whether the economics of a plant would work after it was built.Eligible greenfield CBG projects will receive capital assistance of up to Rs 2 crore for every tonne per day (TPD) of installed capacity.Importantly, the support is not restricted to the core plant.It can also cover critical assets linked to feedstock aggregation, organic manure processing and value addition. Brownfield projects expanding existing capacity will also be eligible.That matters because the economics of CBG depend on the entire supply chain, not just the digester.A CBG plant cannot be commercially successful if its gas cannot reach the market.GOBARdhan therefore provides for cluster-based and standalone pipeline infrastructure connecting plants with trunk pipelines and City Gas Distribution networks.The aim is to reduce evacuation costs, improve reliability and expand the market available to producers.The scheme also attempts to solve the financing problem through a dedicated credit guarantee mechanism.By sharing part of the lending risk, the government hopes banks will be more willing to finance MSME-based CBG projects.This could bring smaller companies, cooperatives, women entrepreneurs and first-time developers into an industry that has so far been dominated by larger players and institutional initiatives.The final component focuses on the problem that often receives the least attention: where will the feedstock come from?The CBG Ecosystem Challenge Fund will support biomass mapping, aggregation infrastructure, district-level development plans, technology adoption, process improvements and organic manure value addition.The objective is to build the local ecosystem around each plant rather than treating the plant as an isolated piece of infrastructure.The government's larger pitch is that farmers should become participants in India's energy economy.Crop residue and cattle dung can become feedstock for CBG plants, creating potential additional income for farmers and local aggregators.The benefit does not stop with the gas.The material left after the biogas production process can be processed into organic fertilisers such as Fermented Organic Manure and Liquid Fermented Organic Manure.This creates a second revenue stream while returning nutrients to agriculture.The government has already been supporting this side of the industry through the Market Development Assistance scheme. Together, these measures are intended to create a cycle in which agricultural and livestock waste becomes an input for both energy and agriculture.That is why GOBARdhan is being presented as more than an energy scheme.It is also a rural infrastructure and waste-management programme.This is perhaps the most revealing part of the government's latest numbers.As of August 6, the GOBARdhan Unified Registration Portal had recorded 1,908 registered CBG/Bio-CNG plants. Of these, 217 had been commissioned, while another 339 were under construction, according to the government.The numbers show both the opportunity and the problem.There is considerable interest in building CBG capacity, but the number of plants actually operating remains far below the number registered.The government says the various initiatives introduced over recent years have helped commission more than 200 CBG plants and establish the initial production and offtake ecosystem. GOBARdhan is now intended to take that foundation to a national scale.In other words, the new scheme is not starting from zero.It is an attempt to make the existing pipeline of projects commercially viable and scalable.That remains the biggest question.Government support can reduce the initial cost of a plant and create a market for its gas. But it cannot eliminate the fundamental logistical challenge of collecting biomass.Bansal cautioned that commercial viability will still vary from project to project because feedstock costs, transportation distances, plant utilisation and financing costs will continue to determine returns.âA project with reliable access to high-quality feedstock can achieve significantly better plant efficiency and returns than a project relying on dispersed or lower-yield biomass resources,â he said.A plant located far from its feedstock source may face high transportation costs. Agricultural residue is seasonal. Competing uses for biomass can raise prices. Plants also need to maintain reliable operations and consistent gas quality.These problems were highlighted by the Parliamentary Standing Committee even before the latest scheme was announced. It pointed to the uneven availability of feedstock, the need for storage and the importance of synchronising CBG production with the national gas grid.This is why the six components of GOBARdhan matter together.A subsidy without a buyer does not solve the problem.A buyer without a pipeline does not solve the problem.A pipeline without reliable feedstock does not solve the problem.And a plant with all three still needs affordable financing and efficient operations.GOBARdhan is effectively trying to solve all of these problems at the same time.The government has set an ambitious ten-year vision.It expects GOBARdhan to deliver nearly ten-fold growth in domestic CBG production, attract large private investment, create rural employment and expand the organic fertiliser economy. It also projects lower fossil-fuel use and significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.These are targets and government projections, not guaranteed outcomes.The more important test will be whether the number of operating plants grows alongside registrations, whether plants remain viable after initial assistance and whether farmers and local businesses actually benefit from the new demand for biomass.If that happens, GOBARdhan could change the economics of waste in India.Instead of paying to collect, transport and dispose of organic waste, communities could potentially build local industries around it.India's CBG journey has already shown that having abundant biomass is not enough.The country had an ambitious 5,000-plant target under SATAT, but financing constraints, feedstock logistics, approvals, pricing uncertainty and weak project economics slowed the industry's development.GOBARdhan is the government's attempt to address those weaknesses through one national framework.At Rs 23,731 crore over ten years, the bet is substantial.But the real significance of the scheme is not the size of the allocation. It is the attempt to connect India's farms, villages, waste streams and gas networks into one economic system.If the model works, cattle dung and crop residue will no longer be treated merely as waste. They could become feedstock for a domestic fuel industry, while the by-products return to farms as organic fertiliser.That would turn the government's âwaste-to-wealthâ slogan into a functioning business model.The challenge is making sure the economics work beyond the subsidy period.For GOBARdhan, success will therefore not be measured simply by how much money is spent or how many plants are registered. It will be measured by how many plants actually operate, how much CBG they produce, whether farmers earn from supplying biomass and whether India's dependence on imported gas falls.India has plenty of waste. GOBARdhan now has to prove that it can turn that waste into a dependable source of energy, income and economic value.

World.title: 'Not said, but presented as if it was': CJI Surya Kant says 'cockroach' remark 'misquoted'
World.content:
CJI Surya Kant said his 'cockroach' remark was 'misquoted and misused' through clipped court videos, warning against misleading social media posts.

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant has said that his oral remarks during a Supreme Court hearing were âmisquotedâ and later used with âmalicious intentâ to mislead the countryâs youth, amid controversy over a comment that sparked the satirical online movement âCockroach Janta Partyâ."My comment was misquoted and misused. What was not said is presented as though it was said. This is extremely unfortunate. Particularly, it is a major malicious attempt to mislead the youth of the country," Kant in a DD News interview.Kant expressed concern over short clips of court proceedings being circulated on social media without the necessary context."You are on social media, print media or any form of media or you are simply a citizen. All of us have rights and constitutional duty and responsibilities," he further said."When we speak of rights, we must also possess the capacity to fulfil our obligations. Therefore, I would urge them to keep their responsibilities in mind; we must all make tireless efforts to ensure that harmony prevails in society," he added.On May 15, while hearing a case in the Supreme Court, Kant had compared certain individuals with fraudulent degrees to âcockroachesâ who become social media or RTI activists to attack the system.The remarks triggered widespread backlash among young people and inspired the satirical âCockroach Janta Partyâ (CJP) movement.The CJP later led protests at Jantar Mantar over the NEET-UG paper leak. The over-a-month-long agitation culminated in a clash between protesters and police on July 20, leaving several people injured on both sides. The protests also preceded the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

World.title: ‘Congress responsible for Partition’: CM Yogi says India would be different if Modi were PM in 1947
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister

has accused the Congress of being responsible for India's Partition and the violence that followed, arguing that the country's history could have been different under leaders such as Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel or Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Speaking at an event in Lucknow marking Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, CM Yogi said the Congress had failed the country by prioritising political power and alleged that the consequences of Partition continue to affect India.

âHad Narendra Modi been the Prime Minister of India at the time of Independence, nobody would have been able to damage India in the slightest,â he was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.

He also invoked Patel, saying that a leader of his stature would not have allowed India to be divided.

âIf a person like Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel were the Prime Minister at that time, nobody would have been able to disintegrate India ... The country had to pay a heavy price for the cowardice of these Congress members -- a character you all witnessed during the CAA protests,â he added.

Adityanath alleged that areas including Sindh, Punjab and Bengal were handed over to Pakistan despite what he described as their Hindu and regional demographic character.





âBengal was Bengali-dominated. All Hindu villages were forcibly given to Bangladesh. This shameful act was committed by the Congress, which was extra-restless for power, and on whom the country had reposed its trust. It repaid that trust with betrayal,â he said.

The chief minister also criticised the Congress over its response to attacks on Hindus in Bangladesh. He alleged that the party remained silent because it was concerned about losing electoral support.

âThey feared that reacting to the events in Bangladesh might cause their vote bank here to drift away. To them, the murder of Dalit Hindus holds no significance; what matters is their own vote bank,â he said.

Adityanath further argued that internal divisions based on caste, region and language had historically weakened India and created opportunities for outside forces.

âWhen such infighting exists, then conspiracy easily creeps in,â he said.

He said the consequences of Partition could still be seen in the form of terrorism, Naxalism, Maoism and extremism. He also questioned the Congress's claims about its role in India's freedom struggle and accused the party of presenting itself as indispensable to the creation of modern India.

âThis also draws our attention to the silence we have all maintained regarding that pre-1947 conspiracy. Yet, even today, these people move before society, acting as if they were the ones who created India, and that without them, India would not have come into existence.

It is a truly strange situation,â he said, describing Partition as the âdarkest chapter of humanity.â

Turning to what he described as the Congress's political legacy, Adityanath said institutions across the country had been named after one political family.

âEvery institution in the country came to bear the name of that very clan. Every single institution was named after that clan, and we all stood by silently, merely watching.

What are they doing even today? What are their actions like now?â he said.

The

also defended the

and attacked the Congress's opposition to it.

âThere was no justification for opposing the act. The act contained a provision regarding Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Bangladesh -- territories that were once part of undivided India and share a heritage spanning thousands of years. It stipulated that if a Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Buddhist, Parsi, or Christian from these countries had been forced to leave and had sought refuge in India for five years, they would be granted Indian citizenship,â he said.

He argued that the legislation did not provide for taking away land or property from Muslims or political parties, and accused opponents of using the issue to provoke protests.

âNowhere did it say that we would seize land belonging to Muslims, the Congress, or the Samajwadi Party. There was no such provision in the Act. Yet, attempts were made to incite agitation across the country,â he said.

Adityanath also targeted the Samajwadi Party, claiming that Uttar Pradesh would have witnessed widespread unrest had it been in power during the CAA protests.

âWhat kind of unbridled mayhem would have taken place? The rioters knew the price they would have to pay, which is why they could not act as they pleased; yet, their audacity was evident,â he said.

âIf you wish to see their true character, you would have witnessed it during the CAA protests, and their silence regarding the recent events in Bangladesh once again puts them in the dock,â Adityanath said.

The event also featured a silent march led by Adityanath and other party leaders from the statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel to Lok Bhavan, according to the Uttar Pradesh government.

World.title: 'First time we did something like this': Former women Naxalites share their Raipur ramp-walk experience
World.content:
Surrendered women naxals walk on the ramp during a participation in a Tribal fashion show programme.

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For nine women from Chhattisgarh's Naxal-affected Bastar region, the stage in Raipur offered a strikingly different kind of experience. Once part of an armed insurgency, they recently walked the ramp in handloom outfits at a National Handloom Day event, as part of efforts to help surrendered Naxalites rebuild their lives.The women, all from Sukma, took part in a Swadeshi fashion show organised as part of rehabilitation efforts for former Naxalites.Sukma SP Mayank Gurjar said the event also gave them an opportunity to promote Swadeshi products.For some of the women, the experience was unlike anything they had done before. One former Naxalite, who had worked with the Pamed Area Committee, said she surrendered in 2026 and travelled to Raipur for six days of training before taking part in the programme."I used to work in the Pamed Area Committee. I surrendered in 2026. We went to Raipur recently. There, we were trained by people who had come from Bombay...prominent ministers also came. The training was of six days...it was the first time we did something like that...we enjoyed it," the former Naxalite told news agency ANI.Another participant, Poonam Devi, said her journey with the Naxalite movement had begun in November 2007.She surrendered on July 12, 2025, bringing that chapter of her life to an end."I surrendered on July 12, 2025. I liked the program...we were trained for it...I joined the Naxals in November 2007 and left in 2025," she said.According to Gurjar, the women's participation reflects the opportunities being offered under the rehabilitation policies of the Central and Chhattisgarh governments to those who surrender and choose to return to mainstream society."As you all know, through the rehabilitation policy of the Government of India and the Chhattisgarh Government, various benefits and advantages are being provided to surrendered Naxalites. In that context, on National Handloom Day, nine surrendered women who had surrendered in Sukma participated in a Swadeshi fashion show," he said.The nine women had held different positions within the Naxalite organisation. Some were associated with the Pamed Area Committee, while others had served as gunners for senior Naxalite commanders in Battalion Number 1. One had worked as a school teacher within the organisation, according to the SP."Among the nine surrendered women, some were working in the Pamed Area Committee. Some worked as gunners for major Naxalite commanders in Battalion Number 1. One of the surrendered women Naxalites was working as a teacher in a school," Gurjar said.Their past also included handling weapons. Gurjar said one of the women had carried an INSAS rifle and that the participants had surrendered around six months earlier.Now, instead of carrying weapons, the women are being encouraged to explore skills and opportunities that can help them build a different future.Gurjar said their participation in the fashion show showed a change in their outlook and suggested that their confidence in the rehabilitation process was growing."They are now actively promoting Swadeshi products and refining their artistic skills," he said.For women who once lived amid the forests and violence of the Naxal movement, walking a ramp in handloom clothing may appear like a small moment. But within the larger rehabilitation effort, it represents something much more significant, a visible step away from an armed past and towards an ordinary life.

World.title: RG Kar victim's 'hurried' cremation: Mob attacks arrested ex-TMC MLA with footwear, eggs, muck; video
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former TMC MLA Nirmal Ghosh, arrested in connection with the alleged âhurried cremationâ of the RG Kar rape-murder victim, was attacked by a mob outside Khardah Police Station in West Bengalâs North 24 Parganas district on Friday.

Ghosh, who was arrested in Odisha a day earlier, was being escorted to a prison van to be produced before the Barrackpore sub-divisional court when the crowd broke through the security cordon and attacked him with blows and kicks. Protesters also threw footwear, eggs and muck at the former MLA.

Police and RAF personnel formed a tight cordon around Ghosh and placed a helmet over his head to shield him from the assault. By the time he was taken to the court lock-up, stains of egg and muck were visible on his white kurta.

The former TMC MLA also faced protests at Barrackpore court, where a group of people waiting outside shouted âchor, chorâ as police rushed him inside.

Another accused in the case, former Panihati municipality councillor Sanjib Mukherjee, was also confronted by protesters while being escorted to the vehicle. Mukherjee, reportedly a close aide of Ghosh, was allegedly present at the Panihati crematorium when the doctorâs body was brought there after the autopsy.

The police have also named former Panihati municipality chairman Somnath Dey as an accused, but he remains absconding.
