The complaint alleges that Ghosh, who was then the sitting MLA from Panihati, used his influence along with Mukherjee and Dey to ensure that his daughterâs body was cremated in haste against the familyâs wishes.

World.title: PoK: Beyond grievance, the politics of mobilisation
World.content:
In 2006, while conducting fieldwork in Muzaffarabad in the aftermath of the devastating earthquake, I stayed with a local family after driving from Islamabad via Abbottabad, through a landscape of shattered houses and tent settlements. One morning, among the volunteers, I noticed a middle-aged man moving slowly on crutches. We eventually sat down together over tea, and I learnt that he had been attacked by activists associated with a rival student movement that would later become central to my understanding of the politics of Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir (PoK).

In 1994, Pervaiz Shraf Magrey lost his leg in a violent encounter with members of the Jamaat-e-Tulba. His group, the Jammu and Kashmir National Student Federation (JKNSF), was challenging Jamaat-e-Tulba’s practice of letting Hizbul Mujahideen militants stay in the hostels of university. For those of us with decades-long familiarity with the nuances and actors of the conflict on the ground on both sides of the Line of Control, it was not difficult to recognise that Jamaat-e-Tulba was the student wing of Jamaat-e-Islami.

Hizbul Mujahideen had acquired considerable prominence on the Indian side of Line of Control around the same time as it increasingly displaced the “pro-independence” Jammu Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF) as the dominant militant organisation. Unlike the JKLF, Hizbul Mujahideen was explicitly pro-Pakistan and advocated the accession of J&K to Pakistan. It also operated with the backing of Jamaat-e-Islami.

Encounters such as these reinforced an enduring lesson: the region cannot be understood through distant observation alone. Its politics are layered, shaped by history, memory, and generations of political mobilisation.

PoK protests, a contrasting narrative

The recent protests in PoK, which unfolded around the 80th anniversary of the Independence of India and Pakistan, have generated sharply contrasting narratives on either side of the border. Within Pakistan, sections of the ruling establishment portrayed the protesters as acting at India’s behest. Meanwhile, outside Pakistan, the protests have frequently been interpreted as confirmation that it is the first major revolt of the region against the Pakistani state.

Both narratives are convenient for their respective audiences, but neither adequately explains what is unfolding on the ground, as complex realities cannot be explained in binaries. There is little doubt that some of the issues being discussed are legacies of Partition. But they have also acquired their own trajectories, shaped by the region’s distinct political, social and historical experiences since 1947.

Approaches that view PoK solely through the prism of India-Pakistan rivalry inevitably miss this complexity. Understanding PoK therefore requires sustained engagement with its evolving political, social and historical dynamics.

The immediate trigger for this latest round of violence appears to have been the killing in June of Shahzeb Habib, a JAAC activist who was travelling with the organisation’s core leader Umar Nazir Kashmiri. Their vehicle was intercepted near Barmang Bridge in Rawalakot, after which an exchange of fire took place. While authorities said armed occupants opened fire first, JAAC supporters disputed the account and alleged that Habib was killed by security-force fire and that Kashmiri was also wounded. The episode illustrates, once again, the limits and ultimately the failure of relying on coercive tactics to suppress political dissent.

In my earlier three detailed pieces on the region for this publication, I have tried to provide a more grounded reading, rather than viewing developments solely through the prism of the India-Pakistan rivalry. While I have outlined the litany of grievances expressed across the region during the protests and traced their historical background, many of these experiences are familiar to other post-colonial states. Questions of political representation, economic distribution, constitutional ambiguity and regional identity have accumulated over decades. Yet an important question remains insufficiently explored – a question I have been asked repeatedly: what explains the mobilisation itself, and why have protesters chosen central PoK as the principal site of protest?

How the movement is sustaining for months

Coming to the first question: why have these grievances, which have existed for years, now acquired the organisational capacity and popular resonance to sustain a movement for months? Who constitutes its cadre, what networks connect its leadership to ordinary citizens, and why have protesters continued to remain in the arena despite arrests, repression and the disruption of communications? The answers suggest that the present mobilisation cannot be understood merely as a reaction to inflation, electricity prices or the immediate political crisis.

The Pakistani establishment has dismissed these protests as being backed by external forces, implicitly pointing to India’s involvement. Some of the same communities that have historically been portrayed as susceptible to Indian influence have also provided substantial manpower to Pakistan’s own security institutions. This makes it difficult to explain the mobilisation simply as an externally sponsored movement.

There is a historical dimension to this mobilisation. The present movement has organisational roots going back several years, with the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee emerging in 2023 as an umbrella platform bringing together traders, civil-society groups, activists and other constituencies. Its demands have subsequently expanded from immediate economic concerns to questions of political representation, governance and the relationship between the region and the Pakistani state. The recurrence of mobilisation in 2024, 2025 and 2026 indicates the gradual construction of an organisational infrastructure rather than a series of disconnected protests.

This historical continuity matters. A protest movement becomes difficult to suppress when grievances are embedded in pre-existing social networks, when local leadership has legitimacy independent of established political parties, and when successive confrontations with the state reinforce rather than diminish collective identity. The striking feature of the present moment, therefore, is not simply the scale of the grievances but the emergence of a political constituency capable of repeatedly converting those grievances into collective action.

That is perhaps the more important story of the current unrest: not merely why people are angry, but how anger has acquired organisation, memory and staying power. The protests need to be located within the longer history of political mobilisation in the region, including the evolution of civil-society networks, the role of traders and local communities, the weakness of conventional party politics, and the unresolved question of political representation. Only then can we understand why a movement that began around economic demands has acquired a much broader political character.

JKNSF: Growing strong since 1967

With the exception of a few figures, namely the traders, the protests were driven largely by a younger generation of activists associated with the Jammu and Kashmir National Students Federation (JKNSF), an organisation that has long unsettled the Pakistani establishment because of its ideological orientation and advocacy of an independent Jammu and Kashmir.

In the Pakistani context, when a group invokes the term “national” or “nationalist,” it can imply a prioritisation of ethnic and linguistic identities over the foundational identity of Islam shared by South Asian Muslims that underpinned the creation of Pakistan. This is often viewed negatively by the Pakistani state, which has historically regarded ethnic or regional nationalism as a potential challenge to the country’s overarching national identity rooted in Islam.

The origins of the JKNSF date back to the early 1960s. Following the partition of the princely state in 1947, student politics in PoK had largely remained dormant. In 1962, a group of pro-independence student activists began touring colleges across PoK to encourage political participation in shaping the future of Jammu and Kashmir. Their efforts culminated in the formation of the JKNSF, whose first convention was held in 1964.

Several pioneers of the movement later entered mainstream politics. One notable example was Mumtaz Hussain Rathore, who eventually became Prime Minister of PAJK in 1990. Ironically, his son, Faisal Mumtaz Rathore, is now presiding over a government as outgoing Prime Minister confronting protests that have resulted in dozens of deaths. This highlights both the historical continuity and the contradictions within PAJK’s political elite.

From its inception, the JKNSF claims that they drew inspiration from socialist and progressive ideas. It viewed the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir as a distinct political entity. The federation also developed close links with progressive student organisations in Pakistan that challenged the political status quo. Many of the individuals active in today’s protests belong to families that participated in earlier waves of mobilisation, illustrating how political activism has often passed from one generation to the next.

The federation’s history is marked by repeated confrontation with the authorities. One of its earliest major agitations occurred in 1967, when students protested against PoK President Abdul Hameed Khan during his proposed visit to the Mirpur College convocation. The state responded with arrests under sedition charges. Several activists were imprisoned for extended periods; Mirpur-born Sabir Ansari, for instance, reportedly spent more than a year in jail. Provisions ordinarily invoked against enemy agents were applied to student activists, reflecting the degree to which the state viewed organised nationalist politics as a security challenge. Now his son Sabar Ansari is now one of the leaders of the current agitation and reports confirm that his family has again faced the crackdown in Mirpur.

The JKNSF also played an important role in the anti-Mangla Dam movement during the 1960s, when many residents opposed displacement and inadequate compensation arising from the construction of the dam on the Jhelum River. Parallel organisations emerged in Pakistan itself, where large numbers of students from PoK were studying. The Jammu and Kashmir Students Organisation, established in Lahore in 1962, sought to mobilise support among progressive and left-leaning Pakistani students for the cause of an independent Jammu and Kashmir. Students from PoK subsequently participated in Pakistan’s wider democratic movements, including the campaign against General Zia-ul-Haq’s military regime during the 1980s.

The JKNSF’s influence gradually came under challenge with the rise of the Jamaat-e-Tulaba. Rivalry between the two organisations frequently spilled onto university campuses, where clashes became a recurring feature of student politics. The balance shifted further during General Zia-ul-Haq’s rule, when independent student unions were banned across Pakistan and PoK. Although the restrictions affected all organisations, the Jamaat-e-Tulaba retained a significant organisational advantage through the institutional, ideological, and financial support of its parent party in Pakistan.

The recent protests therefore did not emerge in a political vacuum. They brought to the surface longstanding grievances, as I’ve outlined in earlier pieces, that have persisted within sections of PoK society for decades. More significantly, they demonstrated that the organisational backbone of much of the mobilisation continues to come from student networks whose political lineage stretches back more than 60 years. Any serious assessment of current developments must therefore examine not only the immediate triggers of the protests but also the historical traditions of political activism that continue to shape the region.

One of the prominent faces of this agitation and its subsequent repression was Sardar Osama Jameel, a PhD scholar at Islamabad-based Quaid-i-Azam University and a prominent JKNSF activist. He died on July 27–28, 2026, after reportedly being shot during protests and security-force crackdowns in Rawalakot. His sloganeering, rooted in progressive political tradition, points to another important dimension of the mobilisation: the presence of a politically conscious student movement with a longer ideological and historical lineage. His participation also suggests that the agitation cannot be understood solely as a response to immediate economic grievances; it draws upon an older tradition of progressive, anti-establishment politics in the region.

A lesser-known aspect of the agitation has been the support it received from various parts of Pakistan. Protesters of PoK origin in several Pakistani cities expressed solidarity with the movement, while 88 of them were arrested and charged under terrorism-related provisions. This wider support is significant because it suggests that the agitation cannot simply be dismissed as a geographically confined or externally sponsored movement.

PoK elections reaffirmed institutional flaws

In this light, the 2026 electoral process in PoK has merely reaffirmed the institutional flaws of the territory’s political system, validating many of the grievances that have fuelled the protest movement. While there were allegations of rigging, mainly raised by the PPP, there was a turnout of 46% in the first phase and 53% in the second phase. The JAAC leadership stopped short of calling for an electoral boycott, but neither did it encourage local residents to participate in the electoral process.

Across the three phases of the election, the ruling PML-N has emerged as the largest beneficiary, securing at least 25 of the 38 seats for which results have so far been announced, much as the party in power in Islamabad has historically tended to perform well in PoK elections. The contrast with 2021 is instructive. Then, the ruling PTI won 26 of the 45 general seats, followed by PPP with 11 and PML-N with six. The third phase, held in Bagh and Haveli, however, has also underscored the unsettled and contested nature of the 2026 process. PPP won LA-17 Bagh-IV, while an independent candidate captured LA-14 Bagh-I; the results in LA-15 and LA-16 remain unresolved, with the Election Commission ordering re-polling at 23 polling stations on August 15. Seven further constituencies in Poonch and Sudhnoti have also been postponed because of the ongoing protests.

The election also produced a striking generational and political turnover: three former Prime Ministers, including Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan, who heads the regional party with a long history, the All Jammu and Kashmir Muslim Conference, were defeated, underscoring the extent to which established political figures and traditional parties have lost their electoral hold. On 19 July 1947, the All Jammu and Kashmir Muslim Conference passed a resolution in Srinagar advocating the State’s accession to Pakistan. This contrasted sharply with the position of Sheikh Abdullah’s National Conference, which had rejected the Muslim League’s politics and was politically aligned with the Congress.

The 12 refugee constituencies remain a particularly contentious feature of the electoral system and of the current agitation. Reserved for people who migrated from the Indian side of Jammu and Kashmir in 1947 and now live elsewhere in Pakistan, these seats, six for Jammu and six for the Kashmir Valley, give voters outside PoK a significant role in determining its government. In 2026, PML-N won 10 refugee seats, while PPP secured 2 seats overall in the currently declared results. Given that the 12 refugee seats constitute nearly 26% of the 45-member elected seats in the Assembly, their political weight is disproportionate to their direct connection with the territory they help govern.

The 2026 election has merely reinforced the protesters’ assertion that retaining these seats in their present form is a negation of democratic representation. The disconnect was particularly visible during the polling for the refugee constituencies on August 2. Although these 12 seats together had nearly 439,000 registered voters, their electorates are scattered across Pakistan, with some individual constituencies representing only a few thousand voters. In LA-43 (Valley-IV), for instance, there were just 3,346 registered voters, while LA-44 (Valley-V), covering refugees in Rawalpindi and Islamabad, had 3,754. LA-39 (Jammu-VI), the largest of these constituencies, had only 20,807 registered voters. The limited participation in these constituencies further exposed the anomaly: legislators elected by small and geographically dispersed electorates, many of whom live hundreds of kilometres outside PoK, can nevertheless exercise the same legislative power as representatives elected by tens of thousands of voters actually living in the territory. This is precisely the democratic contradiction at the heart of the protesters’ objection and not the representation of refugees as such, but the continued use of a non-territorial electoral arrangement to determine the government of a territory whose residents themselves have no say in those constituencies. The fact that the determining composition of the Assembly remains dependent on refugee constituencies only reinforces the broader perception of an electoral system whose institutional design is part of the political grievances being expressed within PoK itself.

These developments have yet again reaffirmed that they are a part of a continuing trend of institutional deceit and falsified claims about the region’s status as an “independent country”. Practically, its political status does not even equal other provinces of Pakistan.

Why are the protests happening in central PoK?

The second question is why central PoK, and particularly hilly Rawalakot, has emerged as one of the main sites of protest. Rawalakot lies within the former Poonch estate, a region with a long history of rebellion against the Maharaja, including the 1955 uprising against the Pakistani state, but it is also an important recruitment ground for Pakistan’s armed forces and has produced several senior military officers. This creates a striking historical paradox: a region that has contributed substantially to Pakistan’s security establishment has also repeatedly been a centre of political dissent.

The social composition of the recent protests reinforces this paradox. One of those reportedly killed during the recent protests was the father of serving Pakistani Air Force officers, while another person killed in firing by security personnel was the son of a former member of the Pakistani army. These connections complicate any simple portrayal of the protests as externally driven. They suggest instead that dissent is emerging from communities deeply intertwined with Pakistan’s own military and security institutions.

The recent protests also offer broader lessons that extend well beyond Pakistan-Occupied Jammu and Kashmir. Across many post-colonial states and developing countries, the political and administrative periphery is often viewed primarily through a security lens rather than as a source of political knowledge and lived experience. As a result, policies are frequently framed in distant capitals with limited appreciation of local realities. The knowledge systems that evolve within peripheral societies deserve greater recognition and accommodation in policymaking. Capitals inevitably become centres of political and bureaucratic power, but they can also develop insulated narratives that overlook the complexities of the regions they govern. This disconnect often delays policy correction and deepens mistrust.

The fact that the epicentre of the protests, including this latest round, has been in central PoK suggests that some of the structural advantages Pakistan enjoyed in this area, as compared to other parts of PoK, have not translated into enduring political legitimacy.

Protesters from other parts of the region have also flocked to the area, turning it into a focal point for mobilisation. One reason may be its geography: the hilly terrain and forested terrain provide protesters with a degree of natural protection and make it more difficult for security personnel deployed from Rawalpindi to exercise effective control. But geography alone does not explain the repeated emergence of central PAJK as the protest site; the area’s strong local networks, martial tradition and history of resisting any real or perceived repression, have also played an important role.

In 1947, geographical contiguity with Islamabad and the relative ease with which Pakistani forces could access the area were only two of several factors that shaped the emergence of PoK. The extensive wartime recruitment of men from north-western British India, including what is today the central part of PoK and northern Pakistani Punjab, particularly the area culturally known as the Pothohar belt, into the British Indian Army created a substantial pool of trained military manpower.

Many served in the European and other theatres during the Second World War on behalf of the Brits, leaving behind considerable military experience that would later shape the region’s political and armed mobilisation. This manpower had also got demobilised after the war. This was one of the key reasons that local forces were able to mobilise quickly and stage an armed rebellion against the Princely state of Jammu and Kashmir in October 1947.

An eyewitness to the tumultuous era of 1947 and an authority on J&K, late Balraj Puri, a Padma Bhushan awardee, records on page seven of his best-selling book Kashmir: Towards Insurgency that the initial discontent in Poonch centred on “some local demands like the rehabilitation of 60,000 demobilised soldiers of the British army belonging to the area.”

According to Puri, as these issues became intertwined with wider political and communal tensions, “the agitation turned communal.” He writes that the state army was deployed to suppress the unrest, but soldiers refused to fire on demonstrators with whom they shared religious and ethnic ties. Some subsequently deserted the army, and, in Puri’s account, the agitation developed into an armed revolt. He further attributes the revolt’s growing strength to “ammunition and other types of assistance from across the border.”

Puri also identifies a longer historical dimension to the 1947 unrest. He argues that the revolt drew on local sentiments of patriotism in Poonch, which, in his view, had been offended when the territory was brought under the direct control of the Jammu Durbar in 1936, following what he describes as a decision of the British courts. Until then, Poonch had retained a distinct status under the descendants of ruler Gulab Singh’s brother for about a century. Gulab Singh was the founder and first ruler of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, which he established in 1846 under the Treaty of Amritsar.

Thus, in Puri’s interpretation, the 1947 upheaval in Poonch was shaped not only by the immediate grievances of demobilised soldiers and the subsequent communalisation of the agitation, but also by longer-standing local political and historical sentiments. Like other princely states or estates of British India, Poonch maintained properties outside the jagir, including the Poonch House in Rawalpindi, which was built by Raja Moti Singh in the late nineteenth century as a rest house for the rulers of Poonch. A historic building known as Poonch House also exists in Lahore, although its institutional history appears to be distinct from that of the Rawalpindi residence.

Following the lapse of British paramountcy in August, the princely ruler initially sought to maintain the State’s independence and entered into a standstill arrangement with Pakistan, while also proposing similar arrangements with India. The State had therefore not acceded to either dominion when the rebellion and subsequent tribal invasion began in October. The Maharaja subsequently sought military assistance from India and signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947, after which India accepted the accession and deployed troops to defend the State. By then, however, large parts of J&K, what is today PoK, had already slipped from the control of the princely government.

Many of those who had served in the British Indian Army possessed both the organisational capacity and political networks necessary to mobilise men, organise resistance and subsequently shape the institutional structures of the territory. Some of the caste and community groups in this area, particularly the Sudhans, have a deeply internalised sense of community pride, honour and justice, reinforced over generations by the martial identity associated with communities that the British classified as “martial races” in British India after the 1857 uprising.

The historical significance of these areas helps explain why their representatives were subsequently given a prominent role in PoK’s political architecture. This area also provided much of the political and military leadership of the region during the early phase of the conflict and became the principal interlocutor in establishing the emerging relationship between the territory and Pakistan. Leaders such as Sardar Ibrahim Khan and Sardar Abdul Qayum Khan emerged from this area and played a central role in the mobilisation and political consolidation of the territory. Initially, however, the region’s political executive was more urban and politically cosmopolitan, represented by figures such as Dogri or Punjabi-speaking Ghulam Abbas, who had migrated from the plains of J&K and had emerged as an important Muslim political leader in the wider Jammu and Kashmir region. His background and political standing also enabled him to enjoy the patronage of the Pakistani state. His followers, who were the migrants from the plains of J&K, were mostly concentrated in Pakistani Punjab and not PoK. Over time, leadership shifted increasingly towards those rooted in the areas where the armed mobilisation had taken place, reflecting the military and political weight that these areas had acquired during the events of 1947. This was further cemented by the Sudhan uprising of 1955–56. Centred in the Sudhan heartland, it reflected grievances over the Pakistani state’s interference in local affairs, the sidelining of Sardar Ibrahim Khan, the absence of representative institutions and demands for greater autonomy. In short, the present dispute over the refugees’ seats has historical roots in the region’s politics apart from other factors.

The part of Poonch that later became central PoK, as noted earlier, had already been one of the principal recruiting grounds for the British Indian Army, a military tradition that continued after Partition with recruitment into Pakistan’s armed forces. Even today, in parts of central PoK, it is common to find families with three successive generations having served in the Pakistani armed forces, including in senior positions. These deep military and social linkages gave Pakistan an advantage that few other parts of PAJK enjoyed. Shared service, institutional ties, and sustained interaction with the Pakistani state might have been expected to strengthen political integration. The Pakistani state’s continuing difficulty in accommodating the overall region’s political and economic aspirations is, in that sense, particularly revealing and points towards a failure of a hard state approach.

A predominantly coercive approach has not resolved underlying political questions; instead, it has contributed to alienation and, in many cases, intergenerational resentment towards Islamabad. Allegations that protests are orchestrated by foreign powers are frequently deployed in official discourse, yet such explanations often obscure the structural grievances that have accumulated over decades. The recent protests have brought these unresolved tensions to the surface. The current phase of protest may eventually be contained through coercive measures, but the scars are likely to endure. Political memories often outlive the events themselves, passing from one generation to the next.

Magrey had told me that none of those responsible for attacking him had ever been arrested or prosecuted because, in his view, members of extremist militant organisations enjoyed official patronage in PAJK and Pakistan at the time. Whether or not one accepts every aspect of his account, it reflects a strand of local memory that has endured across generations and illustrates how lived experiences can diverge sharply from official narratives. It is these accumulated memories, as much as contemporary grievances, that continue to shape political attitudes in the region.

The saga around PoK, which has drawn international attention now, offers a broader lesson for post-colonial entities: coercion cannot substitute for political accommodation. The anger had been building for years before erupting. Apart from being a victim of Pakistan’s enduring obsession with internationalising J&K, which has led it to instrumentalise the region for its foreign policy and portray it as “Azad” (independent), when it clearly is not, the experience of PAJK illustrates these broader dynamics.

A hard state response may suppress unrest temporarily, but its effectiveness diminishes when underlying grievances remain unaddressed. Bureaucratic paternalism and elite perspectives formed in distant capitals must give way to a genuine willingness to learn from those who have experienced these realities firsthand. For post-colonial states facing similar tensions between central authority and peripheral regions, the lesson is clear, though each case has its own historical, legal and political specificities: unless deeper political questions are addressed through meaningful political accommodation, unrest may be contained temporarily, but the grievances sustaining it are unlikely to disappear.

(Luv Puri has authored two books on Jammu and Kashmir namely Uncovered Face of Militancy and Across the Line of Control, the latter published by Columbia University Press based on field-work in the region.)

World.title: Company that signed ₹22,500 crore MoU with Bihar govt. has only ₹11 lakh capital, says Tejashwi
World.content:
The Leader of Opposition in the Bihar Assembly, Tejashwi Yadav, on Friday (August 14, 2026) took a dig at Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary over the Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) signed by the Bihar government earlier this month. He alleged that the company that signed an MoU worth ₹22,500 crore in the nuclear sector has a total capital of just ₹11 lakh.

The Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) national working president, in a press note as well as in a message on X, said a company that does not even have the capital to build the four walls of a house had signed a ₹22,500-crore MoU.

“Wow, what a shame for the Samrat Choudhary government! The Bihar government, through its Industries Department, is beating the drum about signing MoUs for investments worth around ₹51,500 crore with various industrial groups. But why is this government not providing a progress report on the agreements worth over 2 lakh crore from 2024, 2025, and prior years? What exactly happened to those MoUs?” Mr. Yadav asked.

He further said, “You will be shocked and saddened to learn that the company the Bihar government is claiming will invest the highest amount in the nuclear sector — ₹22,500 crore — was established just five months ago in February 2026, and it has a total capital of only ₹11 lakh. In other words, a company that cannot even afford to build the boundary wall of a school or college is now going to set up a nuclear power plant or nuclear research centre in Bihar.”

On August 6, several MoUs worth approximately ₹51,600 crore were signed between the Industries Department and various industrial groups in the presence of the Chief Minister in Patna. The companies included Global Renewable Advanced Clean Energy Private Limited (GRACE), which proposed to invest ₹22,500 crore in Bihar’s nuclear energy sector.

The company’s website mentioned that it has an authorised capital of ₹10,00,000 and a paid-up capital of ₹1,00,000, whereas the date of incorporation is February 25, 2026.

‘Blatant lie’

Mr. Yadav said the BJP-led government should explain “what kind of treasure has suddenly fallen into the hands of this ₹11 lakh company that it’s now going to pour thousands of crores into investments in Bihar?”

“Didn’t the Samrat Choudhary government feel even a shred of shame in telling such a blatant lie to the people of Bihar? The entire Bihar knows how much depth, wisdom, and understanding the Chief Minister possesses with his novice tendencies, but in the presence of so many officials and Ministers, a company walked away with such a massive claim, and no one asked a single question,” Mr. Yadav said,

The former Deputy Chief Minister further asked if fooling the people of Bihar had become the collective goal of everyone. “Were they all silent because, in the future, these paper companies would be handed thousands of crores of free land and subsidies from the State coffers, and they can pocket commissions? By giving subsidies and free land to paper companies in the name of investment, does the BJP government want to sell off Bihar’s resources? If big companies come to Bihar, set up industries and businesses, and invest with their own capital, we will not just welcome them — we will provide every possible assistance,” Mr. Yadav said.

He added that if they [firms] create paper companies, grab land from the government, take grants, and then vanish, the people of Bihar will not tolerate it.

‘Investors wary’

Mr. Yadav further said that for over two decades, the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) had been in power in Bihar. Yet it had not been able to create a conducive atmosphere so that investors develop trust in the Bihar government and its infrastructure.

“Why is no big company willing to make a major investment in Bihar? You can get your praise sung in the media through government propaganda, but you cannot fix the pathetic ground realities. You lack both the will and competence for it. That’s why your fake politics runs on divisive policies in the name of caste and religion, five kg of free grain, and handing out ₹10,000 during elections,” Mr. Yadav said.

After signing the MoUs, Mr. Choudhary had mentioned that, keeping the future energy needs in mind, the government would shift its focus towards clean energy sector, particularly nuclear energy.

World.title: Expert body formed to protect Thamaraikani tank in Sholinganallur, Tamil Nadu govt. tells Madras High Court
World.content:
The Tamil Nadu government on Friday (August 14, 2026) informed the Madras High Court that it has constituted an expert body to protect from encroachments the sprawling Thamaraikani waterbody, located opposite the Infosys campus at Sholinganallur in Chennai.

Appearing before the first Division Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan, Additional Advocate General (AAG) P.V. Balasubramaniam said, the government constituted the committee of experts a week ago.

The submission was made in response to a public interest litigation (PIL) petition filed by anti-corruption organisation Arappor Iyakkam, represented by its managing trustee Jayaram Venkatesan, in 2019 against the construction of a building for the Semmenchery police station on the waterbody.

After the filing of the case, the petitioner organisation amended its prayer and insisted upon removing all other encroachments as well from the waterbody. It insisted upon issuing a direction to the government to evict all the encroachers and restore the waterbody to its original state.

It was brought to the notice of the court that Thamaraikani tank was part of Periya Eri, which was a mosaic of tanks, also consisting of Valaleri and Velalkani tank. Thamaraikani tank was originally spread over 13.47 hectare, as per the Public Works Department’s tank memoir, and it had been irrigating around 250 acres. However, now, there had been large-scale encroachment by private and government institutions.

The AAG told the court that apart from the police station building, whose inauguration had been stayed by the High Court in 2019, there was also an electricity sub-station, a large Aavin milk factory, and a government higher secondary school adjacent to each other, and those institutions had to be protected.

He said, the government had protected the existing extent of the waterbody by demarcating its boundaries and that a committee of experts had also been constituted to suggest the ways and means to protect it from further encroachments in the future.

After recording his submissions and granting four weeks’ time for the government to file a comprehensive status report, the judges ordered that the expert body may also consider the suggestions to be made by the petitioner organisation for the protection of the waterbody.

World.title: A vibrant evening atosphere at Madurai Vandiyur Mariamman Teppakulam, with snacks, shopping, and family fun
World.content:
As the sun sets, the parapet walls around Vandiyur Mariamman Teppakulam slowly come alive . Children stop by colourful stalls selling toys and accessories, families gather to sit and chat , and walkers make their rounds around the tank. On the other side, vendors lay out clothes, jewellery and snacks, hoping to catch the attention of passers-by. During the weekend, the historic tank takes on a new rhythm, buzzing with people, conversations, and brisk sales.

Vandiyur Mariamman Teppakulam was built during the reign of King Thirumalai Nayak and is a big part of Madurai’s annual float festival, known as ‘Theppotsavam’. This festival takes place in the Tamil month of Thai, where the idols of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar are taken around the tank on a beautifully decorated float, along with traditional music and lots of devotees.

On regular days, people come to the Teppakulam to simply simply spend time outdoors.

The growing number of stalls and eateries around the Teppakulam has given people another reason to linger. Stalls selling dress materials and saris, jewellery, and hair accessories line the stretch, while mehendi artists work on intricate desigsn for customers. Some sellers, who run online businesses, use the opportunity to showcase their products in person and connect with potential c

M Yazhni, who runs a stall with her husband, sells dress materials and saris. “We started this stall here only a few months ago. We also sell our products online, but we get more customers here. The weekend crowd helps us reach more people and gives our business a boost,” she says.

A little away, V Tamil Selvi offers mehendi. She says the stall has helped her reach more customers and brought her bridal mehendi bookings as well. For V Durga, who sells jewellery and accessories, setting up the stall is also a way to spend the weekend with her family. “My husband supports me with the stall. I also bring my children along on weekends. They enjoy being here and get to play while I attend to the stall,” she says.

For some, the evening stall has become a regular family routine. R Vellai Ammal and her husband have been selling paniyaram at the Teppakulam for four years. Their stall has become a regular stop for people looking for fluffy and crispy kuzhi paniyaram to eat while walking around the tank.

There are also sellers who see the space as a part-time business opportunity. I Mohammad Azrah has started a food truck and chose this place because evenings are always special here. The weekend crowd also brings more people, which helps the business,” he says.

One can choose from a variety of food options choices range from bread omelettes, bajji and thattu vadai to momos, cakes and ice creams. A few stalls offer homemade brownies. Jigarthanda, a familiar Madurai favourite, is another draw for visitors.

The area grows livelier with college students in the evenings. For many of them, the Teppakulam has become an easy meeting point, a place to catch up after college, grab a snack and spend some time together before heading home.

The Teppakulam is best known for the grandeur of its annual float festival. On ordinary evenings, however, its surroundings take on a quieter role — bringing together walkers, families, students, children, and vendors, each finding a reason to linger by the historic tank.

World.title: Nepal-Delhi charas trail: How social media, bike taxis and autorickshaws helped move drugs
World.content:
From the Nepal border to a bulk storage point in Wazirabad and then into the hands of local distributors, an international charas network had built a supply chain designed to keep the drugs moving while keeping those behind it out of sight.

Delhi Police’s South District police dismantled part of the network, arresting four Nepalese nationals and recovering 106.250 kg of high-quality charas estimated to be worth around ₹109 crore in an operation that stretched nearly 1.5 months.

Editorial | Caught in the middle: On India and curbing drug abuse

The operation began with a relatively small recovery of 8.598 kg at a residence in Kotla Mubarakpur on June 29 this year, leading to the arrest of Bharat Thapa, 32, Govind Budha, 32, and Jyoti Pun Magar, 50. Interrogation, technical surveillance, financial analysis and local intelligence eventually led the police to Roshni Magar, 32, who was operating a massive storage and distribution unit in Wazirabad.

A raid on the premises on August 12 led to the recovery of 97.652 kg of high-quality charas packed in 13 plastic bags. A mixing machine and packing material were also recovered.

Investigators revealed that the network sourced charas through suppliers in Nepal, including the Kakri area of Rukum, and moved it towards Delhi through the Sonauli border. The syndicate relied on road transportation to move the consignments to evade checks and reduce the chances of detection.

Once the contraband reached Delhi, they were stored at various locations, packed into smaller packets based on the demand before being distributed further. Orders were coordinated through social media platforms including Telegram, with payments made both in cash and through digital banking channels. After transactions, the accused deleted digital communications to conceal their activities.

The drugs were then moved through local transport, including autorickshaws and bike taxis, to distributors and customers. Police said the network specifically targeted areas with a high concentration of younger people and demand centres such as Wazirabad and Majnu Ka Tila, with suspected supplies to distributors and customers linked to pubs, bars and hotels in the vicinity.

According to DCP (South District) Anant Mittal, the syndicate has been in operation in Delhi for the past four to five years. Roshni had previously been part of the distribution network involving Thapa, Budha and Jyoti Pun Magar. After the three were arrested in June, she left India and returned to Nepal. Investigators said she recently came back to India believing that the situation had settled and resumed her operations.

The investigation has also opened up the Nepal end of the network. Binmaya, a Nepalese national, has emerged as an alleged key source who arranged transportation of charas from the Sonauli border towards Delhi. Another Nepalese national, Hari, has also emerged as an alleged supplier. Their exact roles, whereabouts and financial links are being established.

Police are now examining the financial trail to determine how money moved through the network and identify other people who may have financed, supplied, transported or distributed the drugs

World.title: A slew of demands raised at Tiruchi DRUCC meeting
World.content:
A host of demands, including augmentation of coaches, installation of CCTV cameras, provision of new halts, introduction of new trains, revision of timings, and enhancement of passenger amenities were raised by members of the Divisional Railway Users’ Consultative Committee (DRUCC) meeting organised by the Tiruchi Railway Division here on Friday.

The nearly three-hour DRUCC meeting presided over by Tiruchi Divisional Railway Manager Balak Ram Negi was attended by senior divisional officers of different railway departments.

T. Saravanan, a DRUCC member based at Papanasam, said he raised long-pending demand of the rail users seeking a halt of the Tambaram-Nagercoil Antyodaya Express at Papanasam in both directions. Providing a halt at Papanasam station for the Antyodaya express, which is operated completely with unreserved coaches, would substantially reduce overcrowding in the unreserved coaches of the Thanjavur-Chennai-Thanjavur Uzhavan Express trains and distribute passenger load, he said.

Installation of closed circuit television cameras at Papanasam station to enhance the security of passengers and augmentation of coaches in the Mayiladuthurai-Tiruchi and Mayiladuthurai-Salem MEMU (Mainline Electric Multiple Unit) services to benefit the growing number of daily commuters were his other demands.

Mr. Saravanan said the revised timing of the Mannargudi-Tiruchi DEMU (Diesel Electric Multiple Unit) service had caused hardship to commuters, students, and office-goers and requested the divisional authorities to restore the earlier timing of 7.55 a.m. at Thanjavur junction for the convenience of passengers.

V. R. Dhanaseelane, a DRUCC member of Karaikal, said he had raised at the meeting the need to install closed circuit television cameras at Karaikal station and deployment of Railway Protection Force personnel on a full-time basis. This demand had remained unsolved since 2014 and its implementation was essential to ensure the safety and security of passengers besides railway property, he said. He requested for the installation of a RO-based drinking water plant at Karaikal station for the benefit of the travelling public.

Mr. Dhanaseelane handed over a memorandum to the Divisional Railway Manager seeking the introduction of a weekly express train between Thirunallar and Tiruchendur via Karaikal, Tiruvarur, Pattukottai, Karaikudi, Manamadurai, Virudhunagar, and Tirunelveli or via Tiruvarur, Thanjavur, Tiruchi, Madurai, and Tirunelveli. The introduction of the service would connect the religious towns of Thirunallar and Tiruchendur.

R. Subhash Chandran, a DRUCC member based in Nagapattinam, said he had sought the introduction of a daily day time express service between Velankanni and Chennai and revision of the timings of the Karaikal-Bengaluru Express to provide a connection with the Mayiladuthurai-Karaikudi passenger train at Tiruvarur junction among others.

Meanwhile, a press release from the Tiruchi Division said the Divisional Railway Manager and the branch officers acknowledged the concerns raised by the DRUCC members and provided responses to the members suggestions.

The Divisional Railway Manager assured the members that the issues raised at the meeting would be examined and appropriate action taken wherever feasible in accordance with operational requirements and guidelines. P. Venkataragavan, Senior Divisional Commercial Manager and secretary of DRUCC, provided an overview of the significant developments and the ongoing projects within Tiruchi Division.

World.title: Mounting criticism in Kerala over Centre’s Mines and Minerals Amendment Act
World.content:
Protests are mounting in Kerala over the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, passed in Parliament, which both the ruling front and the Opposition in the State say completely disregards the federal principles guaranteed by the Constitution.

Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan has termed the MMDR Amendment Act an assault on the federal structure envisaged by the Constitution and urged the United Democratic Front (UDF) government in Kerala to challenge its provisions in the Supreme Court.

On Thursday (August 13, 2026), Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan had stated that the State government would mount a strong political opposition and, if necessary, legal opposition to the Act. He pointed out that the legislation amounted to “a serious encroachment on the State’s constitutional powers over land and poses a grave threat to India’s federal structure.”

‘Encroaches upon States’ domain’

In a Facebook post on Friday (August 14), Mr. Vijayan said the amendment, by restricting the power of States to impose taxes, cess and other levies on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land, encroaches upon the States’ constitutional domain.

Land falls under Entry 18 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule, while taxation of land is also a State subject, he pointed out.

One of the provisions in the MMDR amendment Act gives the Union government control over the regulation of mines and development of mines and “mineral-bearing lands” under the Centre’s regulations.

State levies

Kerala’s concerns assume significance because the amendment empowers the Centre to prescribe conditions and restrictions governing State levies on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land.

Mr. Vijayan said the amendment should therefore be viewed as a direct challenge to States’ fiscal and legislative autonomy. He questioned whether the UDF government was prepared to take a stand against the Centre and protect Kerala’s federal rights.

He also alleged that the legislation formed part of a broader policy to open India’s precious mineral wealth, including strategically important and rare minerals, to private monopolies.

Centre’s argument

The Centre had argued that the new amendment is intended to promote mineral production, ensure mineral security and create a more uniform regulatory framework. Mr. Vijayan, however, alleged that the larger objective was to weaken the public sector and create opportunities for corporates to reap windfall profits.

The Opposition leader also alleged that the UDF government had taken the same approach as the Centre towards the entry of private operators into sandmining. He pointed out that the UDF government’s Revised Budget and the White Paper on the State’s finances had contained proposals to fully privatise beach sandmining.

Rare earth corridors

The Union Budget 2026-27 proposed dedicated rare earth corridors in mineral-rich States including Kerala, with the stated objective of promoting mining, processing, research, and manufacturing. Mr. Vijayan said the State government’s proposed rare earth corridor was a similar attempt to hand over the State’s coastal mineral wealth to private companies. He alleged that the covert moves to “destroy” the State’s public sector undertaking, Kerala Metals and Minerals Ltd., are part of the privatisation agenda of the government.

Mr. Vijayan alleged that KMML’s sandmining activities at Chavara are being curtailed to the extent that the public sector enterprise that was running profitably is no longer able to continue its operations. He pointed out that it was curious and strange that KMML is now being forced to procure more than twice its monthly requirement of raw materials from private firms at higher rates.

Mr. Vijayan said that any move to weaken and close down KMML and facilitate private sector’s control over Kerala’s mineral resources should be resisted tooth and nail.

Fishers’ forum raises issue

The Kerala Matsyathozhilali Aikyavedi has also raised its voice that Kerala’s rich beach sand mineral belt and offshore zone must not be surrendered to big private monopolies, as the Central government is allegedly attempting to do, through the recent MMDR amendment Act.

The organisation said the Centre was amending all existing mining laws to make way for the private sector to gain monopoly in the mining sector.

It said the State government had remained silent about the announcement of a dedicated mineral corridor spanning Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha in the Union Budget, even though the Chief Minister had assured that private players will not be entertained in the mining sector. In the light of the new amendment brought in by the Centre, the State government should now clarify its position regarding the MMDR amendment Act, the fish workers’ organisation said.

World.title: Pakistan's leadership stresses need for unity, reforms as nation celebrates Independence Day
World.content:
Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership has stressed the need for unity and reforms as the nation celebrates 79 years of independence today.

According to state-run Radio Pakistan, the day dawned with a 31-gun salute in Islamabad and a 21-gun salute at the provincial headquarters. A change of guards ceremony was also held at the mausoleum of Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah in Karachi.

Flag hoisting ceremonies were also held at the Supreme Court and the Federal Constitutional Court in Islamabad.

‘Pakistan’s security linked to peace in our neighbourhood’

In his message, President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to Quaid-i-Azam, those behind the Pakistan Movement and those who sacrificed their homes, security and livelihoods in the struggle for a homeland.

“But independence is not only a historic achievement. It is also a responsibility that each generation must carry forward. The Pakistan that was created through the democratic will of its people must continue to grow stronger, more secure and more prosperous. Our task is not only to remember what earlier generations achieved, but to add to it through our own work,” he said.

The president said that the past year had reminded citizens of the strength of the Pakistani nation.

Recalling last year’s brief military conflict with India, he said, “The events surrounding Marka-i-Haq demonstrated that Pakistan seeks peace, but also possesses the resolve and capacity to defend its sovereignty and national interests. The lesson of strength is ultimately a lesson of responsibility. A country that can defend itself must also use its strength to prevent conflict, protect peace and serve the interests of its people.”

He said that the security and stability enjoyed today had come at a great cost, paying tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces, law enforcement agencies and police.

“Their courage and commitment have helped safeguard our nation against external aggression and the threat of terrorism. The people of Pakistan remain deeply grateful for their service,” he said.

He also highlighted Pakistan’s efforts to facilitate dialogue in the region.

“Pakistan has effectively used its channels of communication, its geographical location and diplomatic capital to encourage dialogue and de-escalation at a time when wider conflict could have serious consequences for the region and the world,” he said.

He reiterated that all disputes must be ultimately addressed through dialogue and diplomacy.

“Our security is linked to the peace and stability of our neighbourhood and the world at large. Pakistan will continue to support efforts that reduce tensions, protect regional stability and create conditions for cooperation,” he said.

The president also went on to say that the country must focus on the work that will determine Pakistan’s future.

“We must strengthen our economy, create greater opportunities for our young people, improve education and skills, strengthen institutions through a series of governance, economic and social reforms to ensure that the benefits of development and democracy reach every part and community of the country,” he said.

“Pakistan’s greatest strength is its young people. Across the country and around the world, they are demonstrating their talent in science, technology, business, education and the creative industries. Our responsibility is to give them the education, skills and opportunities they need to realise their potential. By investing in our youth today, we are investing in Pakistan’s future,” he added.

“For ordinary Pakistanis, national progress is measured in practical terms. It means a young person finding the skills and opportunity to build a career. It means a family being able to access quality education and healthcare. It means farmers, workers, traders and businesses being able to plan for the future with greater confidence. The strength of Pakistan will ultimately be judged by whether our national progress improves the lives of its people,” President Zardari said.

He also voiced Pakistan’s support for the people of occupied Kashmir, saying Pakistan will continue to support a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the aspirations of its people and the relevant United Nations resolutions.

On Afghanistan, the president said that Pakistan had always respected and supported the national sovereignty of our neighbour Afghanistan and expected the same reciprocity.

“It is sad that the current interim regime of Afghanistan is allowing and supporting a cocktail of terror groups to use their soil for launching attacks against neighbouring countries including Pakistan. It is sad the Taliban regime of Afghanistan is collaborating with India in launching terror attacks against Pakistani civilians and security personnel. They are doing this to distract us from the peace building efforts of Pakistan, recognised by the entire world,” he said.

“I warn them to stop these evil actions against the people of Pakistan and assure all and sundry that the armed forces of Pakistan are capable of defeating these evil designs,” he said.

He ended his message by calling on the nation to contribute to the country’s progress in whatever field they serve.

‘Pakistan committed to defending its national interests’

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also began his message by paying tribute to the founding leaders of Pakistan, saying the nation owed the fulfilment of its dream of an independent homeland to their vision, statesmanship and sacrifices.

Highlighting the government’s economic achievements over the past two-and-a-half years, PM Shehbaz said the country had successfully navigated challenging circumstances to achieve economic stability and was now moving towards becoming a developed economy.

He noted that remittances from overseas Pakistanis had increased by $11.3 billion over the past two years, which he termed a reflection of their confidence in government policies.

The prime minister said harnessing modern information technology, promoting innovation-driven industrial and agricultural development, creating employment opportunities and establishing a world-class education and skills system remained among the government’s top priorities.

Paying tribute to the armed forces, the prime minister said the military, under the leadership of Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, had demonstrated exemplary unity and courage during Marka-i-Haq, adding another chapter to the country’s history of defence.

He said Pakistan remained committed to defending its national interests, including its right to water resources, and reiterated that the country would continue to play its role as a responsible nation and a stabilising force for regional and global peace.

He cited the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye as testimony to the country’s growing strategic role in the region.

The prime minister also expressed solidarity with the people of occupied Kashmir and the Palestinian people. He said lasting peace in South Asia was contingent upon a diplomatic resolution of the Kashmir dispute in line with United Nations resolutions, international law and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people.

The prime minister also paid tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces and law enforcement agencies who sacrificed their lives for the country, and called upon all segments of society, particularly political parties, to work together for national unity, integrity and the advancement of national interests.

He concluded his message by praying for Pakistan’s continued progress and dignity in the comity of nations.

‘Pakistan’s strength lies in the unity of its people’

CDF Munir, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf and Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu also issued a message to mark Independence Day.

According to Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the armed forces paid tribute to the Quaid and those whose sacrifices resulted in a sovereign Pakistan.

“Their vision, courage and resolve remain a guiding force for the nation and continue to inspire us to uphold the principles and ideals of Pakistan,” the statement said.

“The armed forces of Pakistan respectfully acknowledge the supreme sacrifices of our martyrs, the services of our veterans, the dedication of law enforcement personnel and the contributions of every Pakistani who has served the nation. Their courage and selfless service have bolstered Pakistan’s resilience and safeguarded its independence, security and national interests,” it added.

“As guardians of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, the armed forces reaffirm their unwavering resolve to defend the motherland against all threats, uphold the Constitution and discharge the sacred trust reposed in them by the people of Pakistan. United with the nation, the armed forces will remain steadfast in preserving peace and stability while creating an environment conducive to national progress and prosperity,” the statement said.

“Pakistan’s strength lies in the unity and collective resolve of its people. On this Independence Day, let us renew our commitment to the enduring principles of faith, unity and discipline, strengthen national cohesion, promote tolerance and work together towards a secure, stable and prosperous Pakistan,” it concluded.

Dar reaffirms determination to safeguard country’s sovereignty

In his message on the occasion, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar recalled Marka-i-Haq and reaffirmed Pakistan’s determination to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

“We commemorated the first anniversary of Marka-i-Haq, recalling Pakistan’s resolute and successful response to Indian aggression in 2025,” he said in a televised address to the nation.

“The occasion reaffirmed our determination to safeguard Pakistan’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity while remaining firmly committed to international law, responsible state craft and the pursuit of regional peace.”

At the outset of his address, the deputy PM extended greetings to Pakistanis and expatriates on the Independence Day, saying we commemorate the day “to pay tribute to Quaid-i-Azam whose visionary leadership, unwavering resolve and steadfast commitment transformed the aspirations for a separate homeland into reality”.

He also paid honour to the leaders and workers of the Pakistan movement whose “courage, dedication and countless sacrifices laid the foundations of our independent state”.

Dar said that since independence, the country had made “remarkable strides across diverse fields guided by the enduring principles of unity, faith and discipline”.

“Today we are a resilient nation of more than 250 million people bound together by our shared history, collective heritage and common aspirations,” he added.

He also noted that the country’s achievements in education, science and technology, economic development, sports, culture and other fields “reflect the talent, determination and immense potential of our people”.

The deputy PM also mentioned Pakistan’s “strengthened” position on the international stage over the past eight decades.

“Our expanding diplomatic engagement, growing economic connectivity and partnerships, and deepening defence and security cooperation reflect Pakistan’s confidence and its commitment to contributing to a peaceful, stable and prosperous region and world.”

He also mentioned the defence accord signed by Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia last week, saying the “historic agreement reflects our shared resolve to deepen strategic cooperation, strengthen collective security and address evolving regional and international peace and security challenges”.

He also paid special tribute to armed forces, police and paramilitary forces of the country, saying their “courage, professionalism and unwavering commitment remain a bulwark of our national security”.

Dar noted the country always “stood for peace, dialogue, cooperation and mutual respect among nations”.

He referred to last year’s conflict with India and said the events “underscored the urgent need of peaceful resolution of longstanding disputes, particularly the Jammu and Kashmir dispute which remains a source of instability in our region”.

“Pakistan will continue to extend its principles, moral, political and diplomatic support to the Kashmiri people in their just struggle for the realisation of their right to self-determination in accordance with the relevant UNSC resolutions,” he added.

On the occasion, he urged people to “draw renewed inspirations from the ideals and vision that led to the creation of Pakistan”.

“Let us reaffirm our collective resolve to strengthen our institutions, uphold our national unity, harness the potential of our people and build a stronger more prosperous and peaceful Pakistan for generations to come,” he concluded.

Kashmir stands ‘shoulder to shoulder’ with Pakistan: AJK president

Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) President Chaudhry Latif Akbar, addressing a flag-hoisting ceremony in Muzafarabad, expressed gratitude to Pakistan for standing by the Kashmiri people and advocating their cause at international forums, as well as repeatedly calling for implementation of the relevant United Nations resolutions.

He highlighted the “centuries-old” bonds between Kashmir and Pakistan, saying the relationship was rooted in shared history, culture, religion, traditions and aspirations and had found political expression in the Kashmiri leadership’s July 19, 1947, resolution seeking accession of the princely state to Pakistan.

“Pakistan has also stood with the people of Kashmir through difficult periods and fought wars in defence of its position on the Kashmir dispute,” he said, adding that Kashmiris would never forget Pakistan’s steadfast support.

Akbar reiterated that the people of AJK stood “shoulder to shoulder” with the people of Pakistan and said their destinies were intertwined.

Additional input from Tariq Naqash

World.title: Balochistan home minister unhurt as convoy comes under attack in Mastung
World.content:
QUETTA: Six people, including three police personnel, were injured in an armed attack on the convoy of Balochistan Home Minister Mir Ziaullah Langove in Mastung on Friday.

A senior police official told Dawn that the home minister remained unhurt in the attack, which occurred as his convoy reached the Khad Kocha area of Mastung. He said that Langove was on his way to Quetta from Kalat.

The official added that six people sustained bullet injuries in the attack, three of whom were police personnel.

Nawab Raisani Memorial Hospital’s Dr Sana also confirmed to Dawn that six injured had been brought to the hospital and two of them were in serious condition. She said two of the others were referred to Quetta.

Security forces have cordoned off the area and launched a search operation.

Langove, who is from the Balochistan Awami Party, was sworn in as provincial home minister in March.

Langove had also served as the provincial home minister previously, but his appointment was declared null and void after he was de-notified on August 21, 2024.

World.title: Afghan soil being used against Pakistan, Naqvi tells Norway FM as two discuss counterterrorism cooperation
World.content:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Friday met with Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide, where the two sides discussed counterterrorism cooperation, particularly the use of Afghan soil in terror attacks against Pakistan.

Eide arrived in Pakistan a day earlier on a two-day visit — the first by a Norwegian foreign minister in a decade.

According to a handout issued by the interior ministry, the two leaders discussed strengthening bilateral relations and the regional situation. Naqvi and Eide also agreed to improve cooperation in counterterrorism, prevention of illegal immigration, police training, and mutual legal assistance.

The two sides held discussions on the situation in neighbouring Afghanistan and the activities of proscribed organisations operating from the neighbouring country.

During the meeting, Eide lauded Pakistan’s “constructive and active” role in the US-Iran war. The two sides also discussed measures taken against illegal immigration to Europe from Pakistan.

“Pakistan’s effective measures have led to a 47 per cent reduction in illegal immigration to Europe,” the statement quoted Naqvi as saying, adding that “a zero-tolerance policy has been adopted against illegal immigration”.

He said that Pakistan’s measures against illegal immigration were also appreciated by the European Union.

“Promoting legal immigration is very important for effectively curbing illegal immigration,” he said.

According to the statement, Naqvi told Eide that “Afghan soil is continuously being used for terrorism in Pakistan” and that Pakistan stood “as a wall” between the world and terrorist elements.

“Everyone must work together for the complete eradication of terrorism.” Naqvi was quoted as saying. He also told Eide that his visit would be an “important milestone” in strengthening bilateral relations between Norway and Pakistan.

In the meeting, Eide appreciated the “active role” of the Pakistani diaspora in Norway and their contributions in sectors ranging from politics to health.

Minister of State Talal Chaudhry and other senior officials were present at the meeting as well, the statement added.

On Thursday, Eide held a series of engagements with top civilian and military leadership, where the two sides discussed expanding cooperation in trade, investment, technology, climate resilience, maritime affairs, skilled labour and security, while also exchanging views on regional developments.

World.title: 2 dead, 94 injured in celebratory aerial firing incidents in Karachi on Independence Day eve
World.content:
KARACHI: At least two people were killed and 94 others injured in celebratory firing incidents in Karachi on the eve of Pakistan’s Independence Day, officials said on Friday.

Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed said 17 people were brought to Civil Hospital, 24 were brought to Abbasi Shaheed Hospital and 53 were brought to Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre.

She added that one male from PIB Colony and an infant died in aerial firing incidents. The doctor said another woman was also brought to the hospital with a gunshot wound, who later died. However, police said that the incident was caused due to the accidental firing of a gun.

Earlier Edhi said that 86 people had been injured in aerial firing incidents, including 10 women, 17 children and 59 men. Firing incidents were reported in Lyari, Saddar, Korangi, Malir, Azizabad, North Nazimabad, Nazimabad, Gulbahar, Gulshan-i-Iqbal, Orangi Town, Jamshed Quarters and Defence, it said.

Meanwhile, police in Karachi’s East district launched a crackdown against aerial firing on Independence Day and took 10 suspects into custody from various areas.

In a statement, police said weapons used for aerial firing were also recovered from the arrested suspects. The arrests were made within the jurisdictions of Gulshan-i-Iqbal, Sharea Faisal, Sachal, Gulistan-i-Johar and Site Super Highway police stations, police said.

According to police in Karachi’s West district, three suspects had been arrested for aerial firing on Independence Day.

Incidents of aerial firing are a routine occurrence on occasions such as Independence Day and New Year’s Eve despite bans imposed in the past, often leaving dozens injured .

Last year, three people, including a minor girl, were killed and over 100 others wounded in celebratory gunfire across the metropolis at midnight on Independence Day.

World.title: Cop martyred, another injured in terrorist attack on police post in Bajaur
World.content:
BAJAUR: One cop was martyred while another was wounded after terrorists attacked a police post in Bajaur district’s Barang tehsil in the early hours of Friday.

Mansoor Khan, the district police spokesperson, told Dawn that a group of terrorists targeted the police post in Kohi Sar area with rocket launchers and small weapons.

He said that police personnel at the post immediately responded and retaliated. The official said two police personnel were wounded in the exchange of fire, which continued for several hours.

One of the wounded policemen, identified as Constable Zahir Shah, succumbed to his injuries while being transported to a local hospital for treatment, he said.

The other officer, Head Constable Amir Zada, was reported to be out of danger, he added.

“The police personnel at the post bravely retaliated and successfully foiled the terrorists’ nefarious design,” the spokesperson added.

The funeral prayers of the martyred police official were held at Police Lines in Khar, which was attended by Deputy Commissioner Adnan Farid, District Police Officer (DPO) Khan Zeb Momand and other officials.

Earlier this month, at least 14 people, including police officials, were martyred and at least 18 others injured in a suicide attack on Swat’s Kabal police station.

On July 30, a terrorist attack on a police checkpost in Hangu martyred nine policemen.

KP has seen an uptick in terrorist activity. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies’s monthly security assessment, KP, excluding the merged districts, recorded 154 terrorism related deaths in July, compared with 75 in June, representing an increase of 105 per cent.

World.title: Ex-Sindh minister seeks FIR against ex-wife over AI-edited pictures
World.content:
KARACHI: Former Sindh minister Ghulam Rasool Unnar has allegedly fallen victim to artificial intelligence (AI) technology, claiming that he discovered after his marriage that pictures of his ex-wife that she had shared with him had been edited and altered using AI.

Unnar approa­ched a sessions court seeking registration of an FIR against his ex-wife, Razia Arbab, under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA)

He informed the court that he had come into contact with Ms Arbab through social media platforms. He said that while they were communicating, she proposed marriage to him.

According to the applicant, they later got married through a video call in the presence of witnesses, against a dower of Rs100,000, which had already been paid to her.

The former minister alleged that during the ceremony, his ex-wife did not reveal her face and kept it covered with a niqab. However, after the marriage, when Mr Unnar met her in person, he “got shocked and surprised” to discover that she had allegedly “cheated and deceived” him by “concealing her real face” and sending filtered and AI-edited pictures before the marriage.

He submitted that he subsequently separated from his wife and later divorced her, but she continued posting “fake news” about his death and fabricated images on social media.

He further alleged that she was demanding money from him and sending abusive and threatening messages on WhatsApp, warning him that she would share his personal videos or kill him if he did not pay her.

Asking the court to order registration of an FIR against her, he stated that by posting fake news and spreading false information, levelling false, shameful and baseless allegations on social media, his ex-wife has committed offences under Peca.

He requested the court to direct the concerned SHO to record his statement and register an FIR against his ex-wife. After hearing his submissions, Additional District and Sessions Judge (South) Muhammad Aslam Sheikh issued notices to the SSP Complaint Cell, the SHO of the Defence police station and the proposed accused, directing them to submit their responses before the court on Aug 17.

Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

World.title: Nigel Farage regains UK parliamentary seat, fights off Count Binface challenge
World.content:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage regained his parliamentary seat on Friday in an election he triggered to bolster his position against allegations of financial impropriety, a strategy that was undermined when his main challenger, a comedian dressed as a trash can, won more than a quarter of the vote.

Farage, one of Britain’s leading Brexit campaigners, in a highly unusual move did not turn up at the count in the southern English seaside resort of Clacton because he said the police had advised him that there was a campaign to disrupt the result.

“I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory … and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies,” Farage told supporters at a party before the result was announced.

The election was triggered after Farage resigned from parliament last month to seek a fresh mandate from voters in what he described as a war against an establishment bent on discrediting him over taking undeclared gifts from donors.

After Britain’s main parties pulled out of the race, calling it a self-serving stunt, Farage’s main challenger ended up being Count Binface, a figure created by comedian Jonathan Harvey, who has become a fixture of fun at British elections.

While Farage took 62.8 per cent of the vote, Count Binface, whose policies included capping the price of ice cream cones and conscripting anyone using a speakerphone on public transport, secured 26.7pc.

Reform’s momentum shows signs of slowing

After enjoying a lengthy lead in the opinion polls, Reform has seen its popularity wane, driven partly by the funding accusations made against Farage, who is under investigation in parliament over whether he should have declared a 5 million ($6.75m) gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire investor.

After declaring his decision to trigger the election in Clacton little more than a ploy to distract from those allegations, other British parties pulled out of the race, leaving even some of Farage’s strongest supporters questioning whether the veteran politician had been wrong-footed.

Laura Richards-Gray, a politics lecturer at Birkbeck University in London, said the absence of major-party opponents undermined his attempt to turn it into what he called a “people versus the establishment” contest.

“This has backfired, particularly nationally, as Farage lost control of the narrative,” she said, adding some voters saw the election as “a waste of time and money”.

Farage’s position has not been helped by a rise in support for the governing Labour Party. Since Andy Burnham became prime minister last month, Labour has been enjoying a bounce in ratings, with the party leading Reform 28pc to 25pc.
